2026-10-04

Where a checker trial's time goes

Most of a checker trial's wall time was spent waiting for a newly created worker thread to run for the first time, not in the trial itself or in the driver. Reusing one worker thread across trials roughly doubled checker throughput with identical verdicts.

What was asked

Make checker runs faster without changing any verdict. Checker time was about half of a small-function lane's waiting time, so any saving applies to every lane at once.

What was found

Verified A profile of three contracts of different shapes (one tiny, one with large heap inputs, one with scripted callees and full-data comparison) showed every driver-side stage together costing under half a millisecond per trial: input generation, request encoding, pipe write, response decoding and bookkeeping. A bare pipe round trip measures three hundredths of a millisecond.

Verified The same profile showed the worker's round trip taking about fifty milliseconds per trial for the tiny contract while the worker's own account of the trial work was about twelve. Bracketing inside a scratch copy of the worker split the gap: parsing and preparing a trial take tens of microseconds, creating the per-trial thread takes about sixty microseconds, and then roughly forty-seven milliseconds pass before the new thread's first instruction runs. That lag is constant across contracts while the trial body varies from eighteen to over three hundred milliseconds.

Verified Replacing the per-trial thread with one persistent thread per worker process removed the lag. The full tracked suite runs in about eight hundred seconds instead of about seventeen hundred (about twenty-four trials per second instead of about eleven). All thirty-eight tracked verdicts and all thirty-four mutant verdicts reproduce field for field except timings; one run's retry record differed by a single load-caused entry and a rerun matched fully. Thirty-four lane contracts of varied shapes with their rewrites were compared the same way with the same outcome.

Verified What limits trials now is the trial work itself (both sides executed plus the worker's comparison loops) and scheduler wake latency for the worker thread on a saturated machine, measured at up to about twelve milliseconds per trial. The driver, encoding and pipe remain noise.

Stage of one tiny-function trialMedian cost beforeMedian cost after
Driver: inputs, encoding, pipe, decodingunder half a millisecondunchanged
New thread's first schedulingabout forty-seven millisecondspaid once per worker, hidden in setup
Trial work, both sides plus comparisonabout twelve millisecondsunchanged
Waking the reused threadnot presentzero to twelve milliseconds, load-driven

What was decided or recommended

  • Integrate the persistent trial thread: it is worker-internal, changes no protocol bytes, and keeps the hang behaviour (a timed-out trial still abandons the thread and the worker still exits for a fresh one).
  • Do not pursue batched requests, slimmer responses, or reworked encoding for speed: the stages they would improve sum to under half a millisecond.
  • Running one contract's trials across several workers in parallel is sound in principle (trials are seeded and independent, and results merge deterministically), but it needs a check that every worker mapped memory identically, and it only helps while processors are free. The machine already runs about twenty workers at full load, so pair it with a global worker cap. Not built.

How to reproduce it

Build the worker from the scratch copy in the lane folder, run the tracked suite twice with the stock driver (once per worker binary), and compare the two output folders field by field with the lane's comparison script, ignoring only the two timing fields. Then run the lane's contract runner over its selected contract list, which exercises both workers itself, and compare again. Exact commands are in the lane's change notes.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The starting assumption pointed at the driver and the pipe; the first profile disproved it within minutes. Absolute times swing severalfold with machine load, so only back-to-back pairs are quoted. A first attempt at scanning every lane contract file ran too long and was replaced by checking the cheap filter (a rewrite binary on disk) before parsing. Rebuilding the worker twice into one folder once failed with an access error while no process held the file, so the scratch binary was built under a distinct name.

2026-10-04

Leaderboard team boards named, and a missing id method

All 150 functions in this batch were per-board leaderboard methods for seventeen team and cooperative multiplayer boards, and every one is now named with the same nine-method vocabulary an earlier lane established for the race boards.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and grading each name high, medium or low confidence.

What was found

Verified The batch holds seventeen instantiations of one leaderboard info template, one per team or cooperative board, each with the same nine virtual methods in the same order: a board-name stub, a board-id stub, five column lookup methods, and two schema-mapping methods plus a row builder. Every unnamed entry was attributed to its board by reading that board's virtual table, and all thirty-one attributions matched.

Verified Each board carries a small numeric id used consistently by all of its methods; the seventeen ids were recorded and all siblings agreed, so there were no mismatches of the kind found in the race boards.

Verified One board has no board-id method: its table slot points at a shared encrypted stub, so its id is known only from its seven sibling methods. The batch also ends mid-board, leaving that last board's final two column methods for the next batch.

What was decided or recommended

The earlier lane's method names were reused unchanged, since the code skeletons are identical in shape. The next leaderboard batch should reuse the same table-check procedure: locate each board's table through its first mapping method, confirm the neighbouring slots, then read the two unnamed slots directly. The last board's two remaining column methods should be named with board id noted in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the executable's memory-mapped image, collect the small board-id constant each method passes to the shared schema helper, and scan the read-only data section for the one virtual table holding each board's mapping methods to confirm the unnamed slots. The lane's scratch folder keeps the gathering, analysis and naming scripts plus the full per-function evidence table.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The inventory's subsystem labels for this range are incorrect (they point at unrelated game systems), and one table slot is mislabelled as another class's method, but the virtual tables themselves resolved both cases without ambiguity.

2026-10-04

Naming a run of leaderboard schema accessors

All 150 functions in this batch turned out to be per-board leaderboard schema accessors in a single template family, and all 150 are now named, so the batch is done with nothing left unnamed.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function, with a confidence of high, medium or low.

What was found

Verified The batch holds 18 leaderboard boards, each contributing the same set of small virtual methods: a name getter, a board id getter, column lookup helpers, column size and kind mappers, two cross-list mappers, and one larger row builder.

Verified Thirty-two entries the inventory left unnamed are ordinary members of the same family, not vtables or data: the tiny ones each return their board's leaderboard name string, and the larger ones share the exact shape of the column kind mapper, with board id constants matching their sibling methods.

Verified Every multi-instruction method starts by calling one shared schema helper with its board's small integer id, which makes the board id a reliable cross-check for assigning an unnamed function to its class.

Verified The switch jump tables for the size and kind mappers sit in the padding bytes between functions, each starting exactly where its function ends.

MethodNamedConfidence
name getter17high
board id getter12high
column and row helpers121medium

What was decided or recommended

Method names reuse the convention earlier naming lanes established for this template family, so names stay comparable across boards. The next naming lane covering nearby boards should distrust the vtable boundary label on tiny and mid-size entries there and classify them by code shape first. The shared schema helpers these methods call are still unnamed and would be a useful follow-up.

How to reproduce it

Map the executable in memory, disassemble one board's methods from entry to return, and confirm each calls the shared helper with the same board id constant the id getter returns. Then check every other entry for the same shapes and constants before naming it.

What was confusing or went wrong

One column size method is two bytes longer than its seventeen twins because it computes the switch index with a different but equivalent instruction; it disassembles to the same behaviour and kept the same name. A first version of the naming script failed to match any board ids because it compared the full instruction text against the operand text; fixing the comparison resolved all 32 unnamed entries with no conflicts.

2026-10-04

One ledger for 37,000 functions

Every progress number, queue batch, name and proof record now comes from a single SQLite database that reproduces the current scripts exactly and names fifteen places where they disagreed with each other.

What was asked

Build the project's function ledger: one database with one row per function, an importer that ingests today's scattered sources, proof that it reproduces the current counts and queue, the queries the coordinator needs, and a migration plan that keeps the five-minute loop working throughout.

What was found

Verified The ledger reproduces the scripts exactly: all six headline counts with identical function sets, all 480 code-map slices, and all three queue pools with identical membership.

One batch, two stack surprises: a shared argument slot and reads from unwritten stack

Verifying twenty small task-system functions turned up two stack behaviors worth knowing: one function passes a single pushed word to two calls in a row, and another reads its interpolation factor and one output word from stack slots it never wrote. What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, one function at a time, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the contract can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified A record-kind check function pushes one word, makes an indirect call through an object table, then makes a direct call documented to pop one word. Stack-balance analysis plus the checker's fault report show the indirect callee pops nothing: both calls share the one pushed slot, and the direct callee consumes it. Declaring the indirect callee as taking register and stack arguments without popping (the checker's no-cleanup option) passes one thousand trials with full argument comparison.

Verified Two sibling index state machines return a constant that looks like dead initialization on two of their exit paths. The constant is set once at entry and two paths reach the shared epilogue without overwriting it. Wrong versions returning the plausible constants fail, confirming the behavior and the coverage.

Inferred A route-point interpolation function stores its call result four bytes below where it reloads the factor it multiplies with, and reads one output word sixteen bytes past the value it resembles. Both reads land on uninitialized frame space and caller stack, so the outputs depend on stack garbage and entry alignment rather than on the inputs. This was read from the disassembly three times, including the raw store and reload offsets, but not confirmed by running.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verifying nineteen of twenty, deferring the interpolation function with reason other and the analysis above, rather than shipping a rewrite fitted to the harness fills.
  • When a push sits before an indirect call with no stack cleanup after it, prove which call consumes the slot before declaring conventions; the no-cleanup stub option works for table-planted calls too.
  • Simulate pin and script periods as trial-index arithmetic in the contract generator and assert every path is hit; this caught four silent coverage locks before any trials ran.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch's functions from the executable with capstone through the mapped image, check each call site's pushes against the callee's stack cleanup, and compare the store and reload offsets of every spilled float. The coverage models live in the lane's contract generator scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

The shared-slot function first presented as a checker defect: the original faulted at the pushed heap address on every trial while the rewrite passed. Tracing the stack word by word showed the contract was wrong, not the worker: my declaration made the stub pop a word the real callee leaves. A second function failed on eight trials with the original returning a heap address where zero was expected; the early exit clears the low byte of an address register that still holds the probe pointer, not the flag word that was only compared. Both fixes were one line each.

What was asked

Why experiment lanes had no log files half an hour after their launch was announced, and why nine lanes showed an error exit in the hourly review.

What was found

How the launcher endedWhat happened to its lanesHow it is known
Stopped by handKilled with it. Eight lanes died in the same second.Their logs all end at the moment the supervisor was stopped to change a setting.
Stopped by the two-hour limit on background tasksKilled with it. The assembly lane lost two hours of work; several lanes started by slots went the same way earlier and had been counted only as "not running".The lane's log ends within the minute of the limit; no agent process remained.
Ended normallyThey keep running.A test launcher started a child, exited after eight seconds, and the child kept writing for as long as it was watched.
A short foreground command that starts detached processes and returnsNothing started at all: no log line, no output, no process.Twelve lanes prepared this way had no log file thirty minutes later.

Verified Each row was observed today. The earlier note in this log's operating entry, that a lane outlives its launcher when the launcher is stopped, was wrong; it holds only when the launcher ends normally.

Unknown Why detached processes started from a foreground command did not run. It was not investigated further once a working method existed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Lanes are started only from a long-lived background launcher, which ends by itself before the two-hour limit and is never stopped by hand. Its settings are changed through a file it reads on every pass.
  • A launch is not reported until the lane's log file exists.
  • A lane started directly as its own background task is told to write its results file in the first minutes and keep it current, and to finish well inside two hours. The assembly lane was restarted with that instruction and an 80-minute budget.
  • A lane that dies without results gives its batch back to the queue on the next tick, but never within fifteen minutes of its launch.

How to reproduce it

Start a launcher that starts a child writing a heartbeat line every five seconds. End the launcher three ways (let it finish, stop it, let it hit the time limit) and watch whether the heartbeat continues.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coordinator announced the experiment lanes from the launch script's own output, which printed the lane names it had prepared. Printing a name is not evidence that a process is running. The half hour was lost because the check that would have shown it, whether each lane had a log file, was run only when results were expected.

Black box does not pin down float multiply order

Verified Wrapping one operand of a float multiply in a compiler black box does not stop the compiler backend from swapping the operands, so a rewrite can still pick the wrong NaN payload. Selecting NaN operands explicitly in plain code fixes it reliably.

What was asked

One function in this production batch multiplies two single-precision values and returns the product through the floating point register. One trial in a thousand failed with only NaN sign and payload bits differing, which points at swapped multiply operands: with two different NaNs, the hardware keeps the destination operand's NaN, so operand order is observable.

What was found

Verified The project guidance for this case is to write the operations in the original order and keep the compiler from commuting them with a black box on one operand. That changed nothing: the same seeded trial failed with bit-identical wrong output before and after.

Verified Disassembling the freshly built rewrite showed why. Both multiplies in the function had been emitted with the operands exchanged relative to the source: the value written first in the source ended up as the source operand instead of the destination. The black box only constrains an earlier compiler stage; the later backend pass that assigns the destination register commutes freely either way.

Verified Replaying that trial's inputs by hand confirmed the mechanism exactly: the original returns the destination NaN and the swapped rewrite returns the source NaN. After replacing each multiply and add with an explicit selection (destination NaN wins, else source NaN, else the plain operation, all in ordinary code with no assembly), the same seeded trial passes along with the other 999.

What was decided or recommended

Rewrites in this lane select NaN operands explicitly wherever both inputs of a multiply or add can be NaN. Subtract, divide, compare and negate cannot be commuted and stay plain. Any lane relying on a black box for operand order should re-check: a passing verdict whose trials never combined two different NaNs proves nothing about order, and the build can differ from the source silently.

How to reproduce it

Take a function whose result is a multiply of two f32 values that can both be NaN with different payloads. Write the multiply in the original order with one operand through a black box, build the rewrite, and disassemble the built export: the emitted multiply may list the operands exchanged. Then run a trial with two different NaN inputs and compare the result bits against the original.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first diagnosis looked like an ordinary operand-order slip in the rewrite, and the prescribed one-line fix compiled cleanly, so the identical second failure was genuinely surprising. What unblocked it was stopping trusting the source text and reading the built machine code instead. A second, smaller trap in the same lane: two scratch memory segments overlapped by eight bytes, so random words silently overwrote a pinned value and every trial faulted; the driver does not check for overlap.

The optimizer can silently change NaN results

A rewrite that matched the original on 1099 of 1100 trials failed the last one only because the compiler had packed three independent float computations into vector instructions, swapping the operands of one addition. Where no NaN is involved the swap is harmless, which is why it passed 1099 times. The fix is to fence each computation so the optimizer keeps it scalar and in order.

What was asked

Rewrite two input-handling functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, calls and faults bit for bit.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified, 1100 of 1100 trials each. The larger one transforms eight corners of a box and accumulates a bounding box, with heavy single-precision arithmetic and min/max merging that must match bit for bit, including NaN payloads.

Verified The single failure was a NaN payload mismatch: the original propagated an input NaN unchanged while the rewrite produced a canonical NaN. Disassembling the rewrite showed packed vector arithmetic where scalar operations were written. Restoring scalar order with optimization barriers fixed it, confirmed by checking the generated code contains no packed arithmetic.

Verified A separate coverage trap: when every contract input cycled with period two, all main-path trials took the same combination of branches, hiding the multi-call paths entirely. Mixing period-three and period-two cycles exposed them, and the newly covered paths immediately caught a real mistake in the rewrite.

What was decided or recommended

Float rewrites whose results must match bit for bit should fence independent rows or stages against vectorization and have their generated code checked for packed arithmetic, not just their source reviewed. Contracts should mix input cycle lengths and their branch-shape counts should be read, not just the pass or fail.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's checker contracts for the batch: the verdict files record 1100 passing trials each with full branch coverage. Reverting the barriers reproduces the single-trial NaN mismatch.

What was confusing or went wrong

The NaN failure was confusing at first because the source code had the operations in exactly the right order; the reordering happened invisibly at compile time. An earlier scare about empty disassembly turned out to be simple arithmetic: a size computed as a negative number, which the parsing library answers with empty bytes instead of an error.

The rest split into 183 fragments of other functions, 138 data entries such as jump tables and padding, and 80 that stay unsure. Both naming lanes that had reported doubtful entries were vindicated, one of them only after a second, pattern-specific analysis proved the general method blind in its region.

What was asked

Give a verdict on every game-code inventory entry whose repair class is weaker than fully confirmed: real function, fragment of another function, data, unreadable, or unsure. Calibrate the method against two thousand fully confirmed entries and every verified entry in the weaker classes, which must all come out as functions. Judge two naming lanes' claims of bogus entries independently, entry by entry. Scan the code the inventory does not cover for missing functions.

What was found

Verified The weaker classes are overwhelmingly real: all of the thunk and Ghidra-only classes came out as functions, and the size-corrected and weakly confirmed classes are nearly all functions too. Only the gapfill-invented enclosing starts are mostly bad, at about three quarters fragments or data.

Verified The first naming lane was right on all 33 of its claimed bogus entries: none is a routine start. Twenty-five start in the middle of a machine instruction and eight are aligned interior points of neighbouring factory routines. None appears in the pointer table that references every genuine routine in its region, while all 117 genuine ones do.

Verified The second naming lane was right on all 9 of its claimed data entries, and partly right about missing functions: one claimed function is genuinely missing, swallowed by an oversized neighbouring range, and a set of plausible stub series was found where it predicted lookups. Three of its claimed missing functions turned out to be correctly attributed bodies of jump relays, and one was already in the inventory.

Verified Calibration passed at 2,050 out of 2,052. The two mismatches are genuine exception-handling funclets sitting in the fully confirmed class, the same family an earlier lane had found elsewhere. No verified rewrite sits on a bad entry. Four bad entries reached production batches and about ninety reached naming batches.

Verified The uncovered-code scan lists about seventeen hundred code runs, of which 129 plausibly start functions, holding an estimated 383 nested functions once series of tiny stubs are counted individually. The factory region additionally hides about two hundred true routine starts that the inventory lacks, shadowed by the oversized ranges of the bogus entries.

What was decided or recommended

  • Remove or annotate the 321 fragment and data entries, starting with the few already handed to production and naming lanes.
  • Repair the factory region as one edit: drop the 33 bogus entries and add the missing true starts, instead of only removing.
  • Add the plausible missing runs and the confirmed shadowed function to the inventory.
  • Keep the remaining weaker-class entries in the work queue; the calibration supports them.
  • Re-run the verdict script once the encrypted part of the code is readable; the unsure entries and the funclets hiding in the confirmed class should resolve then.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's verdict script over the repaired inventory with the section-based address mapping, then the tiling analysis for the factory region, then the missing-code scan with jump-table-aware judging. The mapping was proved on three verified functions first, and the call-target count reproduces the published cross-check number exactly. All verdicts, reasons, and the missing-run list are stored as data files with the lane's outputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first version of the method judged the first naming lane wrong on all 33 entries, because the factory region has no analysis coverage and the fallback checks accept any clean-looking decode. A backward test that counted decoding from the entry itself as confirmation made it worse. Only the tiling analysis, which decodes forward from true routine starts and watches the claimed entries fall inside, settled it. The lesson is that empty coverage needs pattern-specific tests, and that a method must be doubted as readily as a lane.

Verified The missing scan first reported over five hundred plausible runs, most of them jump tables that looked targeted because a relocation entry holding a table's own address was mistaken for a function pointer. Skipping table prefixes before judging fixed it. A mid-instruction decode often re-synchronises into plausible code within a few instructions, so a clean decode alone never confirms an entry.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring functions of the input and interface subsystem (between 612 and 1,443 bytes each) in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves like the original, using the stock checker worker only. At least 1,000 trials per function.

What was found

Verified The four functions belong to one module that uploads effect constants: one initialises two record tables and a block of settings, two build constant vectors from a selected record, and one submits a textured rectangle through the getters of two objects. Three were checked with 1,200 of 1,200 trials, the call logs compared word by word, and 14 of 14 hand-made wrong versions (mutants) were caught.

Verified The initialiser stores two floating point values into every record of the first table that it never sets itself. They are leftover stack contents. With a defined zero fill of the stack the rewrite (which writes zero) matches; with a patterned fill every trial fails on the written globals, which confirms that the original reads uninitialised memory. The same is true of one unused word per matrix row in a fourth function. In the shipped game these values depend on whatever the stack held.

Verified The checker can see only the first 8 words behind a pointer argument that points into the function's own frame. The deferred function builds a 16-word matrix in its frame and hands its address to a callee, so only the first two rows are compared. Wrong versions that change the first rows fail (193 of 300 trials); wrong versions that change the third row or the translation row, which holds the most involved arithmetic, pass all 300 trials. A passing contract there is not evidence about those words.

Inferred The deferred function should be finished by lifting the snapshot limit in the stock worker (more than 8 words, or a word offset from the pointer), not by a private worker. The stage-1 rewrite and contract are kept so the next lane only adds the missing snapshots. Until then no result for a function that passes frame buffers of more than 8 words to a callee should be counted as complete unless a mutant in the later words has been shown to fail.

Inferred Contracts for float code should use inputs in a range where small terms survive rounding. A first contract with wide random integers caught one wrong version in only 2 of 300 trials, because a half-texel offset vanishes next to a quotient in the millions; with moderate pixel values the same wrong version fails 221 of 300.

How to reproduce it

  1. Write the rewrites against the checker runtime and build them into the lane's own build folder.
  2. Describe each callee in the contract: calls through an object's table are answered by planted stubs, pointers into the function's own frame are skipped and replaced by a snapshot of the words behind them.
  3. Run the contract on the stock worker; then run hand-made wrong versions against the same contract and check that each fails, including versions that change the words you believe are compared.
  4. Repeat the initialiser's contract once with the patterned stack fill to see the uninitialised reads.

First pilot of the 64-bit lift: what it costs and what gets in the way

Thirty-seven rewritten game functions now exist as ordinary portable Rust with no raw addresses and no unsafe code, and all thirty-seven still behave exactly like the verified 32-bit versions they came from. What was asked

Take one closed cluster of thirty to fifty verified functions and turn them into normal Rust that could compile for a 64-bit target: no raw addresses, no numbered callee slots, no dependence on pointer width. Prove each lift against its 32-bit form without the game, measure minutes per function, and say what would get in the way at scale.

What was found

Verified The chosen cluster is thirty-seven container primitives in three families: intrusive chain operations, indexed slot records, and fixed-stride pool allocators, plus a value-list search and a one-shot table initialiser. Links became indices into explicit arenas, callee slots became callback parameters, globals became struct fields, and vtable stamps became an element-type tag. The whole lift is safe Rust.

Verified Proof runs on both targets: forty differential tests compare returns, full state, and callback call logs between the 32-bit forms and the lifts over thousands of generated inputs on the 32-bit target, and fourteen property tests run the lifted crate on the 64-bit host. All pass. The differential tests caught two of the three authoring mistakes made during the pilot.

Verified One function reads a status byte in a way that also leaks part of a 32-bit address into its result. That part has no meaning on 64-bit, so the lift returns just the byte; the test checks the byte on both sides and pins the quirk's shape on the 32-bit side. Four more functions crash on inputs the original never validates; the lifts panic loudly there instead of crashing or silently guessing.

Verified Cost: about five minutes per plain function and about eleven per function with callbacks, after one-time tooling. Roughly half of the proving work is boilerplate a script could generate from the existing check contracts.

What was decided or recommended

  • Lift leaves first grouped by data structure, then callback-bearing functions, then globals with their owners; cross-cluster references stay opaque cookies until both sides lift.
  • Three rules are proposed for the whole engine: no lifted global state, ever; an unchecked original dereference panics rather than guessing; address-embedding values are narrowed to their meaningful part with the quirk pinned by test.
  • Central estimate for all sixty-six hundred functions is about nine hundred agent-hours with a twofold uncertainty band, plus one-time harness and design costs. The next pilot should sample a callback-dense subsystem, which this one deliberately avoided.

How to reproduce it

From the repository, run the lifted crate's tests on the host and the differential suite on the 32-bit target; both are zero-dependency. Per-function evidence (lifted, proven, minutes, line counts, blockers) is recorded in the lane's results file next to the report.

What was asked

Verified The sift-down never saves two of the twelve record fields it moves. Its final store reloads both from one word of its own stack frame that nothing ever writes, so in the real game those two fields receive whatever the caller left on the stack. The proof defines that word as zero and the rewrite stores zero; anything else about those fields is unprovable.

Verified The unreached function's short path calls what looks like a conditional fatal routine and then returns without restoring its stack frame, so control jumps into frame garbage. In the checker that is a certain, deterministic fault. Because every trial of that path faults, it cannot pass on its own: fault-only trials compare nothing and trip the checker's vacuous rule.

Verified The smoother calls a helper with a constant angle passed as a double in a vector register and reads back a double the same way, which a Rust rewrite can neither pass nor read. The helper is pure over a fixed input, so its exact answer was measured by running the helper itself natively under the checker worker (a one-trial probe with a deliberately wrong rewrite, reading the true answer from the mismatch detail) and folded in as a constant. The value matches a cosine to eight digits.

Verified A smoothing gate that ends in a below-or-equal jump keeps points whose comparison is unordered: that jump is taken for NaN inputs. The natural Rust spelling of the comparison is false for NaN and fails a quarter of trials; only the negated ordered form matches. Three further transcription slips (a dropped doubling, a dropped decrement, a counter incremented before its stores rather than after) were each caught by the first failing trial and fixed.

The four rewrites ship as verified. The uninitialized-slot read and the crashing path are recorded as likely original-code bugs for a later review pass, not fixed. The next lane on the unreached function gets a full retry kit: call conventions per callee, the object graphs to fabricate, the uninitialized slots to define, and the finding that only the whole long path can pass since it has a single exit. Two reusable tricks came out of the batch: probe verdicts to measure exact helper answers natively, and per-word global ranges for first debug runs, since the worker otherwise logs only the range base per changed word.

Each verified function has a contract and verdict file pairing the original with its rewrite export; rerunning the checker driver over them replays the 1,200 trials. The smoother has a second, supplementary contract that forces the mixed inner-loop path every trial with a per-call answer sequence, also green at 1,200. The helper probe is a one-trial contract with a zero-returning export whose expected mismatch prints the true answer.

Unicorn emulation was tried first for the helper's value and dies silently on this host, which is why the probe method exists. Hand-converted 64-bit script words were silently wrong and cost a run; machine conversion only since. A memory-inventory script filtered out register-only instructions and hid the loop-bound decrement for a full debug cycle. A supplementary contract renumbered a callee id the rewrite had hardcoded, faulting every trial until the renumbering was replaced by a per-call sequence.

A callee register the manual calls optional is compared by default

A production batch of three interface functions passed only after its contract listed three callee identifiers with explicitly empty register selections: for object-call convention callees the checker compares the object register even when the contract says nothing about registers.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring interface functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original over at least one thousand trials with the version 4 checker.

What was found

Verified All three rewrites passed one thousand trials with zero failures and non-vacuous verdicts, covering every reachable path combination.

Verified The checker's manual describes the per-call register selection as optional. The worker source tells a narrower story, confirmed by a failing run:

ConventionRegisters compared with no entry
cdecl and stdcallnone
object call (thiscall)the object register
fastcallboth argument registers

This only bites when the object register holds a scratch-frame pointer rather than a real object, which happens for helper calls that take an output buffer in the register. The fix is an explicit empty selection for those callees, which the worker honours as selecting nothing.

What was decided or recommended

  • Contract authors should give every object-call callee an explicit register entry: the register where it carries the object, an empty list where it carries scratch.
  • The manual should state the default selection table instead of calling the option merely optional.
  • The first-mismatch detail should print the first diverging call rather than the first three calls, which usually match.

How to reproduce it

Write a contract with an object-call callee whose register holds a frame address, omit that callee from the register selection, and run any number of trials: the calls check fails on the register while every other check passes. Adding the callee with an empty selection turns the verdict green with no other change.

What was confusing or went wrong

The truncated mismatch detail showed two identical call heads, which sent the investigation toward argument encodings first; dumping the full per-side call logs showed all arguments identical and pointed at the register instead. Two further mismatches on the largest function were genuine analysis errors (a misread argument slot and two caller slots whose overwrite targets had been swapped), both diagnosed exactly by the same call logs.

How strongly is each rewrite proven

Every accepted rewrite now has a proof record with a level from P0 (unproven) to P5 (cross-checked). Of 6,776 rewrites, 6,254 sit at P2 (passing with adequate coverage), 452 at P3 (strict), 25 at P4 (a wrong version was run and caught), and 45 at P1 (coverage inadequate or unshown). The most common gap by far is that 96 percent of functions have never had a wrong version run against them.

What was asked

Define a proof record per rewrite that captures how strongly it was proven, build it for every entry in the rewrite index from the stored verdict and contract files, report which weaknesses are common and which rewrites are weakest, cost a wrong-version run per function, and specify how the index and site should carry the levels.

What was found

Verified The builder matched all 6,776 index entries to on-disk verdicts and contracts; nothing was missing and nothing was guessed. The level counts are P1: 45, P2: 6,254, P3: 452, P4: 25, with P0 and P5 empty.

WeaknessRewritesMeaning
No wrong version run6,515No deliberately wrong variant was ever run and caught
Older checker6,224Verdict came from a checker older than the current one
Narrowed comparison1,809A return channel, check, or call argument was not compared
Private worker250Lane results came from a private copy of the checker worker
Low coverage45Passing verdict but the original rarely completed or a callee never fired

Verified The cheapest lift is a re-run of 4,280 rewrites on the current checker: each needs nothing else to reach P3. A wrong-version run costs a median of under half a second per function because the driver stops after three failures; generation is a script edit, but the rebuild time of each lane crate was not measured. What was decided or recommended

Keep narrowed comparisons below P3 even when they look legitimate, with per-function exemption reasons recorded in the contract. The import step should refuse vacuous verdicts and hash-mismatched contracts, which it does not check today, and a new checker release should demote stale records by query instead of by hand.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane script over the rewrite index; it walks each lane folder for verdict, contract, and wrong-version verdict files, matches them by function, recomputes the contract hashes, and writes one record per rewrite plus the level and weakness tables. A two-contract smoke run of the stock checker confirmed the verdict field meanings and the hash construction.

What was confusing or went wrong

Lanes store verdicts and contracts under many different folder names, and several runs per function often exist, so the builder had to search whole lane folders and pick the best verdict by stated rule rather than by path. The result files use relative function numbers that can look like full addresses, which broke the first matcher until matching compared both forms. The index kept growing while the lane ran, so all counts cite a recorded snapshot hash.

Three task natives read a fourth word they never wrote

Three related task natives each consume four words where only three are defined: the fourth word is read from a frame slot that no store reaches, so it is whatever garbage the stack scratch holds. Verified All three were still verified by pinning the checker's stack fill to zero and storing zero in the rewrite.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small ped-task natives in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares return values, memory, calls and faults.

What was found

All twenty passed one thousand trials each with no failures. While contracting them, three natives turned out to share one suspicious shape: code that moves three argument words onto the frame and then reads a fourth word from a neighbouring slot that is never stored to. Verified

NativeWhat the fourth word feedsStatus
Route table appendStored as the fourth element of the new table rowVerified, rewrite stores zero
Sound level probeFourth word of the coordinate record handed to the sound stagesVerified, rewrite stores zero
Sitting object probeFourth published coordinate and record word for the scan callVerified, rewrite stores zero

Frame arithmetic shows the slot always sits below the incoming stack pointer, in freshly reserved scratch that the caller cannot control, so the value is genuinely undefined rather than a hidden argument. Verified That it is a bug rather than intent is an inference: the surrounding code reads like three coordinates plus a pad word someone forgot to zero, or a read that aimed at the next argument slot and missed. Inferred Whether the garbage word can affect gameplay is unknown: the consumers are scripted stand-ins under the checker, and the real ones were not run. Unknown

What was decided or recommended

The rewrites store an explicit zero for the fourth word, with contracts that fix the checker's stack fill to zero so both sides agree. This is the documented pattern for functions that read stack they did not write, and the verdicts confirm it: all three pass with the garbage eliminated on both sides. A later lane with a running game could check whether the live fourth word ever matters; until then the zero is the honest reading of unknowable input.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the three natives from the mapped executable image and list every frame store against every frame read: in each case three argument words are stored and a fourth neighbouring slot is read with no matching store. Then run the lane's checker contracts for those functions: they pass only because the stack fill is fixed, and changing the fill without changing the rewrite breaks them, which confirms the read is really uninitialised.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two lane-side mistakes cost the most time. First, a Rust precedence trap: a dereference followed by a method call adds to the pointer, not the value, so three rewrites read a far-off heap word instead of adding a small constant; the call logs showed the exact wrong words and one parenthesis fixed all three. Second, the checker's mismatch detail shows only the first three calls of a trial, and these functions make up to nine, so a local-only verdict field carrying the full call logs was added to find the real divergence; it changes nothing compared. Rebuilding the rewrite library twice failed because the previous checker run still held it; waiting a few seconds and rebuilding worked, and no worker was ever stopped.

The stray-write check only runs when full-image comparison is on

A production batch of twenty small handlers is fully verified, and the run exposed a soundness gap in the standard contract template: with the full-image comparison switched off, the check that is supposed to catch writes outside the declared ranges never looks, so a rewrite that scribbles on a neighbouring global still passes.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, using the standard contract template.

What was found

Verified The worker discovers writes outside the declared ranges only when the full-image comparison option is enabled. With it disabled, which is what the commonly copied template uses, the discovery snapshot is skipped and the stray-write count stays zero on both sides no matter what the rewrite writes.

Verified This was demonstrated live, not just read in the source: one rewrite stored its value one slot past its declared target, and every check passed except the missing write at the declared address. Had the bug been an extra write rather than a misplaced one, the verdict would have been a clean pass.

Verified A follow-up probe re-ran all twenty functions with the full-image comparison enabled for fifty trials each: one thousand trials, zero failures, zero stray writes on either side, so this batch's verdicts do not depend on the gap.

Template option Stray writes detected Trial cost seen
Full-image comparison off no, count stays zero fast, tens to hundreds of trials per second
Full-image comparison on yes, fails the verdict on any stray write slow, single digits of trials per second

What was decided or recommended

Keep the fast template for the thousand-trial acceptance runs, and add a short full-image probe of a few dozen trials per function as supplementary evidence; a stray write is deterministic, so a short probe catches it as reliably as a long one. Longer term, either document the gating in the checker manual or run the stray-write discovery unconditionally.

How to reproduce it

Take any passing contract that writes one global, point the rewrite at a neighbouring word instead, and run it with the full-image comparison off: the verdict fails only on the missing declared write, with the stray-write count at zero. Re-run with the option on to see the stray write reported.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified A second, self-inflicted trap from the same run: lists of plain numbers under the explicit-values fill option do not rotate per trial, the whole list is written every trial, so flag-gated branches stayed shut and real writes were invisible until the fills were moved to the cycling fill option. Older lane reports describe value rotors from a previous driver version; the current manual documents both forms correctly, and the manual is the one to trust.

Shared-memory reports name the range, not the word

A production rewrite batch caught the checker misreporting where a changed word lives, which can pass a wrong rewrite. The fix on the contract side is to declare one-word ranges until the worker is fixed.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of medium and large game functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, which compares return values, memory writes, calls and faults over a thousand generated trials.

What was found

Verified When several shared words are declared as one range, every reported change carries the range start address instead of the changed word address. The word index is dropped when the report is built, so only the changed values are compared, not where they were written.

Verified This is a soundness hole, not just a display quirk. A rewrite that stores the right value at the wrong offset inside the same range produces an identical report to the original and passes. Two swapped values at two offsets also pass. Both were confirmed by reading the worker source.

Verified The batch also confirmed two smaller issues. A store address computed into executable code succeeds silently on the original side but is reported as cheating on the rewrite side, because code pages stay writable during original trials and are revoked during rewrite trials. And two fill entries that overlap in one word apply in order, so adjacent flag bytes must be filled as a single word.

What was decided or recommended

All four verdicts in this batch declare single-word ranges, which report exact addresses, so they are not affected. Other lanes should do the same for any multi-word range until the worker reports the true word address. The worker should also re-protect code pages after patching so both sides fault identically on computed code addresses.

How to reproduce it

Declare one multi-word shared range that a function writes once per trial, run the checker, and read the mismatch detail: the reported address is the range start on every trial. Split the declaration into single-word ranges and rerun: the reported address becomes the true store address. The worker source shows the report pushing the range base with the word index unused.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first mismatch looked impossible: both sides reported writing the same unexpected address with different values, an address neither side could compute. It took a byte-level re-read of the function and then the worker source to see the address was the range base and only the value was real. Three genuine rewrite bugs (a misread clamp target, a push-shifted register mapping, swapped flag bytes) were each caught on the first probe run, which is the expected shape of this work.

A bounding-sphere merge that forgets its tag word

One small geometry routine merges two bounding spheres, and on two of its three paths it carries a tag word from the winning input to the output. On the third path, the merge path, it writes no tag at all and instead copies one word of whatever happened to be on the stack.

What was asked

Rewrite the routine in Rust and prove the rewrite behaves identically over at least a thousand generated inputs, including edge values.

What was found

Verified The routine takes two spheres, each a center point plus a tag word and a radius, and returns their smallest shared sphere with a merged radius. When one sphere already contains the other it copies that sphere through unchanged, tag included. When the spheres genuinely merge, the output tag is an uninitialized stack word: the code reads a frame slot it never stored to. The rewrite reproduces this by reading its own unwritten stack slot, so both sides observe whatever the platform left there.

Verified The rewrite matches the original bit-exactly on 1100 trials covering all three paths with finite, infinite and not-a-number inputs, and three targeted mutants (one per path) are each caught within 25 trials.

What was decided or recommended

The uninitialized word is reproduced faithfully rather than fixed, since the project's rule is to match the original's behavior exactly. Whether the tag matters to callers is unknown; the one known caller is a much larger scene-update routine that is still being worked on.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's checker contract for the sphere merge with a nonzero stack fill: the merge path's tag output always equals the fill, proving the original reads a slot it never wrote.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first input corpus looked thorough but almost never exercised the merge path with ordinary numbers, because random 32-bit floats are usually enormous or infinite and take the containment exits instead. A merge-specific mutant passed a hundred trials before this was noticed. The corpus was rebuilt around a deterministic cross product of small, zero, infinite and not-a-number values, after which all three path mutants fail as they should.

Outcome Count Meaning
Named, medium confidence 117 Behaviour and schema verified; the create wording is ours
Unnamed, low confidence 33 Proven mid-routine addresses, left empty deliberately

What was decided or recommended

Disassemble each batch address from the executable using the image base offset, cluster the routines by instruction shape, and collect each routine's direct call targets. The constructor call in each routine resolves to a schema through the class structure records, and the table each constructor installs cross-checks the match. Routine starts are confirmed by a shared head pattern plus a tail jump into the common epilogue; batch addresses failing that test are checked against the surrounding tiling to prove they fall inside neighbours.

The first real-or-bogus check compared head bytes against the long encoding of pushing a small constant and rejected every routine in the batch; the compiler uses the short two-byte encoding, and fixing that turned a zero percent pass rate into the expected split. One batch size was also wrong (listed shorter than the routine truly is), which initially misclassified a real routine as bogus until the check learned to retry the family's two known sizes.

Operating notes: running forty-odd agent lanes on one laptop

These are the working rules the coordinator arrived at over the first day and a half of production, written down so that a later run starts from them instead of rediscovering them. The short form: the limit is the machine's memory, not the model; every published number must come out of a script that runs on a timer; and nothing a lane says about the checker or the inventory counts until it has been checked by something other than that lane.

What was asked

For operational notes that a later session, or another coordinator, can run the project from.

What was found

AreaRuleWhere it came from
How many lanesAbout 45 on a machine with 48 GB of memory. Guard on both free memory and commit headroom before starting a lane.At 74 lanes the machine ran out of commit while free memory still looked fine.
What a lane costsThe agent process is the small part. Wrapper shells, compiler runs and checker workers are the rest: a hundred shell processes held more memory than forty agents.Measured by grouping processes by name.
Inside a laneAt most three checker workers, and small groups of contracts per driver process.One driver process grew to almost 9 GB over a long run before the leak was fixed.
Keeping lanes suppliedSelf-refilling slots: each asks a brief maker for the next batch under a file lock and runs lanes back to back. Large-function lanes start only early in a slot's life.Background tasks are stopped after two hours; a lane outlives its slot, but a slot that starts a long lane late wastes the slot.
StoppingA stop file that slots check before starting a lane. Never stop processes by name.Checker workers from every lane share one name; a lane's test of worker recovery stopped its own regression that way.
The loopOne command on a five-minute timer does everything: import passed rewrites, integrate devlog fragments, rebuild counts, names and the code map, regenerate badges, commit, push.Three published figures went stale because each had been produced once by hand: the named count, the code map and the badges.
TimeRead the clock; never write a time from memory. Lanes guess times in their logs, sometimes by an hour.Status messages ran ahead of the clock several times.
The checkerA pass counts only on the stock checker. Changes to it go through a full read of the diff by the coordinator, a full regression on a fresh build, and only then replace the worker lanes use.Twenty-two lanes had built private copies; one relaxed a comparison.
Reading the executableThrough the mapped image only, and prove the mapping on a known function first.Three lanes read the raw file at a mapped address and two of them concluded that real functions were not functions.
Claims about the inventoryUnverified until an independent check agrees. Screen the whole class, not the one batch.Of three such claims, two were wrong and one was right about 16 entries out of 11,078.
Lists for programsWrite them as data files. Never rebuild a work list from a report meant for people.A survey's printout stopped at 40 names per lane and hid 34 contracts from a re-run.
Replacing a running programBuild into a new folder, rename the running file aside, copy the new one in.A running worker locks its own file; the build fails with access denied.

Verified Each row is something that happened during the run and is recorded in an earlier entry or in the changelog.

Inferred Launching the agent directly from the slot, without the intermediate shells, would free roughly a third of the per-lane overhead and allow several more lanes. Not yet tried.

What was decided or recommended

  • The coordinator's scripts are still outside the repository. They should move in, with machine paths removed, so that the operating layer is not lost with a scratch folder.
  • Any new published figure is wired into the timed loop when it is added, not afterwards.
  • When a counter stops moving for several updates, check its source before reporting it.

How to reproduce it

Start one slot and watch memory by process name for ten minutes; then add slots until commit headroom reaches the guard. The ceiling found that way is the number to use, not a number carried over from another machine.

The first memory guard watched only free memory, because that is what the first incident seemed to be about; the real limit was commit. A guard built from one incident's explanation did not cover the next one, so the watchdog now looks at the things that actually grew: commit, and any single driver process.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the version 3 checker, including several that pass a stack address to a callee as an out-parameter and read the result back afterwards.

What was found

Verified All twenty rewrites passed with one thousand trials each and zero failures, covering every fail point of the multi-stage functions.

Verified The snapshot of a pointed-to call argument is captured before the stub performs the scripted out-parameter write. On stack addresses the two sides' frames legitimately differ, so the snapshot compared unrelated scratch contents while the actual out value, read back by both sides and stored to compared memory, matched. Removing the snapshot and keeping the write plus the downstream store comparison turned the failures into passes with no rewrite change.

Verified One function passes its own incoming argument slot as the out-parameter, so the callee visibly overwrites that caller slot. Its contract runs with the stack comparison off and documents why; the value is still verified through the store the function makes with it. Sibling functions that pass scratch below the stack pointer keep the stack comparison on, because the worker excludes that region.

What was decided or recommended

For out-parameters, declare the write and skip the address, but do not snapshot the pointed-to words; verify the value through whatever the function does with it next. The checker manual should say that snapshots and writes do not compose on frame pointers.

How to reproduce it

Contract any function that passes a stack address as a callee out-parameter with both a write script and a snapshot on that argument, and run a few hundred trials. The call comparison fails on the snapshot while the return value and memory comparisons pass; removing the snapshot passes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first failure looked like a rewrite bug, because the call log showed two different snapshot values. It was the contract: the values were each side's pre-write scratch, which are supposed to differ. Three driver runs also ended with the worker process lost under machine load despite zero failures; all passed on re-run.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the version 3 checker, which compares return values, memory writes, stack balance, outgoing calls and faults over scripted trials.

Verified Three functions passed cleanly at one thousand trials each with zero failures: a vector-math leaf, and two indexed-transform functions that forward their results to a consumer call.

Verified The worker records every write inside a declared global range with the range start address instead of the true write address. Two writes of the same value to different words in one range are therefore indistinguishable, and a rewrite that writes the right value to the wrong word in a range passes. Narrow probes with marker values confirmed the rewrite under test wrote to the right addresses, so its verdict stands.

A bulk initializer making over two thousand calls per trial fills the log with its first callee, so its remaining seven callees never appear in any log and the coverage rule correctly refuses the verdict. The same truncation also means the tail of any long call sequence runs uncompared.

Passing one operand through a compiler barrier did not stop it; only an explicit NaN check reproduced the original's operand order. The one trial in a thousand that caught this had NaN on both sides of the add.

  • Report the global-range address as the true write address, matching the undeclared path. Until then, lanes verifying multi-word ranges should use one range per word or confirm addresses with marker probes.

  • Keep writing float rewrites in the original's operand order, and distrust barriers: disassemble the built rewrite when a NaN-payload mismatch appears.

Declare one global range covering several written words and publish two different values to two of them; the verdict detail lists both writes at the range start. For the float issue, feed a quiet NaN with one payload as the add base and a different-payload NaN as the product, then compare the rewrite's result bits against the original.

The global-range display first looked like the rewrite was storing values at the wrong address, and two probe runs with marker values were needed before the worker line, rather than the rewrite, became the suspect. The call-log truncation first presented as a coverage failure with no failing check, which sent the investigation toward the contract before the log cap was found. The float commutation survived the documented barrier workaround and was only confirmed by disassembling the built rewrite.

A large record-building function with twelve 3x3 float transforms passed 999 of 1000 checker trials and failed one: a single output word was a NaN with the wrong payload. The cause was not a transcription error. The Rust compiler had swapped the two operands of one float addition, which is value-preserving for every input except two NaNs with different payloads, where the hardware keeps the first operand's payload. Pinning the order with an opaque barrier did not fix it reliably: the next build passed the old trial and failed three new ones, because each build reshuffles register choices. The fix that holds decides every NaN case explicitly on the bits (first NaN wins, quieted, exactly as the hardware instruction does) and only runs NaN-free operands on hardware, where swapping is harmless. A follow-up contract feeding every transform nothing but distinct-payload NaNs, infinities, zeros and subnormals passed 60 of 60.

Rewrite one large game function in Rust and prove it identical with the version 3 checker, in stages: the entry path first, then one counted loop at a time.

  • Verified Entry path plus first loop verified: 1000 of 1000 trials agree, all fourteen callees fire, a deliberately planted mutant is caught, and a NaN-torture run agrees 60 of 60.
  • Verified The compiler swaps float multiply and add operands between builds. With two differently-signed or payloaded NaNs the winner changes, so bit-exact rewrites fail rarely and migrate between trials on rebuild. Explicit NaN handling removes the whole failure class.
  • Verified Two checker limits, both worked around honestly and reported: call snapshots cannot start at an offset and cap at eight words, so six computed frame words per loop are review-only; scripted callee-answer sequences cap at sixteen steps while one query site needs twenty-three, leaving one tiny skip-branch uncovered.

What was decided or recommended

Every rewrite with float arithmetic should treat operand order as load-bearing: decide NaN cases on the bits rather than trusting barriers, and run one all-NaN torture contract alongside the random one, because random floats almost never collide two NaNs at one operation. The checker should grow an offset for snapshots and longer answer sequences.

Build any 3x3 float transform in the checker harness with random table inputs over one thousand trials and inspect single-trial NaN-payload mismatches; then replace plain operators with explicit first-NaN-wins helpers and rerun with tables cycling distinct NaN payloads, infinities, signed zeros and subnormals.

Dumping the checker's own trial inputs instead of re-deriving them ended that last one. The rebuilt rewrite file also stays delete-locked long after each run with no visible holder; renaming it aside before rebuilding works.

Correct rewrite fails only on rows returning nonzeroStubbed cookie check overwrites the answer registerLeave cookie checks unpatched; omit them in the rewrite

When the original faults after completing all its calls, check for a stack imbalance tripping the cookie check before suspecting anything else.

Three quiet ways a proof can lie to you

Verifying three memory-subsystem functions surfaced three soundness gaps worth knowing: a contract that forgets to intercept a call silently runs the original machine code instead of failing, heap segment sizes are rounded down to whole words without warning, and ordinary arithmetic in a rewrite can reorder floating point operations and change Not-a-Number results.

What was asked

Rewrite three original game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 3 checker, which intercepts outgoing calls and compares return values, memory, stack and call sequences over at least one thousand trials.

What was found

Verified Two functions verified fully at 1200 trials each with fault parity. The third, a large floating point update, was verified in stages to stage 3 of 5 with 1200 passing trials.

Verified A direct call with no interception record executes the real original code silently: the call comparison sees only intercepted calls and the undeclared-call check stays quiet. A contract that misses a call therefore tests the rewrite against the original plus unknown real side effects, not against the scripted environment.

Verified Heap segment sizes are floored to whole four-byte words when applied. A segment two bytes short left its last bytes uninitialised, which sent the original down a different path with real calls executing, while the rewrite stayed put.

Verified A chain of single-precision additions compiled from plain operators came out in a different order than written, flipping the sign of a Not-a-Number result on one trial in 1200. Scalar helpers with explicit quiet-Not-a-Number propagation and no inlining fixed the order and passed the full run.

What was decided or recommended

The checker should fail a trial that executes a direct call with no interception record, or at least report unintercepted targets. The driver should warn when a segment size is not a multiple of four. Rewrites with chained floating point arithmetic should use explicit ordered helpers, not plain operators, when bit-exact results are required.

How to reproduce it

Build a contract that omits one direct call of a function whose paths depend on heap flags, run it, and observe that the verdict reports only the intercepted calls with no complaint about the missing one. For the segment rounding, declare a segment whose size is not divisible by four and read its last bytes. For the arithmetic, compare a four-term single-precision sum written with plain operators against the original instruction order over Not-a-Number-heavy inputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

The segment-rounding bug initially looked like the interception layer writing to impossible heap addresses, because the real code running through the unintercepted calls wrote where no scripted behaviour could. The floating point failure passed 1199 of 1200 trials and needed the exact trial inputs resolved by hand to see the single reordered addition. A rebuilt rewrite library also stays file-locked after a run; renaming it before rebuilding works around it.

Rewrite twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker. Rewrite six neighbouring routines in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original, checking return values, written memory and outgoing calls over at least one thousand trials each.

Verified Five routines form one family: each normalizes a two-element input vector, mixes table values into two caller structures, normalizes a three-element vector, passes it to a shared helper, and publishes the results plus a table pointer. What was asked

Rewrite five medium and large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 3 checker, or defer with a precise reason and a retry kit for the next lane.

What was found

  • Verified Three functions verified, 1200 trials each with zero failures and full branch coverage: exhaust, fuel tank and glass emitter setups, one with 150 fault parity trials on a scripted null answer.
  • Verified The five functions are one vehicle effects module, not the file and memory subsystem the inventory guessed: they set up particle emitters for helicopter rotors, exhausts, fuel tanks, glass and overheating.

What was decided or recommended

When the original adds two different NaNs, the chip keeps the destination operand's NaN. The Rust compiler may emit the same add with the operands swapped, which is identical for every non-NaN input but keeps the other NaN. Intrinsics do not prevent this: the optimizer sees through them to a plain add and commutes anyway. So a contract that feeds random float bits into transcribed arithmetic can fail on rare trials through no fault of the rewrite. The fix used here was to pin the matrix inputs to a rich set of non-NaN, non-infinite edge values with magnitudes capped so no NaN or infinity can arise mid-computation, and to document the restriction in the rewrite. A software float implementation would close even that gap. Recommended reading for the next float lane: the batch report's NaN section before writing any arithmetic.

How to reproduce it

  • Run the fuel tank contract with a random float matrix fill: a small number of trials fail on the result snapshot with two different quiet NaN payloads.
  • Dump the failing trial's matrix words, then emulate the dot product chain bit by bit under destination-priority NaN propagation: the original's addition order reproduces the original payload and the swapped order reproduces the rewrite payload.
  • Disassemble the rewrite and confirm the emitted add has the commuted order; pin the matrix to exclude NaN and infinity and re-run to green.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two things cost time. First, one callee looked like a single-argument call at its call site but a two-argument call at the next one: an argument word pushed early belongs to the later call, and only the callee's own return cleanup plus global stack balance settle it. The checker's call log, not re-reading the disassembly, gave the right answer both times this happened. Second, the linker intermittently refused to replace the lane's output file with access denied while no process held it; renaming the file aside and rebuilding always worked.

Kind of changeLanesEffect on the comparison

What was asked

Rewrite a gameplay gating function that mixes scalar float arithmetic with scripted helper calls, and prove the rewrite bit-identical to the original over one thousand generated trials, including NaN and infinity inputs.

What was found

Verified The original negates one intermediate value by xoring it with a sign mask read from a global table. Xor maps positive NaN to negative NaN. Disassembling the built rewrite showed why: the compiler recognises the xor as a negation and folds the surrounding add into a subtraction, so the emitted code never contains an xor at all. The optimisation is invisible except on NaN inputs.

Verified Loading the mask from the global table at run time, exactly as the original does, gives the compiler a value it cannot reason about, so the xor survives into the binary. With that one-line change the rewrite passed all one thousand trials with zero failures, and a deliberately flipped comparison was caught within nine trials.

Take any scalar float negation the original implements with xor, rewrite it in Rust with unary minus or an explicit constant xor, and run a differential check with a NaN flowing into the negation. Replacing the constant with a mask loaded from the global makes the xor appear in the binary and the trials pass.

Log capacity256 entriesTrials above this many outgoing calls are affected
Guard shapeskips only when the index is strictly above 256One entry is written past the end of the log
Overflow targetthe callee address tableOnly the rewrite side reads it, so only that side breaks
Unlogged tailcalls past the 256th are answered, not comparedA wrong rewrite could pass on its late calls

Jump after compare(a, b)Faithful RustNaN behaviour
jump if below or equal!(a > b)jump taken

set byte if above or equala >= bcleared

Verified Two related comparison rules also need care. A branch that continues only when one float is strictly above another must be written as a strict greater-than so NaN takes the skip path. A branch that fails only on strictly-greater must be written as a negated greater-than so NaN takes the pass path. Getting either backwards is a silent one-in-hundreds failure.

Every float addition or multiplication in a rewrite whose two inputs can both be NaN now goes through order-preserving helpers, and the built code is spot-checked to confirm the order survived. What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty-five native handler functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Eighteen handlers are plain forwards of up to seven words to one engine call and passed first try on the stock checker, including one with heavy register-and-scratch traffic that still forwards its words in order.

Verified Four handlers coerce a script word to a flag by writing one byte through their own stack slot and pushing the whole word, so the upper bytes are caller-address leftovers. The checker could only compare the full word or skip the argument entirely; skipping would pass a wrong flag value silently.

Verified Two handlers are single-instruction tail jumps to shared implementations. The checker's tail-jump interception records the call arguments one word too low on the stack, because a tail recorder is entered with two return addresses where a normal call has one. The existing proofs only covered thunks with no arguments, where nothing is read, so every contract for an argument-taking thunk failed every trial. It fails closed, never a false pass.

Verified One handler writes its results to fixed addresses that exist only in a running game and cannot be mapped by the checker, so it was deferred rather than verified.

The game-address writer stays deferred.

Separately, a rebuild was blocked for several minutes by an unidentified process holding the rewrite library against deletion while still allowing renames; moving the old file aside unblocked the build, and the holder was never identified. The shared checker worker also died twice mid-contract under load with zero failures recorded, and both contracts passed on retry.
