Float rewrites must guard every add, multiply and subtract against NaN operand order

Verifying a bit-exact rewrite of the biquad filter process routine showed that the Rust compiler picks either operand order for floating point add and multiply, including inside SSE intrinsics, while the hardware propagates the destination operand's NaN payload when both operands are NaN. A rewrite using plain operators is therefore one colliding NaN pair away from a wrong result, and the fix is small explicit guards that decide every NaN case before hardware sees it.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring audio routines in Rust and prove each rewrite bit-identical to the original over at least one thousand checker trials: the biquad filter constructor, its coefficient update, its sample process routine, its parameter apply routine, and the reverb allocation routine.

What was found

Verified The process routine was verified at one thousand trials with zero mismatches. It makes no calls, so the contract is heap state plus edge-biased inputs, including trials where the sample buffer overlaps the effect object itself.

Verified The first green run was vacuous: every trial either took the bypass return or ran with an empty channel mask, because all control pins cycled with the same length and locked phases. Coprime cycle lengths fixed coverage, and a mutant with one dropped term is now caught.

Verified One trial in the full run then failed with the original and the rewrite emitting different NaN payloads at the same six output addresses. Disassembling the rewrite showed the compiler had emitted the output multiply with the operands swapped relative to the source: the hardware keeps the destination operand's NaN, so the swap changed the result. Rewriting the loop with scalar SSE intrinsics produced bit-identical wrong outputs, because the compiler commutes intrinsic operands too.

Verified Twelve targeted probe trials with forced NaN pairs in every sign and payload combination confirm the hardware rule for add, subtract and multiply: the destination NaN wins. The two alternative rules the evidence first allowed (source wins, negative wins) fail those probes.

Inferred Earlier verified float rewrites that used plain operators passed honestly but partly by luck: both-NaN collisions with differing payloads are rare in random corpora, and nothing in their contracts forced one.

What was decided or recommended

  • Float rewrites should route every add, multiply and subtract through helpers that return the destination NaN when it is NaN, else the source NaN when it is NaN, else the plain operation. With NaN-free inputs the compiler's operand choice is invisible.
  • Every float contract should include forced both-NaN trials with differing payloads, not just random floats; random corpora rarely collide.
  • The two deferred routines need checker abilities, not more triage: second-vector-register call logging with a rewrite-side transport, and floating-point-stack call logging with a rewrite-side transport.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane rewrite crate for the 32-bit target, generate the process-routine contract with coprime control pins and aliased buffer offsets, and run the checker for the full thousand trials plus the two small NaN probe contracts. The mutant export with the dropped state term must fail while the correct export passes. Separately, disassembling the built rewrite shows swapped multiply operands versus the Rust source.

The intrinsics fix failing with bit-identical outputs was the confusing step: identical wrong bytes across different code generation proved the bug was in logic the two versions shared, namely reliance on operand order, and direct inspection of the emitted loop then showed the swap. Two environment issues cost time: the freshly used rewrite library stays file-locked for minutes with no visible holder (renaming it aside unblocks the rebuild), and one full run lost its worker near the end and the driver reported zero failures while hiding six real ones, because its early return drops the failure records.

Rewrite twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.

Verified Re-running nine production lanes under checker version 2 verified 180 of 181 functions and caught one version 1 pass that fails under version 2. What was asked

Port every function that nine production lanes had verified under checker version 1 to the version 2 runtime and contract format, and re-run each for at least one thousand trials with the version 2 worker. The batch held 181 verified functions: script native handlers and small game helpers.

What was found

Verified 180 functions pass version 2 at one thousand trials each with no failures and no vacuous passes. One function, a search over many node tables that can make several hundred intercepted calls in a single trial, fails 27 trials out of a thousand: the original side returns normally while the rewrite side faults.

Verified The fault is a worker defect. The recorder stub is meant to stop logging once the 256-entry call log is full, but the emitted comparison skips logging only when the index is past 256 rather than at it. Index 256 therefore still logs, and version 2 places the stub-address table immediately after the log, so that one record overwrites the table with the calling context. The rewrite side then calls through the corrupted entry, jumps to heap memory and faults. Version 1 contains the same wrong comparison but is immune by layout: its smaller log records leave a gap between the log and the table, so the single wayward write lands on unused space.

Verified The rewrite is exonerated. Both checker drivers generate bit-identical trial inputs for the failing contract, the rewrite matches the original guard for guard, every memory access on the failing trial stays inside mapped test buffers, and a throwaway probe confirmed the table holds the corrupted value exactly on trials with enough calls. No change to the rewrite can defend against the worker corrupting the call table mid-trial.

Recommended regression test: a contract whose trial makes more than 300 intercepted calls, which no earlier version 2 proof exercised.

Run the failing contract, a table search with a fixed seed, for one thousand trials with the prebuilt version 2 worker and the batch rewrite library. A minimal probe that reads the first table entry instead of calling shows zero on passing trials and one on failing ones.

The fault signature pointed everywhere except the worker: a privileged-instruction fault at a heap address looks like a bad indirect call in the rewrite, but the rewrite contains exactly one indirect call and every input on the failing trial maps to valid test memory. Most of the diagnosis time went into eliminating rewrite-side causes one by one, including a wrong theory about floating-point call answers and a long detour into how the call target is loaded, before a probe showed the table itself changing between trials. The lesson for future reruns is that an empty rewrite call log next to a full original log means the rewrite died before its first call completed, which points at the call machinery rather than the function logic.

Re-running nine production lanes of script-native rewrites under checker version 2 verified all 205 functions, and caught one whose version 1 pass was empty: both sides had faulted on every trial because the contract set up the wrong global, which version 1 counted as a pass and version 2 exposes.

What was asked

Port the version 1 verified rewrites from nine production lanes to the version 2 runtime and contract format, and re-run each for at least one thousand trials under the version 2 worker. A rewrite counts as verified only when it passes version 2.

What was found

Verified All 205 functions pass version 2 at one thousand trials each, with every trial succeeding on both sides and every declared callee firing.

Verified One timer native passed version 1 on one thousand trials in which both sides faulted identically: its contract prepared a neighbouring global instead of the one the handler reads, so both sides read a zero pointer and faulted on the same store. Version 1 compared only termination and called that a pass. Version 2 records per-trial status, which showed zero successful original trials and flagged the verdict. Pointing the contract at the global the code actually reads makes all one thousand trials succeed and match. The rewrite was correct throughout; the old contract was at fault.

Verified One phone-rotation native read four global words that version 1 left at constant values; the ported contract varies them every trial over float edge values, and still passes fully.

Verified 46 handlers push a boolean flag merged with leftover bytes from their own stack slot; the ported rewrites push the bare flag and the contracts skip that one call argument, since the checker has no byte-level call comparison. Four handlers forward more than eight engine arguments, past the checker's fixed call log; that blind spot is unchanged from version 1 and is documented on each contract.

What was decided or recommended

  • Every rerun batch should mechanically audit version 2 verdicts for zero successful original trials and unfired callees; that audit is what caught the bad contract here.
  • No defect in version 2 itself was found, and no rewrite needed behaviour changes.

How to reproduce it

Build the batch crate for the 32-bit target with the version 2 runtime, run each ported contract for one thousand trials with the prebuilt version 2 worker and driver, then audit every verdict for a full pass count, a non-zero successful-original count, and firing callees. The timer native reproduces the catch: with the original contract both sides fault on all one thousand trials, and with the corrected setup all one thousand succeed.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong in the run itself: all three checker shards exited cleanly with no restarts. The surprise was the direction of the catch: the faulty contract produced identical faults rather than a mismatch, so only the version 2 status counts, not the pass flag, reveal it. A pass flag alone is not evidence.

Verifying a tail-jump native handler whose target takes stack arguments

All twenty-five script native handlers in this batch were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals with the differential checker, including one handler that is a single tail jump to a shared engine routine. The tail jump needed a contract pattern that had not been used before, because the checker's tail stub logs one extra word ahead of the real arguments.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty-five script native handlers and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least one thousand differential trials. One handler in the batch is not an ordinary function body but a single tail jump: it leaves the call context on the stack and jumps to a shared routine that takes the context as a stack argument.

What was found

Verified The other twenty-four handlers share the usual native shape: one context pointer in, script arguments forwarded to one engine call, an optional answer stored into the return slot. Four coerce a boolean flag into the low byte of their own stack slot, a quirk earlier lanes already documented; the same recipe (reproduce the word from the context pointer, skip the stack comparison, verify through the call log) passed first try.

Verified The tail jump works differently under the checker than a normal call. The worker implements a tail patch by turning the jump into a call to a recording stub, so on the original side the stub sees two return addresses ahead of the real argument and logs the inner one as argument zero. That word is a checker artefact, not behaviour: it is the same on both sides but says nothing about what the handler does.

Verified Declaring one more argument than the target takes, skipping argument zero in the call comparison, and having the rewrite pass a documented placeholder word ahead of the forwarded context pointer verifies the real argument exactly. A mutant rewrite that forwarded a null pointer instead of the context failed every trial, and the call log showed exactly the one compared argument, so the comparison is live and not vacuous. The correct rewrite passed one thousand trials with no failures.

What was decided or recommended

Tail jumps whose targets take stack arguments should use this pattern: declare one extra argument, skip the first in the call comparison, and forward the real arguments after a placeholder word. Targets that take register arguments follow the existing register-comparison proofs instead. Nothing in the checker needs to change, but the tail-patch documentation should mention the extra logged word so the next lane does not have to rediscover it.

How to reproduce it

Take any single-jump handler whose target reads its arguments from the stack. Write a contract with a tail patch at the jump, zero outer cleanup, one declared callee argument more than the target takes, and the first call argument skipped. Write the rewrite as a normal call that passes a constant word followed by the original stack arguments and returns the answer. Run one thousand trials, then run a mutant that forwards a wrong pointer and confirm it fails on the call comparison.

What was confusing or went wrong

Rebuilding the rewrite library failed three times with an access-denied error on the old output file while no process appeared to hold it. Renaming the stale file aside freed the path and the build succeeded. Sibling lanes hitting this should rename and rebuild rather than stopping worker processes. Two native-analysis files from other lanes use a different layout than the rest and were skipped; every handler here was simple enough to analyse directly from the executable.

Two audio helpers verified, and four contract gotchas for other lanes

Two adjacent medium and large audio functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over one thousand trials each, but the interesting part is what kept failing along the way: four contract and tracing traps, each of which produced a confusing green-or-red result before it was understood.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring functions as idiomatic Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with checker version two, which runs both sides from identical state and compares returns, memory, calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Both rewrites pass all one thousand trials with bit-exact float agreement and zero faults on either side, and a deliberately wrong mutant of the first rewrite is caught by the heap comparison.

Verified Four gotchas, all confirmed by reading the checker source or by experiment. First, the per-callee write offset in a contract counts words into the stub's private buffer, not bytes into the target, so out-words partway into a buffer need placeholder leading words. Second, stacked input cycles are indexed by trial plus slot number, so a multi-slot path plan must be counter-rotated or the alignment silently shifts. Third, one function jumps into the middle of a shared tail sequence, turning a computation that looks dead into the value that gets stored. Fourth, one clamp's skip-branch lands inside the clamp sequence rather than after it, so the supposedly skipped case still clamps two of three values.

Verified A one-word bug in the checker's restart path crashes the driver on any setup failure instead of restarting the worker; the lane's own copy carries the fix.

What was decided or recommended

The two rewrites are ready to merge under proposed descriptive names. The checker documentation should gain one line about the write-offset units, and the restart-path fix should be folded back into the shared driver. Lanes tracing large functions should re-check any jump that lands mid-sequence and any branch that lands inside a clamp by raw bytes rather than by listing.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's two contracts through the version two checker with one thousand trials each and confirm zero failures, full fault-free histories, and per-callee call counts that match the designed path mix exactly. Flip the sign handling in the first rewrite's error term and confirm the heap check catches it.

What was confusing or went wrong

The dimension ladder looked like a plain range check until symmetric probe inputs showed one axis losing its value exactly when another axis took a particular branch, which first looked like impossible backwards-in-time clobbering and turned out to be the fall-through clamp above. The grid accumulator mismatch survived three rounds of theory before a row-by-row dump showed the outer loop reusing the first outer's scale value. Both times the fix was small and the confusion was large, which is why they are recorded here.

Why commit headroom was falling again with only 39 lanes running, well under the ceiling measured in the earlier incident.

2026-10-03

NaN payloads need explicit handling in float rewrites

Verified A rewrite that used plain floating-point arithmetic matched the original everywhere except in the payload of one NaN result, because the compiler may emit either operand order and the hardware keeps the destination payload when both operands are NaNs. Rewrites that translate floating-point arithmetic now select NaN operands explicitly, and the pattern is proven over thousands of trials.

What was asked

A production batch asked for Rust rewrites of four neighbouring audio functions, each proven identical to the original by the differential checker over at least one thousand trials. One of the four is heavy floating-point code: weighted sums, a reciprocal, angle helpers and running min/max bounds, all in single precision.

What was found

Verified The float-heavy rewrite passed 49 of its first 50 trials. The single failure was a call argument: both sides computed a NaN, but the original produced the canonical quiet NaN while the rewrite produced a NaN carrying a payload. Tracing the inputs showed an addition whose two operands were both quiet NaNs with different payloads. The hardware rule keeps the destination operand payload in that case; the original kept one payload and the compiled rewrite kept the other, because the compiler is free to choose either operand order for the instruction.

Verified The same run confirmed the fix and the boundary of the problem. Non-NaN operands are order-insensitive: rounding is round-to-nearest, and degenerate cases such as zero divided by zero produce the indefinite NaN either way round. Signaling NaNs cannot occur in these trials: generated inputs are quieted and the hardware never produces them. So only the both-quiet-NaN case needs special handling.

What was decided or recommended

Float rewrites now route every arithmetic operation through small helpers with destination-wins NaN propagation: if the destination is NaN return it, else if the source is NaN return it, else execute the real operation. The rewritten function then passed 1000 of 1000 trials with bit-exact comparison, and the helpers are now the recommended pattern for any lane translating floating-point arithmetic. Integer-only rewrites are unaffected.

How to reproduce it

Take any function whose inputs can put different-payload quiet NaNs on both sides of one arithmetic operation, rewrite it with plain arithmetic operators, and run the differential checker with float-edge inputs over a few dozen trials. A mismatch confined to the call-argument channel, with return value, memory and everything else equal, is the signature: the scripted callee answers hide the difference downstream, so only the logged argument differs. Adding the explicit helpers and re-running turns it green.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two earlier mistakes in the same lane are worth recording. First, a different function passed 1000 of 1000 trials with an empty call log: its input cycles were indexed one slot off, so every trial took an early exit. The verdict's call-coverage field exposed it, and the rule going forward is to read that field before believing any pass. Second, a hand analysis of one function's stack frame predicted register garbage that a live trial log refuted within minutes; the arithmetic behind the prediction was wrong (a hex offset misread), not the code. Striking static findings now get a dynamic check before anyone builds on them.

What was asked

Rewrite seven medium and large audio functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the version 2 checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares returns, memory, stack, calls and faults.

What was found

  • Verified Six of the seven functions pass one thousand trials each with zero failures and every declared callee firing.
  • Verified On one function, about four percent of trials end with both sides faulting at an address inside the fabricated heap. Tracing showed the original reads its return address from the wrong stack slot on that path: the caller pushes two words, the callee pops one, and the leftover word shifts every later pop.
  • Verified The rewrite pushes the same two words, drifts identically, and faults at the same address, so the fault agreement is a correct verdict rather than a rewrite bug.
  • Inferred In the real game this path would crash unless real data never takes it; whether it is reachable in practice is unknown.
  • Verified A seventh function could not be verified: its math helper takes two doubles in vector registers and the checker observes only one of them at calls.

What was decided or recommended

  • Accept the six verified rewrites; defer the seventh until the checker can log a second vector register at calls.
  • Keep the fault-agreement verdict for the crashing path, with this note attached, since both sides provably do the same thing.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane rewrite crate for 32-bit x86 with panics set to abort, generate the per-function contract with fabricated bank tables and pinned selector bytes, and run the version 2 driver for one thousand trials. The verdict file records zero failures, the per-callee fire counts, and a small fault-agreement fraction on the affected function. A per-trial probe shows the original side faulting with its instruction pointer inside the heap region on those trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two passing verdicts turned out to be vacuous on first runs: a wide fabricated table silently overwrote two neighbouring globals, and two pin periods aligned so that whole switch cases never ran. Both were caught only by the per-callee coverage counts, which are now checked before any verdict is accepted. A scratch-slot arithmetic slip (an offset of twenty from thirty-two is twelve, not twenty) cost one full debug cycle; the heap diff pointed straight at it.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty-five script native handler functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Twenty-three handlers verified on the stock checker with no changes to it. They share one shape: read script arguments through a call context pointer, forward them to one engine function, optionally store the answer. Special cases the checker already covers all passed: a boolean quirk that borrows the incoming stack slot, an engine answer returned as a floating point value, two handlers passing a stack-built coordinate vector, and one handler passing a relocated code address plus the context itself.

Verified Two handlers pass nine and ten call arguments, but the worker log keeps eight. Reading the worker source confirmed the cap sits in three places (stub emission, log parsing, callee cleanup). Verifying them on the stock worker would have been a weak check, so they were verified on a lane-owned worker copy with the log entry widened from eight to twelve argument slots and the neighbouring tables shifted to make room. Three already-verified contracts re-ran green on the widened worker, both wide handlers pass one thousand trials each, and both tamper mutants (a changed last word, a missing boolean quirk) fail fast on the outgoing-calls channel.

What was decided or recommended

  • Any lane with a function passing more than eight call arguments should use the widened log layout (twelve slots) rather than accept a stock pass that skips words; the exact edit list is in the lane report for folding back into the shared worker.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the version two driver: twenty-three pass on the shared worker binary, and the two wide-call contracts pass on the lane-owned widened worker selected through an environment variable. Each wide-call contract also runs a tamper mutant that must fail on the outgoing-calls channel. The lane report lists every worker edit site so the widening can be folded back and re-proven.

The relocation lookup bug cost one failed attempt: the script added a table base to a value that already included it, so every lookup missed and a relocated constant looked unrelocated. The resulting rewrite failed all one thousand trials, which is the checker working as intended. Re-checking the table with the double-add removed showed the relocation entry, and the corrected rewrite passed. A locked output file also blocked one rebuild; renaming it aside and rebuilding worked, per the recipe an earlier lane left behind.

Rewrite two neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 2 differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares returns, memory, stack, calls and faults.

The large function was deferred rather than contracted with a weakened comparison, since a passing verdict that cannot see an argument is worse than no verdict. Re-running 138 production rewrites under checker version 2 passed all of them, but reading the checker source for the one ten-argument call in the batch showed that version 2 silently compares only the first eight stack arguments of any call, and its manual still says stubs pop the full argument count. The gap is harmless for this batch and the affected verdict is sound, but a future function passing computed values past the eighth argument would pass vacuously on those words.

What was asked

Port every function nine production lanes had verified under checker version 1 to the version 2 runtime and contract format, and re-run each for at least one thousand trials with the version 2 worker, recording verified, failed, or not ported per function.

What was found

  • Verified All 138 rewrites pass version 2 at one thousand trials each with no behavioural difference found; total one hundred thirty-eight thousand trials with no trial where the two sides diverged on faults.
  • Verified The version 2 worker logs at most eight stack arguments per intercepted call, reads back at most eight for comparison, and a non-cdecl stub pops eight words at most, so argument words past the eighth are compared through no channel; the stack comparison only covers words above the incoming stack pointer. The manual's claim that stubs pop the full argument count is wrong past eight, and the cap is documented nowhere.
  • Verified The one affected call in this batch passes literal zeros in positions nine and ten on both sides (confirmed in the original and the rewrite), so its passing verdict is sound despite the gap.
  • Verified Version 2's new per-trial status history exposed a vacuous pass carried over from version 1: one audio flag setter passes one thousand of one thousand with every trial faulting identically on both sides, so its core logic never executed on either side. Version 1 recorded the same pass without the history that would have shown it.

What was decided or recommended

  • Document the eight-argument cap in the checker manual, and either reject contracts declaring more than eight callee arguments or extend the log entry to cover them.
  • Gate acceptance on a non-zero count of trials where the original side returned normally, as the manual already advises, and re-contract the vacuous flag setter with fabricated globals and pinned selectors so its real path executes before it counts as verified.
  • Keep the batch's rewrites as ported: all were byte-identical to the lane sources because every helper name the lanes used already exists in the version 2 runtime.

How to reproduce it

Build the batch crate and run any staged contract with the version 2 driver and worker; declare a callee with more than eight arguments and compare the logged argument count against the declared count in the worker source at the stub emitter, the log reader, and the stub cleanup computation. For the vacuous case, run the flag setter contract and read the status history and the original-ok count in its verdict.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified One sift routine failed its first version 2 run on a single trial. The cause was my own port, not the rewrite: its lane driver indexed stack rotations by trial number, and version 2 indexes stack cycles by trial plus stack position, which broke a deliberate lockstep between a register value and a stack argument on all one thousand trials and generated an input the real program can never produce. Rotating the two staged value lists by their stack positions restored the lane's exact input stream and the rerun passed cleanly. No other contract in the batch pairs a stack cycle with a register cycle, so no other fix was needed.

What was asked

Nine production lanes had proven 146 small rewrites under checker version 1. Version 2 folds the lanes' driver extensions into one driver, one contract format and one runtime, and a rewrite counts as verified only once it passes version 2. This lane ported every rewrite and contract to the version 2 form without weakening any input, built all rewrites as one crate, and ran each contract for at least one thousand trials.

What was found

Verified Counts after the rerun:

OutcomeFunctions
Passed version 2 on the first run145
Failed, then fixed and re-passed1
Not ported or not reached0

Verified The one failure was a small helper that reads a status byte through a linked record and returns it merged over the link pointer's own high bytes. The original does this with a partial-register write; the rewrite source stated the merge plainly. But the release-built rewrite returned only the zero-extended byte on every trial where the link had nonzero high bytes, failing about half of one thousand trials while the original kept the high bytes.

Verified Inspection of the built rewrite showed the merge was gone from the machine code: the optimizer had reduced the whole expression to a single zero-extending byte load. A standalone compilation test of the same load-and-merge sequence folds identically, while the same merge over plain values (no memory loads) compiles correctly, so the fold needs the load context. Rewordings did not help: explicit parentheses, a shift-based merge, a byte-array assembly and a statement form all fold the same way.

  • The rewrite now passes the masked high bits through an optimizer barrier before merging, with a comment citing the evidence. The rebuilt crate contains the merge and the contract re-passes one thousand trials with zero failures.
  • Any rewrite that merges a loaded byte over the high bits of the value its address was derived from should have its built machine code inspected, not just its source reviewed. Source-correct is not enough for this pattern under optimization.
  • Rerun lanes should validate every ported contract with a worker-free dry run before launching workers, and isolate each contract so one bad port cannot kill a whole batch. Both practices paid off here.

How to reproduce it

Compile the helper's load-and-merge sequence (load a word, early-out on zero, load a byte through the word plus an offset, merge the word's high bytes with the byte) with the project's release settings for the 32-bit target and inspect the resulting machine code: the merge is absent and only a zero-extending byte load remains. Compiling the same merge over plain function arguments keeps it. Running the helper's contract with the folded build fails about half the trials on the return channel with the high bytes zeroed; with the barrier in place it passes all trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first surprise was that the source was plainly correct yet the check failed, which first looked like a checker bug. Comparing the built machine code against the source settled it within minutes: the binary did not implement the source.

Earlier in the run, the port script itself had a bug that added an empty word list to heap segments that use fill-driven generation, which the version 2 driver rejects; two run shards crashed on it before the cause was found. The fix was a three-line change, all contracts were regenerated and re-validated, and the ten verdicts already banked were confirmed to still match. The runner now isolates each contract so a single bad port can no longer stop a batch.

This lane is a restart: the previous attempt ran eight workers and the machine ran out of memory. This attempt used three workers throughout and finished all 146 functions with nothing left for another lane.

2026-10-03

Rust does not pin floating-point operand order, and NaN payloads notice

A rewrite that mirrored every arithmetic operation of the original still failed bit-exact comparison on a few trials, with positive versus negative quiet NaN in one output word. The cause was not the algorithm: for a commutative operation such as add or multiply, the Rust compiler may emit either operand in the destination register, and when both operands are NaNs with different payloads the destination operand wins. Plain a + b in Rust is therefore not bit-deterministic in the presence of NaNs, and rewrites of floating-point code need explicit helpers that test for NaN first.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of six fire-audio methods in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with checker version two, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack effects, outgoing calls and faults over at least one thousand trials.

What was found

Verified Three of the six functions verified at one thousand trials with zero failures. The other three were triaged but not attempted before the lane time budget ran out; all use only direct calls and look verifiable with the same checker.

Verified The first floating-point rewrite failed five of fifty shakeout trials even though every operation matched the original in order. Disassembling the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had swapped the operands of several additions and multiplications, placing the right-hand value in the destination register. With two different NaN payloads in one operation, that swap changes which payload survives. Notably, none of the inputs were NaN: an infinity-times-zero inside the function created the first NaN, and a later negation produced the second payload.

Verified Without a NaN operand, scalar add and multiply are fully bit-symmetric, including signed zeros, infinities and overflow. So the fix is small and exact: test each operand for NaN first and return the first NaN found, otherwise do the plain operation. Twelve operations across the three rewrites use these helpers; everything else (subtraction, division-free code, comparisons, square root, negation) already preserves order because the compiler cannot reorder it.

Verified Two further mistakes of mine were caught by the calls comparison, both the same slip: stack arguments run last-pushed-first, so the last push is argument zero. A third mistake was subtler: two per-trial cycles with a shared period (a flag word cycling mod four, an object pointer alternating mod two) conspired so one code path never ran, and a thousand passing trials hid an argument-order bug on that path. Re-cycling the flags mod three exposed it at once. The verdict's per-callee call counts are the check that every path ran.

What was decided or recommended

  • Every lane rewriting floating-point code should use NaN-explicit helpers for variable-by-variable commutative operations, or prove its inputs and intermediate values can never hold two different NaN payloads. Self-products, constant factors and subtractions are order-safe as written.
  • Map pushed call arguments bottom-up: the last push is argument zero. The rewrite must pass them in the same order, because stub-recorded writes and snapshots index by argument position.
  • Keep per-trial cycle lengths coprime across independent dimensions, and refuse a passing verdict whose per-callee call counts show a zero.
  • Comparisons that branch on unordered-or-equal (the jbe form) must be written as a negated greater-than in Rust, since a direct less-or-equal is false for NaN while the original branch is taken.

How to reproduce it

Take any scalar function that adds or multiplies two variable floats, feed it inputs where both operands can be NaN with different signs (an infinity times zero feeding an addition is enough), and compare the Rust output bits against the original instruction by instruction: trials will differ in the NaN sign bit whenever the compiler chose the right-hand operand as the destination. Replacing the operation with an explicit test-first helper makes every trial agree.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first NaN mismatch looked like a wrong algorithm, and hand-tracing the arithmetic kept predicting the original's value for both sides, because the trace assumed the written operand order. Only disassembling the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had swapped operands. The phase-locked cycles were a second blind spot: a thousand green trials felt conclusive until the call counts showed one callee never ran. Both mistakes are now cheap to avoid and expensive to skip.

One of them failed first: the first checker had passed a rewrite whose compiled code drops the high bits of a pointer, because its inputs never exercised the affected path. The strengthened second-version inputs caught it, and a reworded rewrite that computes the identical value now passes.

What was asked

Verified One rewrite passed the first checker and failed the second, for two compounding reasons. First, the old contract's scripted callee answers never included a live pointer, so the interesting path only ever faulted identically on both sides, which counts as a pass. The ported contract mixes null, faulting and live-pointer answers, so the path now executes on most trials. Second, with the path exercised, the rewrite returned the bare tag byte where the original returned the full pointer: the low-byte-insert expression in the source is miscompiled by the project's Rust toolchain on 32-bit x86, dropping the high 24 bits. The miscompile was reproduced in isolation with the same compiler, which emits a bare byte load where the full value is required. Rewording the expression with xor, which computes the identical value by construction, compiles to correct code, confirmed by disassembling the project's own freshly built rewrite library, and the function now passes all one thousand trials.

Verified The reported first-checker weakness in random fills for global data is still present in the second checker's worker: both versions seed the same generator the same way, and trial pairs share bit-identical first words. The thirteen affected contracts in this batch now use explicit per-trial value lists resolved by the driver instead, which vary across the full 32-bit range every trial. Twelve of the thirteen never read the entry value at all; the thirteenth passes it through to a stubbed helper, so full-range values are safe on both sides.

Verified The other two reported weaknesses did not affect this batch: no function calls with more than eight arguments, and no trial faulted on the rewrite side only.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep the xor spelling for the low-byte insert and the strengthened contract; both are now the official form for that function.
  • Keep converting worker-side random global fills to driver-resolved value lists in every re-run batch until the worker seeds its fill generator properly.
  • Other batches should be searched for the same low-byte-insert idiom and their built binaries checked, since the source can be correct while the binary is wrong. Only one toolchain version was tested, so the range of affected versions is unknown.

How to reproduce it

Build the batch's rewrite crate for 32-bit x86 and run each ported contract for one thousand trials with the second checker's worker and driver; every function passes. Reverting the one rewrite to the or-form spelling reproduces the failure within a few dozen trials. Compiling the isolated low-byte-insert function with the same toolchain and reading the emitted assembly shows the dropped high bits without running the game code at all.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first run of this lane used twelve parallel checker shards and the machine ran out of memory, stopping the lane before it could rebuild the rewrite library with the pending fix; the failing verdict on disk therefore tested a binary older than the fixed source. The restart limited itself to three workers, rebuilt first, and confirmed the fix in the binary before re-running. The published first-version contract for the caught function turned out to be unrunnable as filed, referencing resources it never declares, so its intent had to be reconstructed from the rewrite and the failure itself.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the version 2 checker, including two handlers whose whole body is a single jump to a shared implementation.

What was found

Verified Twenty-three handlers verified at one thousand trials each with zero failures. The handlers all share one shape: read script arguments through the call context, forward them to one engine function, and sometimes store the answer in the return slot.

  • Production lanes should keep attempting thunks (the interception is sound for register arguments) but expect this failure for thunks that forward stack arguments.

How to reproduce it

Give any entry-jump thunk a contract with a tail patch site, one stack argument, and a rewrite that forwards the context pointer through the stub table. The calls comparison shows a scratch-stack address on the original side against the heap context pointer on the rewrite side on every trial, while all other comparisons pass.

A function-size table also lists one thunk as hundreds of bytes long because its range swallows neighbouring handlers; the real body is the five-byte jump plus padding.

Rewriting audio code: security cookies and a silent coverage trap

One medium audio function is now rewritten in Rust and verified identical over one thousand differential trials, and the work produced two reusable lessons: compiler security checks are best left unpatched, and contract pins can silently misalign with stack-driven paths so that whole loops never run.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of three adjacent audio functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the version 2 checker, spending most of the effort on the proof contract rather than the code.

What was found

Verified The first function, a bank refresh routine with two paths, seven outgoing calls and a compiler security check, passed one thousand trials with no failures and the original side healthy on every trial.

Verified Leaving the security check call unpatched works better than intercepting it: the real check runs on the original side and passes, and the return comparison then verifies the true return value instead of a scripted stub answer on both sides.

Verified Contract pins and stack-driven path selectors can lockstep invisibly: pins cycle per trial while stack values carry a position offset, so a two-valued pin can anti-align with the second stack argument and an entire loop silently never executes. Predicting exact call counts from the pin math before the long run catches this.

Inferred The two larger functions need no new checker ability; they were not reached only because the lane ran out of time, and their signatures, call tables and float comparison rules are recorded for the next lane.

What was decided or recommended

Future lanes should leave security check calls unpatched with a low-byte or no-value return comparison, always predict coverage counts from pin math before a thousand-trial run, and emulate unsigned float comparisons in a way that treats unordered values the same as the original jump. One known checker limit stands: per-trial constant callee answers cap enumeration loops at a single iteration per trial.

How to reproduce it

Copy the version 2 driver and runtime into the lane folder, build a rewrite crate for the 32-bit target into the lane build folder, write one contract per function declaring callees, pins and snapshots, and run the driver with one thousand trials. Confirm the verdict passes and that the reported call counts match hand-predicted values.

What was confusing or went wrong

A wrong assumption about a library's relocation field produced phantom fixups in the middle of instructions and a brief corruption scare. A struct layout was misread by one word because stores after pushing an argument use a shifted stack pointer; the checker's snapshot diff showed the exact rotation. The DLL could not be rebuilt while an old worker still mapped it, fixed by renaming it aside.

What was asked

Take the functions nine production lanes had verified under checker version 1, port each rewrite to the version 2 runtime and each contract to the version 2 format without weakening its inputs, and re-run every contract for at least one thousand trials with the prebuilt version 2 worker. What was found

Verified The batch held 138 functions recorded as verified under version 1. The remaining 124 were ported, built as one crate, and run.

Passed version 2123all one thousand trials match, original and rewrite

Verified The one failure is a hash-table string lookup. Its contract deliberately feeds full-range random words into table slots to check that wild pointers fault identically on both sides (290 of its 1000 trials do exactly that and pass). On one trial the wild text pointer happened to fall inside the mapped code region. The rewrite side runs with code pages revoked, so it faulted at that read and was reported as cheating. The original side read the code byte successfully, mismatched against the heap string at the first byte, then followed a second wild pointer and faulted one step later. Same inputs, same faithful behavior, different fault points, so the verdict records a termination mismatch plus a cheating flag.

Verified Every link was checked independently of the verdict: the trial inputs were regenerated from the contract seed with the driver's own code and the wild pointer equals the reported fault address exactly; the fault address sits inside the executable's code section; the compared bytes differ at the first byte with no relocation overlapping it; and the worker source classifies any rewrite-side fault in the code range as cheating. The version 1 worker carries the identical rule, so the source lane passed the same contract only because its random stream never landed a dereferenced word in that range. Porting shifted the stream (a string fill became a random fill with a pinned terminator) and this run drew the short straw: roughly one trial in a thousand for this contract shape.

What was decided or recommended

The function is recorded as failed under version 2 with the mechanism above, and its rewrite is kept out of the passing set but preserved in the lane folder so it is not lost: no faithful rewrite of this function can pass that trial, because any code that reads the same wild pointer faults the same way. Three follow-ups are recommended for the checker owner, in increasing order of work: capture both sides' fault records in the verdict so the next analyst need not re-derive them; when the rewrite side faults inside the code range, re-run that side once with the page readable and compare the second fault against the original's; and add a word spec for random-but-outside-the-image so wild-pointer contracts can exclude a sliver of inputs that is unjudgeable by design rather than untestable by accident.

How to reproduce it

Run this lane's version 2 contract for the hash-table lookup with the prebuilt version 2 worker at its recorded seed. Trial 644 of 1000 fails deterministically with the original faulting and the rewrite flagged for touching original code, while all other trials pass. Regenerating the trial inputs from the seed with the driver's own input code shows the dereferenced wild pointer matching the reported fault address.

The first confusing fact was the pairing itself: the rewrite flagged for reading original code while the original faulted. A rewrite bug would show matching fault points or a behavior difference, not this split. The split made sense only after tracing both paths past the first read: the original does not fault where the rewrite does, it faults one step later. The second surprise was that the faulting instruction address sat below the rewrite library's base address seen in later probes, which briefly suggested a third module was involved; it is consistent with the library loading at a different base in each worker process and does not affect the finding. Separately, the first attempt at this batch ran eight checker workers at once and the machine ran out of memory and stopped the lane; the rerun used three workers and completed without incident.

Production batch: a tail-call logging bug and two contract lessons

All twenty rewrites in this batch verified, but the checker needed a one-line fix first: its tail-call recorder logged stack arguments from the wrong slot, failing a correct rewrite on every trial.

Rewrite twenty small behaviour-task functions in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the version 2 checker, including a jump thunk, a recursive collector, two broadcast loops over scratch arrays, and a large message router.

What was found

  • Verified The tail-call recorder reads stack arguments one word too low. A tail call arrives with two return addresses on the stack, so the first argument sits one word higher than in a normal call, and the recorder captured the trampoline return address instead of the argument.

Rewrite a batch of small game functions in Rust and prove each bit-identical to the original with the differential checker, including several floating-point helpers (a clamp-and-interpolate routine, two vector interpolation routines, and a threshold subtraction).

Verified The cause is an operand swap by the compiler. The original's scalar instructions have fixed destination/source roles and propagate a quiet-NaN destination first, else a quiet-NaN source. A plain Rust multiply lets the compiler exchange the operands, which is unobservable for ordinary numbers but selects the other NaN when both are NaN.

Verified The fix is a small explicit router around every float operation: if the destination is NaN return it, else if the source is NaN return it, else perform the operation, using the original's exact roles. After the fix all four float rewrites pass 1000 of 1000 trials, including the previously failing trial.

Case Plain same-order Rust Explicit NaN router
Ordinary numbers Matches Matches
One NaN operand Matches (only one payload to propagate) Matches
Two different NaNs May diverge (compiler picks the roles) Matches (roles pinned)

What was decided or recommended

  • Inline assembly would also pin operand roles but is forbidden; the router is plain safe code with no performance cost on the game path.

Take any routine that multiplies or adds two values that can both be NaN with different payloads, rewrite it with plain Rust operators in the original's order, and run the differential checker with float edge inputs until a two-NaN trial reaches the operation. FactValueWhat it means
Lanes running at the time74Thirteen of them were the new re-run lanes
Commit in use85.6 of 86.8 GBThe operating system had already grown the page file twice; the next large allocation anywhere would fail

Slots now wait for both at least 5 GB of free memory and at least 14 GB of commit headroom before starting a lane, with a random delay so they do not all start in the same second. The numbers come from the operating system's memory counters and per-process private memory, grouped by process name, read while the machine was under pressure.

Six re-run lanes were stopped mid-work to recover; their ported rewrites were on disk and they were restarted one at a time with instructions to continue. Stopping the lanes took over ten minutes because the machine was thrashing. The coordinator had described 60 lanes as the ceiling on the strength of free memory alone and then added a wave of heavier lanes on top; it should have measured what a lane of the new kind costs before launching thirteen of them.

The first reading looked like a possible hidden float argument, since the value is moved with vector instructions into four evenly spaced fields. Checking the frame arithmetic slot by slot ruled that out: no alignment makes the read land on an argument, the return address or the saved frame pointer. A second trap in the same batch was a conversion loop that skips one source offset; the first rewrite assumed contiguous inputs and the checker caught it on the first run.

Rewrite behaviour mismatchnone in twenty thousand trialsall verified

The surprise was in four of them: the original coerces a script boolean by scribbling the 0/1 result into the low byte of its own incoming argument slot and pushing the whole dword to the engine, so the engine call receives the call-context pointer with its low byte replaced instead of a clean boolean.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original using the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Every handler in the batch follows one calling pattern: a single pointer to a call context holding a return slot and an argument array, one direct engine call, and either no stored result or one store through the return slot. They fall into a few shapes:

ShapeCountBehaviour
Forward11Pass the script arguments to one engine call and keep no result
Byte result6Store the low byte of the engine answer through the return slot
Full result2Store the whole engine answer through the return slot
Boolean coercion4Forward, but one argument carries the slot-surgery value described below
Global lookup1Resolve an object through globals, call, invert and store the answer
Jump thunk1A bare jump to the engine function, nothing to intercept

Verified The four boolean handlers reuse their own dead argument slot as scratch: the 0/1 result overwrites the low byte of the incoming context pointer, and that modified dword is what the engine receives. Since a real context address is never small, the value the engine sees is always nonzero even when the script passed false. Whether the engine reads the full dword or only the low byte decides whether the false branch works at all.

Verified One further handler passes eleven argument words to its engine call, which exceeds the checker's eight-word call record, so its last three arguments could never be compared and it was deferred rather than stamped with a gap.

What was decided or recommended

  • Rewrites reproduce the slot-surgery value exactly, and the pushed value is compared on every trial with the context placed at an address with a nonzero low byte so the masking is exercised.
  • The stack comparison is disabled for those four contracts only, because the original's write lands on its own incoming slot where no Rust rewrite can follow without inline assembly; the value itself is still checked through the call record.
  • The jump thunk and the eleven-argument handler were deferred with explicit reason codes instead of verified with holes.
  • The checker driver should restart a lost worker mid-run and resume remaining trials; two runs died environmentally with zero failures and passed cleanly on rerun.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble any of the four boolean handlers and watch the incoming argument slot between the comparison and the engine call: the low byte changes to 0 or 1 while the upper bytes keep the old pointer value, and the pushed engine argument is that combined dword. The lane scratch folder holds the contracts, verdicts and rewrites behind these numbers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first full-batch run died twice with the worker process vanishing mid-contract and no failures recorded; both contracts passed a thousand trials on immediate rerun with identical inputs, which pointed at machine load rather than the trials. Running one contract per worker process contained it.

Inferred The slot reuse looks like a compiler saving one stack slot by recycling dead space, not hand-written code: it is identical in all four handlers and serves no purpose a plain push would not.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handler functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, running at least one thousand trials per function including edge values.

These six were deferred.

Verified One handler is a five-byte jump to engine code with padding after it, so there is no handler body to rewrite. It was deferred as a jump thunk.

Disassemble any deferred handler from the original executable and look for a boolean test whose result is stored into the incoming stack argument slot before the engine call. Attempting the C-variadic workaround fails at compile time on this toolchain.

A whole batch that ends in jumps, not returns

This production batch verified nothing, and that is the finding: all twenty functions were destructor fragments that hand off to the next destructor with a tail jump, a shape the checker cannot intercept, so the only honest outcome was to defer every one.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty small game functions from the animation task subsystem in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker.

What was found

Verified Every function in the batch takes an object pointer, writes one or two table pointers into the object, sometimes releases one owned field, and then jumps to another destructor instead of returning. There is not a single return instruction in the batch. About half make one ordinary call first; the rest only store and jump.

Verified The checker's worker only intercepts ordinary call instructions and refuses anything else, which its own source states plainly. A tail jump therefore cannot be observed or scripted: running the original would execute unrewritten game code, including further chained jumps, and no honest rewrite can reproduce that.

Verified The batch had been classified as checkable. The classifier counts ordinary calls but does not look at the final instruction, so it mistakes jump-chained destructors for plain checkable functions.

All twenty functions were deferred with a stated blocker and no checker runs were made, since there was nothing the checker can express. Two recommendations went to the coordinator: exclude functions ending in a jump from checkable batches, and consider a future worker feature that turns a terminal jump into an observed call so this whole class becomes verifiable.

Disassemble any function in the batch and read its last instruction: it is a direct jump to another destructor, which itself ends the same way. Read the worker source function that installs call patches: it rejects any site that is not an ordinary call. The batch list, the repaired inventory sizes, and the merged destructor names all agree on what these functions are.

What was confusing or went wrong

A first relocation check wrongly reported that none of the table addresses are relocated, because the script added the page base twice. The corrected check confirms they all are. The lesson, already learned by earlier lanes in both directions: when a small script disagrees with an established proof, suspect the script.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty neighbouring functions that operate on a shared table of forty fixed-size records, and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares return values, memory writes, stack behaviour, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Eighteen of the twenty functions were verified with one thousand trials each and zero failures, covering record copies, flag sweeps, jump-table state machines, float range tests with edge values, and multi-call watchdog logic.

Verified One function was deferred without an attempt because it calls through an object's function table, which the checker cannot intercept by design.

The only consistent model is that the built stub zeroes the upper half of the value instead of merging the scripted lower half as the worker sources describe. Under that stub a rewrite that always returns zero passes vacuously, and under a transparent stub a rewrite would bake in behaviour that is wrong for real execution, so no faithful rewrite is verifiable until the stub is reconciled.

Verified The checker caught two genuine rewrite bugs on first attempts: a copy loop whose last element is copied in place rather than shifted, and a sweep whose flag update is skipped for non-matching records. Both one-line fixes passed on retry.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of script native handlers in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the differential checker, which compares return values, written memory, stack behavior, and outgoing calls over one thousand trials per function.

What was found

Verified Twenty-three of twenty-five handlers verified with zero failures in twenty-three thousand trials. Two were deferred: one is a single trap instruction and the other is a bare jump to its engine function.

Verified The vehicle-attach handler passes nine words to its engine call (three handles and flags plus two by-value vectors). The checker stub that records outgoing calls keeps the callee id plus the first eight stack words, so the ninth word never appears in the call comparison. A rewrite that passed a wrong ninth word would still get a passing verdict on every check.

Verified Seven bool-taking handlers build their engine argument inside their own dead incoming-argument stack slot, so the pushed word keeps the context pointer's high bytes with the low byte replaced by the bool. The rewrites reproduce that exact word and the call comparison checks it, but the stack comparison is disabled for those seven because the dead-slot clobber itself cannot be reproduced without inline assembly.

What was decided or recommended

The nine-word rewrite was accepted as verified with the eighth-word-plus gap stated in the lane report: it passes all nine words and every machine-checked comparison passes. The recommended fix is a worker extension that widens call-log entries beyond eight stack words, after which this function should be re-verified with no contract change. Other lanes with handlers forwarding more than eight words should state the same caveat until then.

How to reproduce it

Read any verified contract whose callee declares nine stack arguments and compare the recorded call log against the pushed words: the log holds the first eight only. The worker source states the eight-word cap where it emits the recorder stub.

The first run of the vector-scratch handler failed on the return register: the original reloads it from the context for the return-slot store, so it returns the slot pointer rather than the engine answer. Native handlers smuggle booleans through their own stack slot

Many script native handlers pass a boolean to the engine by overwriting the low byte of their own incoming argument word on the stack and pushing the whole word, so the engine receives the context address with its low byte replaced by the flag. Rewrites must reproduce both the pushed value and the clobbered stack word, and the checker observes both.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker.

What was found

Verified Six handlers in the batch coerce a script argument to boolean with a set-byte-on-stack pattern: compare the argument word against zero, set the low byte of the incoming argument slot to 0 or 1, then push that slot. The pushed boolean therefore carries the call context address in its high bytes. A seventh handler spills a float argument over the same slot. The checker's stack comparison covers incoming argument words, so a rewrite that only computes the pushed value still fails on the stack diff.

Verified Safe Rust cannot name its own incoming argument slot without the stack pointer, so the rewrite cannot reproduce the write unassisted. The worker derives the incoming stack address deterministically from the scratch stack base it already reports, and the driver passes that address into a dead word of the call context that the original never reads. Both sides start from identical state, the original ignores the extra word, and the pushed value is independently verified through the outgoing-call comparison.

What was decided or recommended

Other native lanes should expect the same set-byte pattern wherever a handler coerces a boolean, and reuse the incoming-address harness word rather than disabling the stack comparison. Two handlers that pass a pointer to their own stack frame to the engine were deferred instead, because excluding that pointer from the comparison would leave the marshalled data unverified.

How to reproduce it

Run any boolean-coercing native handler under the checker with the stack comparison on: the original shows one stack write the naive rewrite lacks. Resolve the worker's reported stack base plus its fixed offset to the incoming slot address, feed it to the rewrite as input, and confirm the stack and call comparisons both pass over one thousand trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first attempt failed most trials on the stack check with no hint of which word differed beyond the count; reading the worker source showed incoming argument words are compared and only the callee frame below them is excluded. A later batch run also died partway when its worker process was lost under machine load, so the driver now restarts the worker and retries instead of crashing.

Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker.

Rust reader: audio banks and their ADPCM streams

A pure-Rust reader now parses and decodes every audio file in the game — archives, bank and streamed containers, wave headers, IMA ADPCM to 16-bit PCM, and the versioned audio configs — and its output matches the reference decoder sample-exact on seventeen channels and streams spanning every container and codec variant. The last unknown block-header word turned out to be an ignorable signed drift marker, confirmed by byte-searching the reference output in the raw file.

What was asked

Write a clean, dependency-light Rust library for the game's PC audio containers: the audio archives and the bank or stream format inside them, the wave headers, and IMA ADPCM decoding written from scratch, validated sample by sample against vgmstream output. Also parse the versioned audio configuration files as far as their structure can be determined, and report bank and wave counts, sample rates and channel layouts.

What was found

  • Verified The game ships 45 audio archives holding 3,286 entries: 1,869 bank files containing 140,293 short streams, and 1,417 streamed files with 3,045 channels. Thirty sample rates appear, one channel layout reaches seven channels, and all of it parses and decodes with zero failures.
  • Verified Three codecs exist: IMA ADPCM for nearly everything, 16-bit PCM for radio music and some effects, and exactly one Ogg Vorbis stream, which the reader refuses cleanly as unsupported.
  • Verified The IMA step table matches printings except one entry, found by searching the executable for the table: using the printed value causes plus-or-minus-one drift in loud passages, while the stored value matches the reference decoder bit-exact.
  • Verified The block channel word once called unknown is a signed drift marker, nonzero in 52 PCM files only. Each channel's seek table stays continuous regardless, so linear playback ignores it — proved by an exact reference match on a file with nonzero markers.
  • Verified Three files defeat the reference decoder, not the reader: on short last blocks it reuses the first block's header size and skips a payload entry, and on one file with lopsided seeks it reads a fixed stride, bleeding one channel's bytes into the other and zeroing a channel from the third block on. Byte searches in the raw file prove both mechanics.
  • Inferred The per-channel trailers (a short header plus three bytes per data sector) carry seek or state data, but six candidate encodings were tested and rejected, so their contents stay unknown with zero effect on decoding.
  • Unknown What the game itself plays for the one file with oscillating block sizes; the reference output there (a channel dead for most of the file) is not plausible as authored audio.

Its verdicts and enclosing functions are void, though its suggested rejection rules remain sound hygiene.

  • Two self-inflicted bugs (a relocated address used as a literal, two swapped parameters) each cost one attempt; both were caught by the first mismatch detail.

What was asked

Bisecting this exposed a checker bug: the per-trial random fill for globals seeds its generator with the trial number directly, so consecutive trials produce near-identical values and global-driven branches go one way on nearly every trial. Mixing the seed first restored uniform fills and took deep-path coverage to 64 in 200 across every input kind.

None is known to have passed a wrong rewrite, but every verdict issued before the fixes will be re-run under the upgraded checker before it counts.

The inventory's real error rate is being measured separately; the alarming number was an artefact. The coordinator repeated the claim to the project owner before it was checked, which was a mistake.

Lanes sharing one build output folder overwrote each other's libraries when two crates had the same name, and fifty lanes building at once queued on one lock. The rewrite order: levels, clusters and what the checker can take today

Bottom-up rewrite order is computed: every function sits on one of 45 levels, level zero alone holds over fifteen thousand game functions, and just over half of all game functions are checkable with the checker as it stands today. Verified

What was asked

Work out the order in which the executable's functions should be rewritten, and how many the checker can verify today. That meant building the complete direct call graph from the Ghidra pairs plus a fresh instruction scan, condensing it into strongly connected components, assigning every function a bottom-up level, classifying every game function as checkable now, checkable after a named checker extension, or needing the running game, folding byte-identical duplicates, histogramming sizes, and packing the queue into batches of twenty to forty functions.

What was found

The union graph has about seventy-three thousand edges over some forty-five thousand functions. Verified The fresh scan independently re-found nearly ninety-eight percent of the usable Ghidra edges and added about fifteen thousand more, mostly from callers the Ghidra pass had not covered yet.

Condensation gives about forty-five thousand components, of which only thirty-five hold more than one function, and the longest dependency chain is forty-five levels deep. Verified The two large mutual recursion clusters hold about a hundred and about sixty functions each, mix several subsystems, and are confirmed by both edge sources, so they are real cycles that must be rewritten as units. Level zero holds over nineteen thousand functions in total, of which fifteen thousand are game code, so rewriting can start wide; the top eleven levels together hold only about a hundred functions.

Checkability splits as follows. Verified

CategoryFunctionsShare of game bytes
Checkable by the current checker as it is18,90517%

Unknown (zero-size entries, no code)540%

The byte shares matter more than the counts: the as-is half is mostly small leaf functions, while the extension bucket holds three quarters of all game bytes. Verified The three named extensions unlock the middle bucket in this order, each count marginal to the ones before it:

ExtensionWhat it addsFunctions unlockedCumulative checkable
Per-callee scripted answersa separate scripted answer per callee instead of one shared value9,06379%

The running-game bucket is almost entirely functions using processor-local storage or structured exception handling, plus a few dozen using operating system traps or timing instructions. Verified No game function reads its own code bytes or modifies itself, and none uses locked atomic instructions; atomicity goes through imported operating system functions instead. Verified

Two findings shape the schedule. First, about ten thousand game functions call into the still-encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so their callees can be stubbed but their calling conventions cannot be read yet. Verified Second, duplicate folding finds four hundred forty-five groups of byte-identical functions covering over five thousand functions, nearly all tiny template-like bodies, saving about four thousand seven hundred rewrites. Verified

Sizes are heavily skewed: three quarters of game functions are under one hundred fifty bytes but hold under a fifth of the bytes, while one hundred giants over four thousand bytes hold nearly a tenth. Verified The queue packs into one thousand one hundred eighty batches of twenty-nine to thirty-one functions each, grouped by subsystem and class and level-adjacent in the call graph. Verified

What was decided or recommended

  • Dispatch the rewrite queue in level order using the per-function level map, so callees exist before their callers; start with the wide, small level zero.

  • Treat each mutual recursion cluster as one rewrite unit rather than splitting it across lanes.

  • Build the three checker extensions in per-callee, indirect-call, custom-convention order, which reaches ninety-six percent checkable.

  • Fold duplicates before dispatching: each group needs one rewrite, not one per copy.

  • Plan contract authoring for the ten thousand functions calling encrypted callees around inference or a decrypted image, since conventions there cannot be read from bytes.

How to reproduce it

Take the function inventory, the Ghidra caller-callee pairs, the virtual table list, and the checker capability notes as inputs. Disassemble every function outside the encrypted range with capstone using the inventory boundaries, collect direct call targets and the instruction feature flags, and union the found edges with the Ghidra pairs. Run an iterative Tarjan pass for components, assign levels by longest path over the condensation, classify each game function against the checker rules, hash masked bytes for duplicates, and pack batches by subsystem, class, and level. The lane reran this pipeline end to end several times; the scripts and their JSON outputs sit together in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

The disassembler reports resolved absolute call targets rather than raw relative offsets, and the first scan double-added them, producing a hundred thousand bogus edges that agreed with Ghidra in only two cases. Verified Comparing five known edges by hand exposed it in minutes.

Jump tables live inline in the code section here, so the first code-read rule flagged over sixteen hundred innocent functions as self-inspecting. Restricting the rule to pure absolute reads cleared all of them. Verified

Two smaller traps: some mnemonic names are shared between string instructions and vector instructions and can only be told apart by operand shape, and the tool folds repeat and lock prefixes into the mnemonic text, which hid both string instructions and any locked atomics until the matcher was fixed. A renamed loop variable then shadowed the image base and broke a whole rescan; the per-function error field caught it immediately. The final surprise was genuine: there really are no locked atomic instructions anywhere in the scanned code. Verified

What was asked

Rewrite two randomly sampled very large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each function is roughly five hundred instructions with sixty or more outgoing calls.

What was found

Verified The first function is a message dispatcher: it parses an incoming message through a helper, then switches on the message id across nine arms, each validating and routing. It makes sixty direct calls plus six indirect ones, touches a dozen global words, and uses no real floating point.

Verified The second function is a copy-style constructor for a pooled world object: it stores a type tag, initializes about two hundred bytes of fields, and queries the source object through virtual calls, with real single-precision float math. Half of its sixty-eight calls are indirect, starting thirty-six instructions in.

Verified Three new checker gaps, each independently fatal for the dispatcher, proven by reading the checker worker source against the disassembly:

  • The fail path returns an uninitialized stack word. The worker fills the stack with an address-dependent pattern, so no faithful rewrite can reproduce the value.
  • The call log compares raw stack addresses. The function passes addresses of its own locals to callees from its first call, and any rewrite frame sits at different addresses.
  • Stubbed callees return one value and write nothing, but the parse helper's whole job is filling a struct through two pointers, so all nine dispatch arms are unreachable in testing. Running the real helper instead is impossible because it sits in the encrypted range.

Verified Two known gaps also proved decisive: indirect calls cannot be intercepted, so the constructor's virtual-call body would pass only vacuously through fault equivalence; and all stubbed sites share one scripted answer per trial.
