Both functions are deferred, not attempted blindly: a rewrite that cannot be checked would only produce a fake data point for the schedule estimate. What was asked

Rewrite three sampled game functions of 600 to 1,500 bytes in idiomatic Rust, prove each one behaves identically to the original with the project's differential checker over at least 1,000 trials including edge values, run one honesty test with a subtle planted bug, and record honest per-function timings including failures.

What was found

Verified The middle-sized function, a record-table refresh routine making eleven direct calls to two callees, was verified with two contracts totalling 1,300 trials and no failures. Its behaviour in words: for each of four slots it asks whether a record exists and either copies the sixteen-byte record into a global table row or zeroes the slot, runs three more conditional queries into a second table, then always copies one record out to the caller with the third word forced to zero. All float traffic is bitwise copies with no arithmetic.

Verified The honesty mutant, which stores the third word instead of clearing it, fails quickly through the heap comparison, exactly as designed.

Verified The largest function, a blend-weight and quaternion-blending routine of about 390 instructions with heavy vector float arithmetic, was deferred. Its stack-allocated scratch buffers are filled by callees whose scripted stand-ins have no memory effects, so both sides would read different garbage; its loop bounds come from unconstrained inputs that would hang trials; and one scripted answer per trial cannot serve its four callees.

Verified The smallest function, a probable animation-channel constructor, was deferred. It makes eight register-indirect calls, which the checker cannot intercept, and reads thread-local storage twice, which the checker cannot virtualise. Both are documented checker gaps with no quick fix.

What was confusing or went wrong

The functions were worked out of order: after recon showed only the table refresh was fully expressible in the checker, it went first so the lane would bank one verification instead of spending the hour on a likely deferral. Timings are recorded honestly regardless of order.

The first attempt failed only on the lane's own contract: one declared global range was twenty bytes short, and the checker's undeclared-write scan caught it on both sides before any rewrite bug could hide behind it. Widening the range fixed it with no rewrite change.

The shared scripted-answer limitation meant all four existence queries in one trial had to agree, so mixed present and absent patterns within a single trial went untested. Each slot's both paths are covered across trials and the slots are independent copies of the same code, which made this acceptable, but it is a real coverage hole worth closing with per-callee answers.

Four of six sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals over a thousand differential trials each; the other two turned out not to be leaves at all, which is itself a useful scheduling signal.

What was asked

Rewrite six randomly sampled small functions in idiomatic Rust, prove each one behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, and record honest per-function timings, including failures.

What was found

Verified Four true leaves passed every trial: a gated readiness flag combining a state word, two flag bits and two float threshold compares; a four-float field setter; an insert-if-absent pair table holding up to a thousand entries; and a conditional linked-list counter.

Verified Two samples were mislabelled as having no calls. One makes four register-indirect virtual calls in a search loop; the other chases a pointer chain from a global and ends in a computed tail jump. The checker can intercept only direct calls, and a faithful rewrite would trip its anti-cheat, so both were deferred with documented unblockers.

Verified A deliberately introduced one-bit mistake in the first rewrite was caught by the checker within a hundred trials.

What was decided or recommended

For scheduling, count roughly a third of nominally call-free samples as needing indirect-call support, since static call counts miss virtual calls. Three small driver extensions should be folded back into the checker: scripted stack values, scripted heap words, and scripted heap-pointer values for linked structures. Two worker features would unblock the deferred class: interception of register-indirect call sites, and a way to aim globals at checker-owned memory.

How to reproduce it

Each function has a JSON contract describing its calling convention, inputs and compared outputs, and a Rust export in the lane crate. The checker runs the original and the rewrite from identical state over a thousand generated inputs, including edge values, and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults. The pair-table case aims its object pointer below a small owned heap segment because the real struct is larger than the worker heap.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The linked-list counter failed its first run because the argument sense was read backwards from the branch order; the very first trial exposed it and a one-line fix passed. Rebuilding the rewrite library twice failed on a transient file lock that cleared by itself after half a minute; waiting briefly before rebuilding avoids it.

What was asked

Rewrite five assigned leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with at least one thousand random plus edge-case trials, record the time honestly including failures, and run one honesty test with a deliberately planted bug.

What was found

Verified All five rewrites matched their originals on every trial: a byte-string to UTF-16 expander, a small object reset, a float setter, an integer getter, and a random-range float generator with generator state.

Verified The native execution method from the harness lane works for differential checks once extended with heap prefills, so each trial starts from controlled random memory instead of a fixed pattern.

Verified The compiler's thiscall convention matches the originals exactly: the object pointer arrives in the expected register, extra arguments sit on the stack, and the callee cleans them up. This was confirmed by reading the compiled output of the rewrite crate itself.

Verified The honesty test worked: a rewrite copy with one stripped bit flag was caught on 991 of 1028 trials, with only the empty string and short all-ASCII inputs passing.

Inferred The random-range function draws from a multiply-add generator state and interpolates between its two bounds; its constant multiplier table entry equals exactly two to the minus twenty-third.

What was decided or recommended

The five rewrites are proposed for integration as written. Two comparison details are recommended for the checker lane: expect a leftover return-address word on the stack after callee-cleaning returns, and compare floating-point results through the 80-bit return register encoding rather than as text. Rebuilding the rewrite binary while trials execute it must be sequenced, never overlapped, because the operating system locks running programs.

How to reproduce it

From the lane scratch folder: build the harness fork and the rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows, then run one check script per function. Each script runs its trials with parallel workers, compares written memory byte for byte plus return values and stack discipline, and prints an agree count. The honesty test re-runs the first function's script in mutant mode.

The first check of the float setter failed on the check side, not the rewrite: the script expected the wrong stack-pointer advance and missed a constant leftover word the harness leaves behind. Reading the harness trampoline explained both, and the corrected check passed without touching the rewrite. A rebuild also failed once with an access-denied error because trial processes were still executing the old binary; sequencing builds after checks fixed it. Trial throughput was far below the harness lane's solo measurement because the shared host was heavily loaded.

Pilot lane 06: five functions rewritten and timed

Five small original functions were rewritten in Rust and each rewrite was compared against the original over more than a thousand trials: every trial agreed, and a deliberately planted bug was caught every time. The honest cost was about seven minutes per verified function, most of it spent running the comparisons rather than writing the code.

What was asked

Rewrite pilot functions 26 to 30 as clear Rust, prove each one behaves identically to the original with at least a thousand random plus edge-case trials, record how long each step takes, and run one honesty test showing the comparison actually catches mistakes.

What was found

Verified All five rewrites agree with the originals on every trial: 5,182 agreements out of 5,182 trials. The set covered an object field-copy routine, two small object initialisers, a table-indexed word store, and a bounded string comparison.

Verified The honesty test worked: a one-word typo planted in a copy of the first rewrite failed 200 out of 200 trials, each time at exactly the differing memory location.

Verified Total time was about 36 minutes for five verified functions, roughly seven minutes each. Understanding and writing took minutes; running the thousand-plus native comparison trials per function took most of the time.

Verified One pilot function reads a global data table, even though the pilot list described its entries as touching no global data. The leaf-selection filter has a gap for tables that live in zero-initialised memory, and a specimen has been handed to the coordinator.

Inferred The string comparison function looks like a statically linked C library routine rather than game-specific code, based on its structure and behaviour. Its identity is unconfirmed but its behaviour is fully covered by the trials.

Function Trials Attempts Outcome
Field copy 1037 3 verified
Header stamp 1028 2 verified
String compare 1090 1 verified

What was decided or recommended

  • Comparisons should check the full final memory state, not just the list of reported writes, because writing a value that is already there is invisible to write-listing.
  • The checker must compare relocatable pointer constants modulo the image load offset rather than raw, or every such function will mismatch.
  • The leaf-selection filter should treat reads into zero-initialised global memory as global-data reads.
  • Simple functions budget at about seven minutes each with current single-shot tooling; a persistent comparison worker would shrink checking to seconds.

How to reproduce it

Build the 32-bit harness and the rewrite crate from the lane scratch folder, then run the five check scripts, each of which drives the original function natively and the Rust rewrite over the same seeded random and edge-case inputs and compares return values and touched memory bytes exactly. The honesty test rebuilds the crate with a one-word error and reruns a subset of trials. No game process is launched at any point.

What was confusing or went wrong

Every failed attempt was a bug in the test driver, not in a rewrite, and each one taught something real: the harness shows its own return address on the stack for one calling convention, pointer constants must be normalised before comparing, a mis-shaped test input silently corrupted a table, and huge table values do not always crash because 32-bit address arithmetic wraps around. One early file read also misidentified the contents of the global table by reading past the end of its section; checking section sizes corrected it. These fixes are all in the final scripts.

Pilot lane 03: five functions rewritten and timed

Four of five small game functions were rewritten in Rust and proved identical to the originals over about a thousand trials each, in forty minutes of work; the fifth was deferred over a genuine floating point corner with the cause fully characterised and a fix scoped.

What was asked

The lane was given five leaf functions from the pilot list and asked to rewrite each in Rust, prove identical behaviour against the original with at least a thousand random plus edge-case trials, record honest per-function timings for the project schedule estimate, and run one honesty test showing the comparison catches a deliberate mistake.

What was found

Verified Four rewrites pass full differential comparison: a clamped table-slot address function, a flag-byte predicate, a byte conversion, and a five-path linked-record select, each agreeing on every trial.

FunctionWhat it doesTrialsOutcome
113-element vector transform1052deferred: NaN payload order
12clamped slot address1019verified
13flag byte predicate1063verified
14byte conversion (exact identity)1024verified, exhaustive
15linked-record select1050verified

Verified The vector transform writes a fourth output word from uninitialized stack data: nothing stores to the slot it loads, the value never changes across input-varying trials, and it equals the test harness's own stack fill pattern at that slot. It is not a function of the inputs and was excluded from comparison.

Verified The deferred function is bit-exact except when two different NaN payloads meet in one accumulation row. Probing showed single-NaN cases always agree and only payload conflicts diverge; the mechanism is operand-order canonicalization of floating point addition by the toolchain, which changes which NaN payload survives. The fix is pinned instruction order, left for a follow-up.

Verified The honesty test mutated a clamp constant by one in a copy of the slot-address rewrite; exactly one trial in 1019 failed, the boundary input, confirming single-trial sensitivity.

Verified Two rewrite bugs were caught by the machine check and fixed: a signed-versus-unsigned comparison, and a pair of swapped branches. Both fixes passed on the first retry.

What was decided or recommended

  • The uninitialized fourth output word is excluded from that function's contract; no caller can depend on it.
  • NaN payload conflicts need a project policy: they are the only float class where portable Rust codegen observably differs from the original, and the observed quieting behaviour comes from emulation, so matching it needs a deliberate decision.
  • Input domains belong in the queue record next to each verdict, since one function's wildest inputs read wild memory in the original and are untestable by construction.
  • Per-lane test binaries need unique names: the shared build cache silently replaced one lane's binary with another's.

How to reproduce it

Each rewrite is an exported Rust function with the original calling convention in the lane's scratch crate, with a batch test binary beside it. Drivers run the original through the native execution helper with crafted stack and register inputs, run the same cases through the Rust binary, and compare integers exactly, floats bit-exactly, and pointers by expected relocated address. Random seeds, trial counts, and per-function timings are recorded in the pilot results file in the same folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full test run faulted on every trial because functions with a frame pointer read their stack arguments one word off from frameless ones; the helper's fault record pointed at the exact store and the layout was fixed in minutes. A shared-cache binary collision, a transient link lock, and a publishing-tool timestamp quirk each cost a few minutes and are documented as tool traps. The largest surprise was the NaN finding itself: full-random bit patterns inject signaling NaNs no float literal can express, and without them the operand-order issue would have stayed hidden.

Pilot lane 01: five functions rewritten and timed

Five small original game functions were rewritten in Rust and each rewrite was shown to behave identically to its original over at least a thousand differential trials, with honest per-function timings recorded for the schedule estimate. Verified All five passed; the comparison caught one genuine rewrite bug, one driver bug, and a deliberately planted mutant.

What was asked

Rewrite the first five pilot leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original by native execution comparison, and record exactly how long each one takes, including failures. The schedule estimate will be built from these timings.

What was found

Verified All five rewrites agree with their originals on every trial: 5,100 matching trials in total plus 13 fault-parity trials where both sides fault identically on wild inputs.

FunctionWhat it doesTrials agreedAttempts

Verified The comparison is strict: return values, every written word, stack pointer movement, untouched registers, and exact stack artifacts are all asserted per trial. The two simplest functions return relocated addresses, so their rewrites take the load base as an explicit parameter rather than baking in an address.

Verified The table-append function re-reads its row count before every store, which matters when a wraparound count makes an early store land on the count slot itself. The first rewrite read the count once and failed 28 trials; the fixed rewrite matches on all of them including dedicated aliasing trials.

Verified The table-copy function reads from uninitialised-image memory that is zero in a fresh process, so each trial sets the entry under test to a known value first. Its byte shuffle provably reproduces its input for every possible word, and the rewrite expresses the net copy directly.

Verified A deliberately planted one-bit mistake in a copy of the first rewrite was caught on all 1010 honesty-test trials.

Verified Lane time was about 52 minutes for five verified functions, roughly 10 minutes per function including write-up, or about 8 minutes excluding it. The comparison runs were the largest cost at 18 minutes; single-shot trials cost a fraction of a second each under load.

What was decided or recommended

  • Rewrites that need a game address take it as an explicit parameter (load base or table pointer) instead of baking in a value. This worked for three of the five functions and keeps the Rust portable.
  • Wraparound counts and indices stay in every future corpus: the one genuine bug this lane found only triggers on a wraparound input.
  • The checker should record memory diffs on faults too, so faults after partial writes become comparable; this lane had to exclude that case and cover the same code path with mapped trials instead.
  • A persistent checker worker that maps the image once would cut the largest time cost, the per-trial process setup, to nearly nothing.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's extended 32-bit harness and the rewrites crate for the 32-bit Windows target, then run the comparison driver, which executes both sides over edge values plus a thousand seeded-random trials per function and asserts identical observations. A separate script confirms the built library exports all five symbols with the expected callee stack cleanup. All scripts, seeds, and expected trial counts are recorded with the lane's scratch outputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified A first probe of the relocation table double-added the page base and wrongly concluded the absolute addresses were unrelocated. The running functions contradicted it immediately, and a corrected probe settled every site. Lesson kept: a cheap runtime check beats re-reading library docs.

Verified A first dump of the copied table read past the end of the file-backed data and returned bytes belonging to a later section. The table actually lives in zero-filled memory, which changed the test design: every trial now sets the entry under test explicitly.

Verified One driver assertion wrongly claimed a register holds the result at return; the register actually carries the result mid-function but is saved and restored. It failed all 1018 trials while the rewrite matched on every stored word, which made the driver bug obvious.

Merging the class layouts into one set of Rust types

All class layouts recovered so far are now one consistent set: about thirty eight hundred classes merged from the family lanes, the script native lanes, the RTTI hierarchy and the public headers, with ten thousand resolved conflicts, thirteen hundred open ones, and a draft Rust crate of three hundred forty layout structs that builds for both thirty two and sixty four bit targets.

What was asked

Combine every recovered class layout into a single set of structure definitions, resolving conflicts explicitly, and generate Rust types with compile time size and offset checks.

What was found

Verified every expected source file was present: all fifteen family layouts, all twenty two native field lists, the RTTI hierarchy and the public header names. Nothing is waiting on a missing lane.

Verified the merged set holds about thirty eight hundred classes and about eleven thousand fields after deduplication, with roughly three thousand high confidence fields and a similar number at medium confidence. About three thousand classes now carry base class links, mostly from RTTI.

Verified the draft crate holds three hundred forty structs covering about fifty six hundred fields, with explicit padding for unknown ranges and pointer fields that stay four bytes wide on sixty four bit hosts. It builds cleanly for both targets, and a deliberately corrupted assertion was shown to fail the build, so the checks are live.

Verified the largest gaps: the player object has only a handful of fields, the top level game and world objects have no records at all, physics instances are thin, and vehicle layouts are rich but about half low confidence.

What was decided or recommended

  • Inherited fields are recorded once, on the owning class. A first rule that moved fields by size comparison was tried and rejected because it pulled derived only members into their bases; the shipped rule moves a field only when two independent child subtrees agree on it, or drops it as a duplicate with its evidence transferred to the owner.
  • Sizes from the lanes are lower bounds, so each Rust struct asserts its size rounded up to four byte alignment and is documented as a prefix of the true layout.
  • About seventy observations turned out to be global variables rather than struct fields and were split into a separate globals file for a later lane.
  • Recommended next analysis: allocator and pool stride work for true sizes, a dedicated pass for the game and world objects, and targeted review of the twenty high confidence kind conflicts listed in the conflicts file.

How to reproduce it

Run the merge script in the lane scratch folder to regenerate the merged structures, conflicts, globals and moves files, then the generator script for the crate, then build the crate for both the thirty two bit and sixty four bit Windows targets. The merge log records each decision class with counts.

What was confusing or went wrong

Each lane used its own schema for sizes, bases and fields, including one off wrappers and word widths such as dword and vec3, so the first merge attempt miscounted several hundred fields until every spelling was normalised. Absolute memory addresses disguised as field offsets inflated some layouts to tens of megabytes before the globals split caught them. The first base attribution rule looked principled but was circular, because base sizes already contained misattributed bytes; spotting train only and ped only members landing in their bases is what exposed it. The Rust generator initially produced over a thousand assertion failures from implicit padding before alignment aware typing fixed them.

Replacement loader built and tested without the game

The loader that will live inside the running game and swap original functions for Rust rewrites is built, and every part of it passes its tests without the game ever launching. The proxy library forwards the full set of system library exports, the hook engine replaces functions behind individual on/off switches, and a watched control file drives toggling, bulk operations and bisecting. What remains is running it against the real game, which only the owner can do.

What was asked

Build the 32-bit replacement loader as Rust crates: a proxy library that stands in for a system library the game already loads, a hook engine written from scratch (function-start hooks with trampolines, virtual table slot replacement, import table slot replacement), a registry of replacements with run-time switches driven by a watched control file, logging with timestamps, a crash handler recording which replacements were active, and a safe mode. Prove it all with unit tests that run without the game, including a small 32-bit test program with several kinds of functions hooked under concurrent calls from several threads.

What was found

Verified The proxy library forwards every export of the system library it stands in for, with names and ordinals matching exactly, and the forwarding table is generated from the real library at build time rather than hand-written. The library itself imports only core system libraries, so it cannot load itself in a loop.

Verified The hook engine handles the calling conventions the game uses, including class methods, through small generated adapter stubs. Hooks install, call through to the original, toggle on and off, and remove cleanly, including while four threads call the hooked function and the main thread toggles a hundred times. Creating a hook on an unsuitable target (too short, undecodable, unreadable, out of range) returns a clean error and touches nothing.

Verified The readiness gate works as designed: in the test program, which has no game code in it, the loader waits, times out, stays fully disabled, and logs the whole sequence. The log from that run shows startup, the readiness checks, the timeout, and a clean shutdown with all hooks off.

Check groupChecksResult
Decoder and planner unit tests12all pass

Inferred The design is ready for live testing against the game, starting with the proxy alone and adding one trivial hook at a time.

Unknown Whether the game's start-up protection objects to an extra module in the process or to patched code. Nothing in the static analysis answers this; it is the first thing live testing must establish.

What was decided or recommended

  • Exports for the proxy are declared through the linker's directive section, the same mechanism the C compiler uses. A separate definition file and command-line export flags were tried and cannot resolve the generated symbols; this is documented in the build script so nobody rediscovers it.
  • No third-party hook library is used. The engine is hand-written, which keeps the dependency list empty and the proxy's own imports limited to core system libraries.
  • The hook table ships empty. No game target is registered until its live address and expected bytes are confirmed with the game running.
  • Live testing follows a fixed eight-step order: proxy alone, coexistence with the community loader, timing calibration, first trivial hook, toggle mechanics, debugger etiquette, protection reaction, and a memory snapshot diff. Each step stops at the first surprise.

How to reproduce it

Build the workspace for the 32-bit Windows target and run the host unit tests, then run the 32-bit test program with the path to the freshly built proxy library as its argument. The program prints one line per check and a final pass and fail count with a matching exit code. Comparing the proxy library's export table against the system library's export table confirms the forwarding is complete. All commands and the eight live-test steps are written up in the loader manual kept with the lane's work.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • The proxy refused to link for a long time: the linker reported every generated stub as unresolved even though the symbols were provably present in the object files. A minimal probe showed even plain Rust symbols failed the same way, which pointed at the export mechanism rather than the code. Switching to directive-section exports fixed it on the first try.
  • The first version of the class-method adapter passed the wrong second argument to the replacement function; a live capture showed it receiving a code address instead of the test value. The stub was rewritten to rebuild the argument frame properly, and the test now asserts the values end to end.
  • A caller-side adapter turned out to be callee-pops, so calling it with the wrong prototype corrupted the stack silently and crashed later. The prototypes were fixed and a register-preservation check was added that would catch any repeat.
  • One confusing hour came from a self-inflicted cause: a probe build script left in a non-empty state made cached linker flags look like a build-tool bug. Reading the file on disk settled it immediately.

Pilot lane 10: five functions rewritten and timed

Three of five pilot functions were rewritten in Rust and proved bit-identical to the originals over about a thousand native trials each; the other two were deferred with a concrete blocker, and the pilot surfaced a gap in the leaf-selection filter. Verified

What was asked

What was found

The five functions and their outcomes:

FunctionWhat it doesOutcome
Bucket mappermaps a float sample to one of eight bucketsverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree
Float trackerupdates a timestamped smoothing state with init, predict and clamp pathsverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree on the second attempt
Slot store and slot copywrite through a table-selected offset into an objectdeferred: the table is runtime-initialised global data
Small clearerzeroes twelve bytes and returns the objectverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree

Verified The deferred pair reads its offset table from writable global data whose file image is unrelated text, so the game must fill the table in at run time. A rewrite can only take that table as a parameter until runtime bytes exist, and running the original against file bytes would only exercise wild offsets. The leaf-selection filter missed these because it only screens plain absolute reads, not indexed ones; the candidate pool should be re-screened.

Verified Two subtleties needed exact handling: the bucket mapper's float-to-integer step returns a special indefinite value for out-of-range inputs where Rust saturates, and the tracker's comparisons use ordered float semantics that differ from min and max on NaN. Both are covered by targeted edge trials plus uniform random bit patterns.

Verified The honesty test confirmed the comparison catches a plausible mistake: a mutant that trusted Rust's saturating float-to-integer cast failed 174 of 1020 identical trials.

What was decided or recommended

  • Ship the three verified rewrites; keep the two table-dependent rewrites parameterised over the table and marked unverified until runtime bytes or a table-patching runner exist.
  • Re-screen the leaf pool for indexed absolute reads of writable data before assigning more pilot functions.
  • Budget pilot comparisons at a few trials per second per machine with single-shot runners; batching would change this substantially.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's twin crate for 32-bit x86, then run its parallel driver: it feeds identical edge and random inputs to the original through the native runner and to the Rust twin, and compares return values bit-exactly, floating-point results bit-exactly, written memory byte-exactly, and the stack pointer after return. Machine records of every trial batch are kept with the lane's data files.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three unaligned-pointer trials for the small clearer first appeared to fail, but the original was correct: a twelve-byte zero at an unaligned address spans four partial double-words, and the driver's comparison had assumed aligned writes. The driver was fixed to compare byte-exact images and the trials re-run. The tracker's first attempt missed ten trials because the original's floating-point return quiets signalling NaNs while the rewrite passed them through; the rewrite now quiets at return and keeps raw bits in the store. The candidate record for the bucket mapper also lists a register input that its own code zeroes before reading; the rewrite treats it as clobbered, not input.

Native handlers ATTACH_PED_TO_CAR to CLEAR_ROOM_FOR_OBJECT: what they reveal

All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled and matched against the public native database and the decompiled mission scripts. Nearly every handler is a thin wrapper that unpacks script arguments and calls one engine function, and the engine functions resolve script handles through a single shared pool lookup. Four public param counts are wrong, one documented return value never reaches scripts, and the shared pool lookup sits in the encrypted part of the executable so it could only be observed, not read.

What was asked

Recover engine names and meanings from a batch of 140 script native handlers, propose names for the functions each handler calls, record object fields the handlers touch, and note stubs, shared handlers and encrypted code.

What was found

Verified Every handler receives one pointer to a call context. Slot zero of that context points at the return-value slot and the third slot points at the argument array. No handler in this batch reads anything else from the context, and none writes back into the argument array. Twenty-five handlers return a value; the rest are void at the script level.

Verified Most handlers share one shape: read the arguments, call a single engine function, store the result if there is one. Ten handlers are a bare jump to the engine function, three are jump chains ending in a few inline instructions that flip a global flag, and two attach handlers pass through a shared second-stage unpacker. The breakpoint native is a lone trap instruction and is never called by shipped scripts.

Verified Forty-three engine functions resolve script handles through one shared lookup routine, always with the pool pointer in the same register and the handle on the stack. The same routine serves the ped, vehicle and object pools. It lives in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so its internals stay unknown; only its call pattern is established.

Verified The observed argument counts agree with the public database for all but four natives. The travel-distance native reads six arguments, not seven; the mission-entity check reads three, not zero; the ceiling function reads one, not two; and the event-precedence clear reads two, not zero. The decompiled scripts agree with the binary in each case.

Verified The camera-sequence progress handler calls its engine function but never stores the result, so whatever the engine computes never reaches scripts. No shipped script calls that native. Separately, three decision-maker natives share one identical handler, and the two cell-camera visibility natives share one engine function.

Inferred Field meanings proposed from single-purpose wrappers include the two car colour bytes, the last-damage bone and last-weapon-damage fields (the latter at the same offset on peds, vehicles and objects, so it sits on a shared base class), ped flag words for blocked animations and cover behaviour, per-bit player damage flags, and a stat-id range that decides which stats can carry a string.

What was decided or recommended

Engine wrapper functions are proposed for naming after their native, with the shared pool lookup, the second-stage unpackers and the pool and manager globals proposed as cross-lane shared names. The four wrong public param counts and the dropped progress return should be fed back to the native documentation. The encrypted pool lookup needs the decrypted executable before anyone can go further.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone, follow jumps to the end of each chain, record argument-array reads, direct calls and return-slot writes, and compare the highest argument index against the public param counts. Then disassemble one level down from each engine function and record which pool or manager global it loads before resolving handles. The per-native records, proposed names and proposed fields ship as JSON alongside the lane report.

What was confusing or went wrong

The disassembler prints small numbers without a base prefix, so an early version of the analysis script misread offsets and found no arguments at all until the parser was fixed. A register-tracking bug then tagged the wrong values until stack loads were excluded from propagation. The shared pool lookup initially decoded to two plausible instructions before its bytes were recognised as ciphertext, and those two phantom instructions were thrown out. A script-usage scan over the decompiled missions took far longer than planned because of per-native regex passes.

Verified Throughput is a few milliseconds per trial for simple functions, rising to around a tenth of a second when every writable data section is scanned for undeclared writes. The full twenty-function proof runs in a few minutes. The host slows noticeably under sustained load, so every verdict records its own timing.

What was decided or recommended

The verdict file format matches what the work-queue acceptance tool expects, and all twenty verdicts pass its validator. Recommended next steps: per-callee scripted answers for functions calling several routines, interception of register-indirect calls, a faster undeclared-write scan, and one worker process per processor core.

What was found

  • Verified The call context layout: handlers receive one pointer, and the script argument array hangs off it at a fixed offset, one 32-bit slot per argument. Two neighbouring slots are never touched by any handler in this batch, and since no native here returns a value, the return slot stays unknown.
  • Verified 135 of the 138 readable handlers call exactly one engine function. Two day-shift natives share a five-call tail, and one pool-physics native branches on its argument. Two natives share an unreadable stub handler with 44 other debug and stripped natives.
  • Verified Three argument marshalling idioms: integers pushed directly, booleans normalised through a compare and set instruction that overwrites the saved context pointer on the stack, floats moved through vector registers into reserved stack slots.
  • Verified No handler resolves a script handle itself. Handle to pointer lookup always happens one level down inside the engine function, through a shared pool lookup reached with the pool in one register and the handle on the stack, seen at vehicle and ped call sites.
  • Verified The public documentation is wrong about SET_TIME_ONE_DAY_BACK: it claims the native does nothing, but the handler holds a complete day-decrement path with month rollover and weekday update, and the shipped main script calls it.
  • Verified The public database lacks signatures for seven natives; handler evidence fixes their argument counts, including two for the vehicle alarm duration and four or five for the trip-skip family. Script call sites confirm the alarm duration is passed in milliseconds.

What was decided or recommended

  • Inferred 139 engine functions proposed for naming, most with high confidence since each maps one to one onto a documented native; area prefixes such as vehicle or ped come from code region and documented meaning.
  • Inferred Nine structure fields proposed, strongest the vehicle alarm time and the clock date globals; the rest are medium or low confidence single-sighting proposals.
  • Inferred Later lanes should expect handler, setter, then pool lookup, not handler straight to lookup, and a lane with value-returning natives still needs to pin down the return slot.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each listed handler with Capstone from the executable, tag the context pointer and argument array with a small abstract interpreter, compare argument counts against the public native database, and grep the public decompiled mission scripts for call sites. Targeted disassembly of a dozen engine callees confirms the pool lookup pattern and the clock arithmetic. The encrypted prefix of the code section is never disassembled.

What was confusing or went wrong

The boolean idiom initially looked like handlers passing their own context pointer to the engine; it is actually a normalised zero or one written over the saved pointer slot. One door-state native shows both four and six argument call sites in the decompiled scripts while the handler reads six, so its signature either grew between builds or the decompiler merged two same-named natives. Ten sampled natives are never called in the shipped scripts at all.

Rust reader: texture dictionaries (WTD)

Every loose texture dictionary in the game now parses with a new pure Rust reader, and every texture in them decodes to plain pixels: 205 files, 2,286 textures, zero parse failures.

What was asked

Write a clean Rust reader for the texture dictionary format: the dictionary structure, the texture records, decoding of every pixel format found in the game to RGBA8, and an in-memory DDS export for inspection in tests. Report the format and size distribution across every reachable dictionary.

What was found

Verified All 205 loose dictionaries share one container design: a small header naming the resource type, then a single compressed payload that expands into a structures segment and a pixel-data segment. Each dictionary holds a hash table and a pointer list over texture records carrying name, dimensions, mip count, format code, stride and a data pointer.

Verified Exactly five pixel formats appear, with this distribution:

FormatTextures
DXT51389
DXT1862
DXT318
A8R8G8B8 uncompressed16
L8 uncompressed1

Verified Three layout rules were pinned down that public documentation did not state: stride times height always equals the top mip level size including compressed formats, the name hash is computed over the short title rather than the stored name, and every dimension is a multiple of four though many are not powers of two. Most textures carry a single mip level; the deepest has eight. One dictionary is empty.

Verified The new decoders were cross-checked against an independent image decoder on real textures: four of five formats match byte for byte, and the fifth differs only by one brightness step in one colour channel on some texels, a known rounding-convention difference.

What was decided or recommended

The crate keeps unknown fields as raw values rather than guessing meanings, and sizes mip data with block rounding, which is the principled rule even though shipped files never expose the difference. Dictionaries inside encrypted archives stay out of reach until the archive work lands; the next texture step is to run this reader over those once extraction exists, since map and vehicle textures will extend the distribution. Cube and volume textures were not observed and stay unsupported until one is found.

How to reproduce it

Build the crate and run its unit tests, which use only hand-built byte vectors. With the game directory in an environment variable, the integration test parses every loose dictionary, checks the stride and hash rules, decodes the top mip level of each texture and builds a DDS in memory; it reports exact counts and fails on any error. A worked example program prints a one-file summary to standard output.

What was confusing or went wrong

The public wiki page for this format is a stub with no layout, so the field order came from reading an open-source parser, then confirming every field against real files. A first guess at the hash input matched nothing until the short-title form was tried. Two words first read as padding turned out to be capacity counts. One calibration script reused a single output file without an overwrite flag and silently re-read stale bytes, briefly suggesting large decoder differences that vanished on re-run. Every format lane named its example program the same thing, so a test run silently executed another lane's binary until the example was renamed.

The script interpreter, mapped end to end

The whole script virtual machine interpreter is now mapped: every opcode handler, the thread layout, the functions around it, and the first behavioural test of original engine code on this project, which ran a tiny synthetic program and left the right answer on the script stack.

What was asked

Map the script virtual machine interpreter precisely: find its opcode dispatch, enumerate every opcode with its stack effect and operand bytes, describe the thread context as the interpreter uses it, identify the surrounding functions, and if possible run the original interpreter in isolation on a synthetic program.

What was found

  • Verified The interpreter is a single function that fetches one opcode byte and dispatches through a jump table of 78 entries, one per named opcode.
  • Verified High byte values are not looked up: each pushes its own value minus a constant, giving small integers directly. Only two byte values are invalid and abort the thread.
  • Verified All 78 handlers were read individually. Their behaviour matches the public instruction names in every case, with five quirks a rewrite must copy, including division by zero leaving the dividend in place and a supposedly unsigned push that sign-extends.
  • Verified Native calls are bound when a script loads, not looked up while it runs: the loader overwrites each native hash in the code with the handler address, writing zero for unknown hashes, and the interpreter simply calls whatever address it finds.
  • Verified The thread layout derived from the handlers agrees with the layout published by the open-source script debugger on every field, with no disagreements, including the five thread states and the order of the five virtual functions.
  • Verified Eighty-two related functions were identified with roles, including the per-frame scheduler, thread reset, kill and spawn, the program and native tables, the loader, the native binder, and the game-specific thread overrides.
  • Verified The original interpreter bytes executed a synthetic program (push two numbers, add) and produced the correct stack, plus both error paths. The per-instruction budget, the saved instruction pointer and the restored globals all behaved as the static analysis predicted.
FactValueWhat it means

Push-immediate byte values176each pushes a small integer with no operand bytes
Invalid byte values2both abort the thread with the same error
Related functions identified82scheduler, lifecycle, tables, loader and overrides
Behavioural tests passed3arithmetic plus both error paths on real interpreter bytes

What was decided or recommended

A Rust rewrite should implement the loader-time native binder rather than any run-time hash lookup, reproduce the five arithmetic quirks exactly, and take the text-formatting helper and the log sink as engine-provided hooks, since both live in the encrypted part of the executable and cannot be studied statically. The three behavioural tests are the seed vectors for the rewrite's test suite. Two small corrections for earlier survey notes: the script file extension string does appear in the executable, and opcode zero is invalid rather than a no-op.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the interpreter function with a standard x86 disassembler and follow the single computed jump to the opcode table; each entry leads to one handler whose stack traffic can be read directly. The instruction-length helper next to it confirms every operand size independently. The behavioural test maps the interpreter's code pages into a scratch process with relocation fixups, builds a synthetic thread, program and bytecode program on a scratch heap, calls the interpreter entry point with a small instruction budget, and reads back the thread state and stack words.

What was confusing or went wrong

The Python emulator crashes on this machine even for two trivial instructions, so the planned unicorn demo was rebuilt as a small native runner instead, which took several iterations of mapping and relocation work. The native call path looked impossible at first: the handler calls the operand with no lookup in sight, until the loader's binding pass explained that the operand is already a handler address by run time. A block of composer-data code just past the interpreter was briefly mistaken for script thread management until its virtual table gave it away.

What was found

Verified The family is flat: one root with mostly direct children, plus small nests for movement, combat subtasks, scenarios, vehicle subtasks, condition waits and wandering. Tables hold 21 to 26 slots.

Verified Slot zero is the scalar deleting destructor in nearly every class: destroy the object, then return it to a pool when a flag is set. About one in seven classes inlines the pool arithmetic; the rest call a shared pool helper.

Verified Over 460 constructor and destructor functions were identified by the order of base calls versus vtable stores. Optimizer output complicated this: many constructors pass the object pointer in registers other than the usual one, and some destructors are fully inlined into their deleting wrappers.

Verified About a third of all vtable slots point into the encrypted range, but these are only a few dozen shared stubs, not class-specific code. Every overriding function examined is readable. The one family-critical encrypted dependency is the shared pool-free helper used by task destruction.

Inferred The root class adds one pointer-sized field past its base, most likely the subtask pointer. One virtual slot returns a per-class constant in the few classes that reduce it to a stub, which reads like a task-type identifier.

Unknown Most virtual slot meanings beyond the destructor, exact object sizes for the majority of classes (current figures are lower bounds; pool element sizes would settle them), and one odd unaligned secondary-table entry.

How to reproduce it

Scan the readable code for each class vtable address as an immediate, keeping only hits backed by a relocation entry; attribute each hit to its function via exported function bounds; disassemble with capstone; classify constructors versus destructors by whether the base call precedes the vtable store; confirm deleting destructors by the destroy, flag-test, pool-free shape; collect field offsets from object-pointer accesses in each class's own methods. Scripts and JSON data sit with the lane's scratch outputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first scan found almost nothing because of a relocation bug that added the image base twice; fixing it raised the hit count from 4 to over 500. A first classifier mistook branching constructors for deleting destructors until a real deleting destructor was read. The longest wrong turn was misreading deleting destructors as clone methods for about an hour; the call target is the plain destructor and the order is destroy-then-free, which settled it.

Ninety-four script-native handlers were disassembled and every one is now understood: most are thin wrappers that turn script handles into engine object pointers through shared pool lookups, while a few inline helpers, tail jumps and shared particle-effect unpackers cover the rest. What was asked

Disassemble the handlers of the ninety-four natives from TASK_TIRED to WRITE_LOBBY_PREFERENCE, recover the call-context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions and object fields they touch, with confidence levels.

What was found

Verified Every handler receives a single context pointer holding a return-slot pointer and an argument-array pointer; no handler checks an argument count. Handlers fall into five shapes: thin wrappers, tail jumps into context-taking engine functions, fully inline helpers, shared particle-effect unpackers, and one handler in the encrypted range that was skipped.

TimingThe wait natives accumulate either warped frame time, a fixed sixty-hertz step, or warped time that pauses with the game; the unwarped step is a hard-coded constant.

What was decided or recommended

Proposed names were recorded for over eighty engine functions and twenty object fields with per-native evidence, so later lanes can confirm or correct them against decrypted code. The pool lookup, task allocator, particle spawn core and several network implementations sit in the encrypted first megabyte and need the decrypted view; the teleport native's fifth parameter cannot be resolved from shipped scripts and needs a live test.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone using section-aware address mapping, stopping at returns and unconditional jumps while keeping code reachable from forward branches; dump the first hundred or so instructions of each direct callee; read argument indices, boolean normalisation, by-value vector construction and return-slot writes from the instruction stream; and cross-check parameter lists against the public native database and call sites in the public decompiled mission scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first extraction pass stopped at the first return instruction, which silently dropped code after conditional branches in the wait natives and bled neighbouring handlers into tail-jump stubs. Fixing the disassembler to respect branch targets and unconditional jumps changed several call attributions. Argument-index tracking also needed two iterations before register reuse stopped misclassifying reads. Both traps are worth knowing for the remaining native batches.

What was asked

Disassemble the handler behind each of the 140 natives from SET_CAR_PROOFS to SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_STANDING_STYLE, work out the call context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions called and meanings for the object fields touched, using the public native documentation and the public decompiled mission scripts as the source of meaning.

What was found

Verified The call context carries a pointer to the argument array eight bytes in; every handler in the batch reads all of its arguments through it. Boolean arguments are normalised to zero or one and floats travel through vector registers, both with recognisable instruction idioms.

Verified Of 137 distinct handlers, 136 were disassembled and each calls exactly one engine function, all different. Four natives share one handler that sits in the encrypted part of the executable and was skipped.

Verified One shared lookup routine resolves script handles to object pointers for 114 of the 136 engine functions, taking a pool pointer plus a handle. The pool used splits exactly by native family: character natives use one pool, vehicle natives another. Two natives that take two handles look up twice, including one that consults both pools, which confirms the split.

Verified Character behaviour flags live in a run of flag words on the character object, with 47 single-bit assignments mapped to named natives and no two natives sharing a bit. Damage immunity flags sit at the same field with identical bits on both characters and vehicles, so that field belongs to a shared base class, with two relationship-based damage modes that actively clear each other.

Verified The nine decision-maker attribute setters share one code shape: convert the handle to an index, range-check it against 54 slots, lazily create a manager object, then write one field. Six attributes pack as bit ranges into one word and three are single bytes or bits, all mapped.

Verified All six coordinate setters route to one teleport function, differing only in flag constants. The money native sends its amount to a helper and sets only a flag bit inline. Health setting clamps to a maximum and consults the streaming system rather than storing blindly.

About one native in seven is never called by the shipped mission scripts, mostly multiplayer or edge-case natives, but all still have real engine bodies.

Three analysis bugs each silently corrupted a whole pass before they were caught: disassembly bled through padding bytes into neighbouring functions because inventoried sizes overestimate, inflating one five-instruction body to 185 instructions with ten foreign calls; every handler's argument count came out one too high because the context-pointer load looks exactly like an argument read; and float stores to memory were first classified as reads, hiding a health write. Each was fixed by re-reading the bytes more carefully, and the fixes are recorded so the next lane does not repeat them. The core entity classes are also absent from the project's RTTI table, so object classes are named by pool rather than by verified class name.

No two natives in this batch share a readable handler.

Linear disassembly initially ran past tail jumps into neighbouring functions and mis-attributed their calls; bounding each decode at the first return, tail jump or padding fixed it. Synthetic relocation round-trip Pass, four load shifts including zero and overflow

Estimated full game capture time About five seconds for twenty-six megabytes

Inferred The live capture is expected to take about five seconds, from timings measured on the file's own bytes and on timed memory reads. Unknown Whether the running game carries any run-time patches outside the encrypted range, and which helper libraries are loaded while it idles at the menu. Both questions are answered the moment the tool runs against the real game.

What was decided or recommended

  • A plain script on the project's existing Python setup was chosen over a compiled tool, because the cross-bitness memory reads it needs are supported by design and the self-test proves them on this machine. No new dependencies and nothing to build.
  • Differences outside the encrypted range are recorded as findings, never as failures: a mismatch there would mean the game or its wrapper patches code at run time, which is itself valuable to know.
  • The reconstructed executable the tool produces is for static analysis only and must never be launched, since the start-up wrapper would try to decrypt already-decrypted code.
  • Any future code that lists a 32-bit process's modules from a 64-bit tool must query both the toolhelp snapshot and the process-modules call with the 32-bit filter, or it will silently miss half the process. The first version of this tool did exactly that.
  • The capture outputs never leave the private folders and are never published; the public record carries only counts and conclusions.

Run the tool's self-test subcommand with the project Python from the repository root: it prints each stage and ends with a pass or fail line. The module-listing gap was the real surprise: the first listing looked complete at seven modules, and only the absence of the most basic system library gave away that every 32-bit library was missing. It took a second enumeration call to see them. Less dramatically, the test program kept landing at the same shifted load address on repeated launches, so the retry loop built to catch varied shifts never saw variation; the synthetic round-trip covers that gap instead. The relocation table is fine; three lanes read it wrong

Earlier lanes disagreed about the executable's relocation table: one called it garbage, one found twenty thousand anomalous entries scattered through the code, one counted exact import matches, and one saw no entries at all in the encrypted region. A verified from-scratch parser shows the table itself is healthy, with just under two hundred ninety-two thousand entries that all check out, and each earlier disagreement traces to a concrete reading error, all now corrected.

What was asked

Settle the contradiction between four earlier lanes about the relocation table, produce the definitive relocation list and statistics, and map the whole code section page by page to find every encrypted or non-code pocket.

What was found

  • Verified The relocation table parses cleanly: only the two expected entry types appear, the bytes consumed match the directory size exactly, and every fixup site is backed by file content.
  • Verified The "garbage table" verdict was a scripting bug: the lane added the page address twice, scattering all sites to wrong locations. Re-running the bug reproduces its numbers digit for digit.
  • Verified All twenty thousand odd-looking entries sit inside the encrypted first megabyte, and their on-disk values are ciphertext, confirmed by uniformity tests. There are no scattered high-entropy pockets; an earlier lane misread its own location histogram.
  • Verified The encrypted region holds over twenty thousand fixup sites, not zero as reported; only their values are opaque, while their positions are exact and probably form the start-up stub's own fixup list.
  • Verified The import-table cross-check of about two thousand entries reproduces exactly, and a handful of references from code to the file headers are genuine.
  • Verified Page-by-page mapping finds no second encrypted region: two hundred fifty encrypted pages, sixteen pages of jump and pointer tables, and everything else code, including some zero-heavy initialisation code and tiny stub functions first mistaken for padding.
  • Verified Both function inventories contain entries inside ciphertext that must be excluded: several hundred in the new Ghidra export (which at least labels the region) and a few thousand in the lane estimate.

What was decided or recommended

The new relocation list replaces all earlier counts as the source of truth, with on-disk values inside the encrypted region marked as ciphertext. Downstream tools must drop ciphertext function entries from both inventories. The stub-fixup theory and the exact table seams inside mixed pages are left for a runtime lane and the function-inventory lane.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane scripts in order with the project Python: a boundary scan by page entropy, a manual relocation-directory walk cross-checked against the parsing library, a bug-reproduction script, uniformity tests on the odd values, and a per-page classifier combining entropy, pointer density and aligned fixup runs. Outputs are a compact relocation list and one record per code page.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two page-classification metrics failed before the third worked: plain linear disassembly misfires whenever a page starts mid-instruction, and resync disassembly then proved too permissive since nearly any bytes decode as something. Pointer density plus runs of consecutive aligned fixups turned out to be the reliable table signal. Separately, several dense initialisation pages first classified as tables or padding and were only corrected by reading their bytes.

The third-party libraries in the executable are now mapped to exact lists of functions instead of rough address ranges: just over a thousand functions, about half a megabyte, are identified as library code that the rewrite queue can skip or replace, and the two middleware packages that must be rewritten from scratch are sized with entry points.

Verified The linked zlib is the compress side only, twenty-four functions: the checksum, the window filler and the three compression levels were confirmed by reading the code, but the decompressor, the checksum-table code and the gzip helpers are absent from the readable code. Pinning down where decompression happens is left open.

Most codec internals are reached through method tables rather than direct calls, so the full extent needs indirect-call analysis.

Verified The TLS stack covers about three hundred functions with dozens of callers from game code; hash code is present but the symmetric cipher is not found in readable code. The target neighbourhood turned out to mix library code with game code that parses text formats, so every range-based assumption had to be replaced with call-graph evidence. Tools: shaders

All of the game's shaders can be extracted and translated to validated SPIR-V with free tools that now live in the project's tools folder. The game ships 102 shader programs in 6 graphics-card variants (612 files), all using shader model 3.0 bytecode inside a simple container. After removing duplicates there are 969 distinct shader programs. The recommended path is a small extractor, then the DXVK project's shader compiler to SPIR-V, then SPIRV-Cross to Metal shading language, with the official SPIR-V validator as the gate.

What was asked

Establish the game's shader container format from file headers and public documentation, count the shaders, and find, test and where allowed install the tools the project needs: an extractor for the container, disassemblers and translators for Direct3D 9 shader bytecode, and SPIR-V tools. Recommend a pipeline from the game's shader files to SPIR-V and to Metal shading language.

What was found

Verified The shader files sit as loose files in the game's shared shader folder, so no archive tool is needed for them. Each container starts with a four-character magic word, then a list of vertex-shader fragments, then pixel-shader fragments; every fragment carries its parameter names and a size-prefixed bytecode blob, followed by technique metadata. A purpose-written extractor parsed all 612 files with zero failures and every blob checked out as well-formed shader model 3.0 bytecode with full parameter tables.

Verified The six card-specific folders are mostly copies of each other: two are byte-identical, two more differ from the base set in only one or two files, and the remaining two carry cheaper variants of a few dozen shaders. Deduplication leaves 969 distinct programs out of 10,134 blobs.

ToolJobResult on all 969 programs
dxbc-spirv (the DXVK shader compiler)Bytecode to SPIR-VAll outputs pass the official validator with no fixes needed
MojoShaderBytecode to GLSL, SPIR-V and MetalReads everything, but its SPIR-V needs trailing junk trimmed and 4 programs fail validation on a gradient bug
SPIRV-CrossSPIR-V to Metal and HLSLEmits both languages; some shaders need a newer Metal version flag
SPIRV-ToolsValidate and inspect SPIR-VUsed as the pass/fail gate for every translated shader
fxc from the Windows SDKDisassemble for inspectionClean disassembly with parameter tables; inspection only
rage_fxc_extractorContainer extraction (reference)Despite targeting console files, it reads every PC file and matches the purpose-written extractor byte for byte
glslang and nagaGeneral shader compilersBoth work, but neither fits this chain: one cannot read the generated GLSL dialect, the other rejects fragment shaders

Verified One named candidate was rejected after testing: a DirectX 11 shader decompiler errors out on these older bytecode files and its disassembler crashes on them. It only understands a newer bytecode format, so it was removed again.

Inferred The PC and console containers share one layout, since the console-oriented extractor reads every PC file including its quirks.

Unknown The technique and pass tables at the end of each container are not fully decoded yet, only their name strings. The Metal output from both translators is unvalidated because no Metal compiler exists on this machine.

What was decided or recommended

  • Standardise on this offline pipeline: extract and deduplicate to 969 programs, translate with dxbc-spirv, require every module to pass the SPIR-V validator, then convert to Metal shading language with SPIRV-Cross.
  • Keep MojoShader as a second source for cross-checking, with workarounds for its two known defects, and keep glslang and naga only for newly written shaders.
  • Use the SDK disassembler for inspection. Do not adopt the DirectX 11 decompiler.
  • Before translated shaders can run, not just validate, the renderer team must settle how shader resources and inputs are bound, because the translator's output follows DirectX 9 conventions the new renderer has to mirror.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's extractor over the game's shader folder (read-only), which should report 612 files parsed and 969 distinct programs. Then run each translator over the extracted programs and check every output with the SPIR-V validator. The exact scripts, command lines, tool versions and licences are recorded in the lane's report and tool manifest in the project scratch area.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • An earlier survey reported a different container magic word; re-reading all 612 files showed it was misread, and its shader count had double-counted each program. Both are corrected in the lane report.
  • The first batch test reported hundreds of MojoShader failures that turned out to be a bug in the test script's file mapping, not in the tool. After the fix all three language profiles passed everything.
  • MojoShader's own example programs corrupt binary output on Windows by printing it as text. A 40-line helper that writes bytes to a file fixed it, and that helper is what all validation here used.
  • Two plausible pipeline links failed for instructive reasons: generated GLSL uses too old a dialect for the Vulkan compiler, and the Rust shader compiler rejects fragment shaders from both translators. Both findings are recorded so the next lane does not retry them.

Tools: running, debugging and tracing the game

All eight runtime tools are installed from their official sources and start on this machine, and scripted tracing with Frida is verified end to end against a 32-bit test program. The bad news is graphics: the display driver ships no 32-bit Vulkan support, so the translation layer that could make frame capture possible has almost no chance of working here.

What was asked

Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for running, debugging and tracing the game later: an interactive debugger, a scripted instrumentation toolkit, a frame capture tool, a Direct3D 9 translation layer, two system and API tracers, a plugin loader and a community patch baseline. Every download had to come from the project's own official release page, install portably without admin rights, and be tested without touching the game.

What was found

Verified Frida attaches from emulated 64-bit Python to a 32-bit test process and runs full instrumentation: architecture detection, module listing and memory reads all returned correct results.

Verified The 32-bit debugger GUI and the API tracer GUI both start under emulation, respond and show a main window. The frame capture tool prints its version cleanly. The system tracer was deliberately not launched because its first run loads a kernel driver; its package includes a native ARM64 build.

Verified A small probe program showed that 32-bit processes on this machine see exactly two Vulkan devices, both provided by the system's Vulkan-on-Direct3D-12 layer at Vulkan version 1.2, and no native graphics driver device. The installed driver ships Vulkan support for ARM64 processes only.

Verified That finding blocks two tools. The frame capture tool does not support Direct3D 9 at all, so it can only see the game through the translation layer. Current translation layer releases need Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4, which the 32-bit path does not offer; only the legacy 1.10 line, which needs Vulkan 1.1, passes the version check, and running it stacked on emulation is untested by its authors.

Verified The plugin loader, the community patch and both translation layer builds have the right architecture and the expected entry points. The community patch bundles its own loader, its own translation build and about two hundred megabytes of replacement assets.

Original functions can be executed for comparison, but not with Unicorn on this machine

The planned checker approach works, with a different engine than planned. The Unicorn CPU emulator crashes on every execution attempt on this machine, so the lane built a small 32-bit harness that runs original functions natively through the operating system's own compatibility layer instead. Fifty small functions were executed with hundreds of random inputs, most ran cleanly, and two trial Rust rewrites matched their originals on all 200 inputs each.

What was asked

Prove or disprove that original game functions can be executed outside the game for comparison testing of Rust rewrites. The plan named the Unicorn emulator: map the executable, set registers and stack inputs, run each function until it returns, and record the return value and memory effects. The lane was also asked to cover harder cases (calls between functions, global data, system imports, floating point, object methods), measure speed, and design what agreement between original and rewrite means.

What was found

Verified The emulator engine is unusable here. Every execution attempt crashes the whole process, including a minimal test of one trivial instruction with no hooks attached, and including non-x86 guest code. The fault is inside the emulator's own library, with a different crash code on different runs.

Verified A 32-bit helper program built with the project's Rust toolchain runs original functions correctly. It loads the executable's bytes with standard relocation fixups (a count cross-checked against an independent tool, matching exactly), calls one function at a time with chosen inputs, and reports registers, flags, floating-point state and changed memory as structured output. Faults are caught inside the process and reported with the failing location instead of crashing.

Verified The first of the code section's megabytes is encrypted or compressed on disk (entropy near the theoretical maximum, undecodable as instructions), while the remaining nine megabytes are normal code. Functions in the encrypted part cannot be executed from file bytes at all.

Verified Of 50 sampled small leaf functions run 8 times each, naive random inputs completed only about one run in eight, while shaped inputs (pointers aimed at scratch memory) completed over half, and a follow-up with better stack inputs brought 43 of 50 to fully passing. All failures were memory access faults, never illegal instructions. Repeated runs were bit-identical.

Verified Harder cases behave as needed: a real nested call between two game functions executed end to end; a global data read returned the correct startup value; an unresolved system import faulted deterministically at exactly the expected address, which is what makes it interceptable; legacy and modern floating-point instructions both work and their outputs are captured.

Verified Two hand-written Rust twins of original functions agreed with the originals on all 200 random inputs each, including calling-convention stack accounting on a stdcall function.

FactValueWhat it means
Small leaf functions foundAbout 1800 in the readable codePlenty of easy first targets for the checker
Leaf trials passing with shaped inputs43 of 50 functions fully passingInput shaping matters more than engine choice
Relocation entries appliedAbout 292 thousand, matching an independent countThe harness loads the program the way the OS loader would
Single call costRoughly a tenth of a millisecondExecution is cheap; process setup dominates and should be batched
End-to-end trial cost todayA few hundred millisecondsA persistent worker running many trials per process is needed for speed
Twin agreement200 of 200 on both trial rewritesThe full compare loop works in principle

What was decided or recommended

The checker should use native 32-bit execution, not Unicorn, on this machine: one worker process owns the relocated original plus the linked rewrite, calls either side through the same trampoline, and compares return values, stack accounting, written memory, outgoing calls with arguments, and floating-point state. Bitwise floating-point equality should be the default, with per-function tolerance only where declared. Functions in the encrypted region and functions needing live operating-system state are out of scope for the checker and should be tracked as blocked rather than failed.

How to reproduce it

Build the scratch helper and twin crates for the 32-bit Windows target with the installed Rust toolchain (offline build, no extra dependencies), then run the driver scripts in the lane's scratch folder: one maps the executable and samples leaf functions with a disassembler, one runs each leaf with random and shaped inputs and records structured results, and one compares the two Rust twins against their originals over 200 seeded inputs. The design document in the same folder describes the contract, the input generation policy, and the per-case handling.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first leaf scan produced nonsense instructions because it started inside the encrypted region; an entropy map showed the boundary clearly and the scan was restricted to readable code. The emulator failure looked at first like a harness bug and was only settled by a minimal one-instruction test with no hooks. The native harness then crashed in its own trampoline for several rounds: the fault addresses first suggested an emulation quirk, but disassembling the generated bytes plus an in-process fault handler proved it was an ordinary stack bookkeeping bug (the host stack pointer saved on the wrong side of two push instructions). Low memory also turned out to be unmappable in 32-bit processes on this host, which forced relocation support earlier than planned. Each of these cost time but left a checkable artifact in the scratch folder.

In the first 33 minutes of phase 0, 37 agent lanes finished 545 lane-minutes of analysis and wrote about 104,000 words of findings: roughly sixteen times faster than one agent working through the same tasks in sequence. That speed is real, but it was measured on the kind of work that parallelises best. The rewrite itself has not been timed yet.

What was asked

The owner noticed the project was moving faster than expected and asked for an analysis, an estimate of when it could finish, and a note on what swarm working is like in practice.
