Concurrency limit reachedNone yetUp to 38 lanes ran at once with no rate limiting from the model provider. Each lane used about 180 MB of memory; the laptop had 9 GB free at the peak.
Mistakes caught by a second lane3 in the first hourThe encrypted code range the coordinator missed, an emulator that crashes on this machine, and a disagreement about the relocation table that is still being settled.

Why it was fast

  • Verified The tasks were independent. Each lane read the same file and answered a different question, so no lane waited for another.
  • Verified Every lane got the same written contract: where it may write, what it must deliver, how to label evidence, and a progress log to keep. The coordinator did not have to explain anything twice.
  • Verified Publishing was automated behind a check. A script refuses any devlog fragment containing addresses, local paths, byte dumps or code, so the coordinator could integrate fifteen entries at a time without reading each line first.
  • Verified Overlap between lanes was useful, not wasteful. Lanes that measured the same thing a different way are what caught the three mistakes above.

What slowed it down or went wrong

  • Verified The coordinator is the bottleneck. Lanes finish faster than one coordinator can read their reports properly. In the first hour most lane reports were read only as fifteen-line summaries.
  • Verified Lanes cannot be corrected once they are running. When the encrypted code range was discovered, sixteen lanes had already started without knowing about it, and their numbers have to be checked afterwards.
  • Verified Pushing every commit separately broke the project site for several minutes. See the entry on site build collisions.
  • Verified Lanes disagree. Two independent function counts differ by about fourteen thousand, and two lanes describe the same relocation table as clean and as mostly garbage. A swarm produces contradictions at the same speed as findings, and each one costs a further lane to settle.
  • Inferred Quality varies with how much of a lane's evidence comes from running code against the real file. Lanes that measured were reliable; the one lane that worked mostly from forum posts was corrected within hours.

The estimate, and how much to trust each part

These are estimates made on the first evening, before any function has been rewritten through the full pipeline. The pilot in phase 2 replaces them with measurements.

PhaseEstimateBasis and main risk
0. MeasureFinished within a dayMeasured: most of it took an hour. One megabyte of code is encrypted on disk and can only be read once the owner has started the game.
1. Harness2 to 4 daysThe side-by-side runner is proven on simple functions. It still needs stubs for outgoing calls, since 70% of functions call other functions. This work is mostly serial, and everything after it depends on it being right.
2. Pilot1 to 2 daysMeasures functions per lane per hour and the false-accept rate. Every estimate below is a guess until this exists.
3. Rewrite2 to 5 weeksAssumes 30 lanes, each completing 4 to 10 small functions an hour around the clock. 82% of functions are under 256 bytes and about 13,000 are duplicates of one another, which favours the low end. The hard tail (about 1,700 functions over a kilobyte, about 900 with non-standard calling conventions) and the provider's usage limits favour the high end.
4. Standalone2 to 4 weeks moreIntegration debugging is serial and does not speed up with more lanes. The Xbox 360 recompilation projects spent months here.
5. 64-bit and platform layer3 to 5 weeks moreNo comparable project to measure against.
6. Renderer and macOS6 to 12 weeks moreThe longest phase in every comparable project. Shader translation already works, which helps.

Added up: a rewritten game that runs on its own with the original renderer in roughly 6 to 11 weeks, and a 64-bit build with a new renderer on three platforms in roughly 4 to 6 months. The first figure rests on one comparable project, the agent-driven Modern Warfare 2 decompilation, which took about ten weeks to become playable with fewer agents, fewer functions and the benefit of symbols.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep lanes independent and overlapping. Do not remove overlap to save tokens; it is the swarm's error correction.
  • Measure before estimating. The phase 2 pilot is short on purpose.
  • Move routine coordination, such as integrating finished lanes and posting status, onto cheaper models or scripts, and keep the coordinator for decisions and review.
  • Treat phase 0's speed as the ceiling for analysis work, not as a forecast for the rewrite.

How to reproduce it

Each lane's log records when the coordinator launched it and when it exited. Subtract the two for each lane, add up the durations, and divide by the wall-clock time between the first launch and the last exit.

Tools: building for the three target platforms

One Rust code base can already build and run for both Windows targets on the project machine, and macOS builds belong on macOS runners, not on this machine. A hello-world crate compiled for all three Windows targets and each binary ran. A macOS binary also linked locally through a cross-linker, but only a Mac can run, sign, or ship it.

What was asked

Work out how the project builds one Rust code base for Windows on x64, Windows on ARM64, and macOS on Apple silicon, from the project machine and from continuous integration. Test the local toolchain, try cross-compiling to macOS, and research runners and their cost, the Vulkan SDK and MoltenVK in CI, macOS signing, and how similar projects set up their builds.

What was found

Verified The local machine builds and runs all three Windows targets with no extra setup. The compiler ships native linkers for each one.

TargetBuildRun
Windows ARM64yesyes, native
Windows x64yesyes, emulated
Windows 32-bit x86yesyes, emulated

Verified Static linking of the C runtime removes the need for a redistributable install. The test binary then depends only on core system libraries.

Verified Cross-linking a macOS Apple silicon binary on Windows works for a trivial program using the Zig linker driven by cargo-zigbuild, with no Apple SDK installed. The output has the right Mach-O header for an ARM64 executable.

Inferred That cross-linked binary is a compile check, not a shippable build. Anything using macOS frameworks needs the real Apple SDK, whose licence restricts it to Apple hardware, and nothing here can run the result. Real macOS builds must happen on a Mac or a macOS CI runner.

Verified Standard CI runners are free with no minute cap for public repositories, so the three-platform build matrix costs nothing once the project is public. Suitable runners exist for each target, including an ARM64 Windows runner and current Apple silicon macOS runners.

Verified The Vulkan SDK is a free download and MoltenVK is permissively licensed, so neither needs buying. Both install in CI through maintained setup actions or direct downloads, and macOS runners can also install them from Homebrew.

Verified Ad-hoc signing is enough for development builds on macOS, but a clean first launch of a downloaded release needs paid developer membership, a distribution certificate, and submission to Apple's notarisation service, which is itself free.

Verified Three similar projects were read: a Sonic recompilation, an open game engine, and a GTA IV recompilation. All build each platform natively on its own runner, cache dependencies and compiler output, pin tool versions, sign macOS builds ad-hoc in CI with real signing reserved for releases, and ship Apple bundles as compressed tarballs rather than zip files.

What was decided or recommended

  • Build Windows targets locally and in CI with plain cargo; keep the C runtime statically linked so there is nothing to install.
  • Use the Zig-based cross-linker locally only as a macOS compile check, and do every real macOS build on a macOS runner.
  • Standardise CI on one runner per target, a pinned Rust toolchain with a shared build cache, a pinned Vulkan SDK installed by a setup action, and ad-hoc macOS signing, adding paid signing and notarisation only for tagged releases.
  • Organise the Rust code as one workspace with a crate per boundary: shared types, platform layer, renderer, engine subsystems, the 32-bit replacement library, the checker, and packaging tasks.

How to reproduce it

Install the missing Windows target with rustup, then build a hello-world crate for each of the three Windows targets and run each binary. Rebuild with the static C runtime flag and confirm the system library list shrinks. Install cargo-zigbuild, add the Apple silicon Rust target, and cross-link the same crate for macOS, then inspect the output header to confirm it is an ARM64 executable. The full commands, versions, hashes, and CI sketches are in the lane report.

What was confusing or went wrong

The cross-linker first failed to find its own Zig binary because a system launcher stub shadowed the real interpreter; pointing it at the project interpreter fixed it. The first Zig download arrived truncated and had to be retried with hash verification. A system tool that locates compiler installs reported nothing even though the compilers work fine, which cost a short detour before plain builds proved the linkers were there all along.

Tools: reverse engineering helpers

Most of the helper tooling works on this machine, but two things failed plainly: neither demangler handles bare type names without a wrapping trick, and the bundled emulator crashes on every run. The project now has tested commands for diffing, listing, disassembling, parsing and demangling, and a clear note on what to avoid.

What was asked

Find, install and test the tools that complement the main disassembler for this project: an object differ, a relocatable-object exporter, shipped library-identification and similarity data, LLVM-style listing tools, two portable analysis suites, seven Rust crates for disassembly, parsing, hooking, emulation and demangling, plus the demangler in the installed build tools. Every tool had to be run on this machine, not assumed to work, and the demangling command had to be proven on twenty class names from the executable.

What was found

Verified The object differ runs natively and diffs 32-bit objects correctly, flagging a single changed constant with a near-total match score, but it refuses 64-bit ARM objects. The relocatable-object exporter ships an exact build for the installed disassembler version, confirmed from its manifest but not yet activated.

Verified The disassembler ships ready-made library fingerprints for five compiler generations in both 32- and 64-bit flavours, including the one matching the executable's linker generation, plus similarity-search scripts and weights. No queryable database exists yet; one must be built after analysis finishes.

Verified The installed build tools contain native listing and demangling programs but no LLVM listing tools. An official portable LLVM build for this processor exists (a large download) and was deliberately skipped.

Verified One portable analysis suite runs natively and reads the executable fully (machine type, section count, debug path, build date); the other runs emulated and agrees, additionally naming the linker generation. All Rust parsing and disassembly crates built and agreed with each other on headers, sections, imports and entry code.

Verified Both hooking crates refuse to build for the native processor and both build and run their tests for the 32-bit target the game uses, including an enable-and-disable hook round trip. The emulator package imports and maps memory but crashes hard on every emulation start in both 32- and 64-bit modes, so it is unusable here; its Rust twin shares the same engine core and licence and was not built.

Verified A scan found 1688 type names in the executable (1579 classes, 109 structs). Neither demangler reads a bare type name directly: one echoes it back or emits garbage, the other errors or keeps a prefix. Wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form before demangling fixed both engines, scoring twenty out of twenty on each, with matching results.

What was decided or recommended

  • Use the object differ for object-level comparisons, the build tools lister for headers and imports, and the native portable suite for second opinions.
  • Use the tested Rust crates for disassembly and executable parsing, and the tested demangling wrapper recipe in both Rust code and one-off commands.
  • Use the safe Rust hooking library for 32-bit targets with the C-based one as fallback, both fenced off from native builds.
  • Tag library code with the shipped fingerprints matching the executable's linker generation, and run similarity search against a local database once analysis lands.
  • Do not install the portable LLVM bundle, do not use the emulator on this host, and do not link copyleft-licensed emulation code into the project.

How to reproduce it

  1. Run the differ with two 32-bit objects, one symbol and dash for stdout; expect a structured diff naming the changed instruction.
  2. List the executable with the build tools lister and either portable suite; all three should report the same machine type, section count and import count.
  3. Build the small Rust test programs from pinned crate versions and run them against the executable; parsing results should match the listers exactly.
  4. Demangle twenty type names by stripping the leading dot, wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form, and running either demangler; expect a plain class line from each after removing the descriptor suffix.
  5. Build the hook tests for the 32-bit target and run them; expect the detour to reroute and then restore the call. Confirm the native build of the same tests fails.
  6. Start any emulation call in the bundled emulator package; expect the process to die without an error message.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Downloads silently landed outside the repository because a child shell did not inherit the working directory; the files were moved back and re-verified by hash. Future work should use absolute paths everywhere.

Verified The first disassembly test decoded from the wrong offset and produced nonsense; decoding from the real entry point produced a clean result. The first demangling tests also failed until the wrapping trick was found by trying the descriptor form directly.

Verified The emulator failure was silent: no exception and no output, only a dead process. Unbuffered step-by-step runs isolated the crash to the emulation start call itself.

How our code can get into the game

Our replacement functions can ride into the game as a proxy system library placed next to the executable, the same way community plugins already load, and nothing in the game's own checks looks at such a library or at patched code. The one thing that needs care is the start-up wrapper: the entry code loads a helper library from the game folder that prepares hidden start-up data before the real game begins, so our loader must wait until that finishes before touching anything.

What was asked

Work out, by research and static analysis only and without launching the game, how a project-built 32-bit library can be loaded into the running game and replace individual functions: which community mechanism to reuse, which libraries the game loads early enough to proxy, whether any integrity check would notice, and how the loader itself should be designed.

What was found

Verified The game statically imports three proxyable system libraries early enough to carry our loader, and none of them ships in the game folder, so a file placed next to the executable is picked up automatically. The community loader defaults to one of those names and recommends it in its readme; our loader should take a different one so both can coexist.

Verified Community plugins load inside library initialisation, before any game code runs. The community loader also has a deferred mode that waits for the game's first system call, but only other game titles use it; this game uses the default early path.

Verified The game's signature verification checks exactly one thing: the Rockstar Social Club library in the Program Files folder, confirmed as Take-Two signed. Save-game encryption uses the data-protection API and is unrelated. No code path was found that verifies the game executable itself, lists loaded modules for checking, or watches for patched bytes.

Verified The entry code resolves system functions by hand, loads a helper library from the game folder, calls into it in a retry loop, then invokes start-up callbacks that are all zeros in the file on disk (so the helper must fill them in at run time) before jumping to the real game code. The helper's imports show process and module inspection, memory reading, debugger checks, and the ability to end the process.

Verified The community fix project finds game code purely with named byte patterns (over a thousand collected, with per-version alternatives and no hardcoded addresses or version checks) and waits with watcher threads when code is not visible yet. Searched against our build, about half match exactly once and form named anchors; the rest belong to other game versions, plus a small set matching more than once that needs disambiguation.

FactValueWhat it means
Proxyable early importsThree system librariesOur loader can enter before any game code runs
Files the signature check verifiesOne: the Social Club libraryOur library and patched code are not covered by it
Named patterns collectedOver twelve hundredA large pool of candidate anchors
Patterns matching exactly onceAbout six hundredUsable anchors for the hook table
Helper library reaction to our codeNot known staticallyTop question for the first live run

What was decided or recommended

  • Build the loader as a project-owned proxy under the system library name the community loader does not use, with the small set of used functions forwarded to the real system copy; also support running as a community-loader plugin from the same codebase as a fallback.
  • Do almost nothing at load time; wait with an anchor-watching thread until game code is provably final, then install hooks, each behind an on/off switch driven by a start-up file and a local command channel, failing closed on any mismatch.
  • Use the pure-Rust detour library (permissive licence, native per-hook enable and disable) as the primary hook mechanism, small assembler adapters for class methods on the stable toolchain, direct slot writes for virtual tables, and mid-hooks only for observation.
  • Never touch the helper library's memory or threads, and assume it can see our module until a live run proves otherwise.

How to reproduce it

List the executable's import table with a PE parser and confirm which system libraries it resolves at load time and which files exist beside it in the game folder. Disassemble the few hundred bytes at the entry point and note the hand-rolled library loading, the helper-library calls, and the manual start-up callback invocation. Map every cross-reference to the signature and crypto imports and disassemble around each call site to see which file path is built and checked. Collect the community fix project's pattern strings, match each against the code section with wildcard support, and count exact, multiple, and zero matches.

What was confusing or went wrong

The start-up callbacks being all zeros in the file looked like missing data until the entry code's manual callback loop made clear they are filled in at run time. Two early readings of the entry code were wrong on first pass (how the helper name is encoded, and an address-range slip that briefly suggested odd export locations) and were corrected by re-parsing the bytes precisely rather than by hand. Web page fetches kept truncating, so both community projects were read as local copies in scratch instead, and only the pattern facts were kept. Most pattern variables in the community source share one generic name, so anchors are identified by file, line, and bytes rather than by a meaningful name.

Verified The executable holds about 45,200 functions in its readable code, with at least 1,170 more hidden in an encrypted first region, measured by recursive-descent disassembly with capstone. What was asked

Produce an independent estimate of the function count and sizes without waiting for the Ghidra analysis: recursive descent from the entry point, direct-call targets, relocated code pointers, and exception tables; then size and complexity distributions, duplicate detection, and a comparison with the public Xbox 360 counts.

What was found

Verified The code section has two sharply divided regions. The first 1,000 KiB is encrypted and unreadable on disk; the remaining roughly 9.5 MiB is ordinary compiled code. A small loader stub at the entry point resolves imports at run time and jumps to the real entry; it was not reversed further. Switch tables live inside the code section rather than in data, which the scan had to learn (see below).

The wrapper is treated as out of scope: no decryption was attempted and none should be. The per-function data file is ready for the library-tagging lane, which should shrink the count, and for Ghidra cross-checking once that analysis lands. How to reproduce it

Parse the executable headers, split the code section by per-block entropy, and collect seeds from direct-call targets, relocated pointers with trustworthy sources, and the exception handler table. Run capstone recursive descent over the plain region, resolve index-scaled jump tables validated by relocations, merge case blocks back into their owners, and hash functions with address bytes masked. The lane's scan script repeats the full pass in about two minutes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first entropy sample covered only the start of the code section and briefly suggested the whole thing was encrypted; a full block scan corrected that within minutes. A 256-byte entropy threshold then missed the boundary entirely because small samples cannot reach high entropy values, and the first full run decoded 64 KiB windows through a disassembler call that decodes eagerly, running twenty times too slow. Both bugs were fixed the same hour. The genuine surprise was switch tables stored in executable code, including one region of 481 identical functions that first looked like a data island.

Subsystem survey: physics and collision

The game's physics is RAGE-native collision code over a statically linked Bullet broadphase and narrow phase, with NaturalMotion Euphoria driving ragdolls, and no Havok anywhere. The survey counted 94 physics-owned classes, 792 related strings, and at least 789 physics functions in readable code, concentrated in one large engine block plus fragment, material, and entity-glue regions.

What was asked

Survey the physics and collision subsystem of the original executable by working directly on the file with Python: extract its classes from run-time type information with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, identify its operating system and library dependencies, compare against public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and leave rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.

What was found

Verified The subsystem owns 94 classes: 19 collision bound types from boxes and spheres up to composite, mesh, and octree bounds; live instances, three collider types, joints, rope, constraints, archetypes, materials, a simulator, sleep management, a level world, broadphase variants, Bullet narrow-phase algorithms, and a fragment family for breakable objects. Sixteen more classes in other systems carry physics names, and 24 Euphoria behaviour classes plus two fragment render dictionaries sit at the boundary.

Verified Both the broadphase and the narrow phase are Bullet-derived, with Bullet class names appearing both under the engine namespace and without any namespace. Euphoria appears as behaviour, effector, and engine classes in a dedicated animation namespace, reached through dedicated physics instance types. No Havok class or string exists in the binary.

Verified Game entities attach through a single physics entity class with 72 virtual functions, the parent of pedestrians, vehicles, and objects, with matching network mirror classes. Fragments use multiple inheritance with the largest tables in the subsystem at 65 and 66 slots, while the simulator exposes only 8 virtual functions and the level world only one, so most of their interface is non-virtual.

Verified Of 792 related strings, the most revealing are resource paths for fragments and natural motion data, ragdoll state messages, task parameter asserts for ten Euphoria behaviours, debug dump formats for collision state and velocity, 19 wheel friction surface names, tuning keys for damage, inertia, and self collision, and broadphase debug text. Collision file extensions, Havok names, and physics source file paths are all absent.

Verified Relocation clustering plus virtual function targets attribute at least 789 functions and about 309 kilobytes of code to the subsystem across 168 clusters, with disassembly spot checks passing on 94 percent of sampled sites. About two-thirds of the attributed functions sit in one large engine block covering bounds, colliders, joints, rope, archetypes, both Bullet phases, and the simulator, with separate regions for fragments, materials, and game-side glue.

Verified The subsystem calls almost no operating system functions directly: only thread synchronisation primitives and a thread affinity query were found in its code. The C library is statically linked, file access goes through the resource system, and both Bullet and Euphoria are statically linked.

Inferred The physics stepper takes variable frame time as a parameter rather than using a fixed-step constant, since no frame constant is referenced from physics code. This matches public reports that running above 60 frames per second breaks vehicle handling, ragdolls, object physics, and helicopters, which community fixes address by restoring frame-rate scaling.

What was decided or recommended

A rewrite should proceed from bound primitives and mesh bounds with a bounds-file reader, through instances, broadphase, narrow phase, colliders, joints, the simulator, the level world, fragments, and game attachment, leaving the Euphoria bridge for last together with the animation work. Pure geometry queries, solver steps, and broadphase operations can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation, while stepping, level queries, streaming, entity glue, and behaviours need the running game. Fixed-step-only simulation would be a behaviour change, so the rewrite must reproduce variable frame-time quirks, and field layouts, file formats, and the behaviour interface still need to come from debugger work or community sources.

Four scripts in the lane scratch folder run in order with the project Python environment: an environment check that verifies the encrypted prefix against its mirror section, a class scan that filters the shared type inventory and measures every virtual table through relocations, a string scan that filters the shared string inventory with physics patterns, and a cluster scan that groups code references with slot targets and spot-checks them with the disassembler. Each script reads only the original executable and the shared probe inventories and writes only to the scratch folder, finishing in about ten minutes. The class, string, and cluster data files it produces hold every address and count behind this entry.

What was confusing or went wrong

Several name filters misfired before review caught them: audio hardware voices, pixel-shader fragments, render phases, camera graph parameters, and a particle attribute all matched physics patterns and had to be excluded by hand, while one iterator class lost its enclosing scope to a name printer bug and had to be re-read from its mangled form. Tiny clusters pairing two type descriptors turned out to be data tables embedded in code rather than functions. A text search over the single-line string inventory hung and had to be replaced with a JSON load. Two Euphoria behaviour name strings looked like noise until the matching behaviour classes confirmed them, and the absence of collision file extensions was checked three ways before being trusted.

Verified The project now has a working script pipeline: an open-source tool built from source on this machine decrypts and disassembles mission scripts from our own copy of the game, and a small project script extracts all 940 of them from the game archives without needing any key material.

What was asked

Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools for the game's script files: decompilers, compilers and disassemblers. What was found

Verified Scripts ship inside two archives per episode (main and network), six archives in total, holding 940 scripts. The archives use a newer format than the classic one: only their directory is encrypted, while the script data itself sits raw, so scripts can be recovered by their headers alone.

Verified Every script on this PC build is encrypted but not compressed, with a versioned header carrying code, statics and globals counts. The decryption key is derived locally by the tool from the owner's own executable at run time; no key material was copied, printed or stored anywhere.

Verified The decompiled reference set holds 869 scripts and about 3.8 million lines across the three episodes, making 621,220 calls to 2,206 distinct native functions. The most called natives are injury and death checks, debug print helpers, the timer, and the wait call, which appears in 829 of 869 scripts. The reference predates our game build, so its counts differ by two scripts and its native names need re-mapping.

Tools: the future Rust engine's libraries

A survey of Rust crates and C libraries for the future 64-bit engine found a maintained, permissively licensed crate for nearly every need, with three licence flags and one platform risk to resolve. Verified Seventy-three crates were checked against the package index, twenty-two repositories had their build configurations read, and every recommendation below names its version, licence and maintenance state as of the survey date.

What was asked

Find the best maintained Rust crate or C library with bindings for each need of the future engine: Vulkan bindings and allocators, Metal bindings, windowing and input, audio output and 3D audio, decoding, physics, maths, compression, archive parsing helpers, networking, scripting, profiling and the upscaler SDKs. Check which build for Windows on ARM64 by reading build configurations, flag every licence outside the permissive set, and end with a recommended dependency list. Research only; nothing was installed.

What was found

Most of the stack is uncontroversial. Vulkan goes through the long-standard binding whose repository is still active, with a pure Rust allocator beside it. Windowing and gamepad input collapse into a single C library that already supports Windows on ARM64 and Apple silicon. Audio output, the game mixer, physics, maths, compression, parsing helpers, networking and the profiler each have a maintained crate with recent releases. The 3D audio answer is the maintained wrapper around the now open source Steam audio SDK.

Four findings needed more care. First, only one crate in the survey tests Windows on ARM64 in its build configuration; everything else is trusted there because it is pure Rust on what is now a top-tier compiler target, while crates with C build steps each need one compile check. Second, the audio decoding library is pure Rust and complete but carries a weak copyleft licence that needs sign-off, and it cannot decode the game's videos, so a video library is still required for those. Third, the physics engine the original game derived from has only tiny or stale Rust bindings, so the maintained pure Rust physics engine wins despite the family resemblance. Fourth, upscaler bindings are new or placeholder, except for the Metal ones, so thin project-owned bindings are expected later.

Licence flags, all Verified from package metadata or primary sources:

  • Audio decoding: weak copyleft, file level. Usable inside a larger work but needs an explicit decision.
  • Video library: copyleft terms that depend on build options; a minimal build keeps obligations small but they still exist, and only this library decodes the game's videos.
  • OpenAL: rejected. Its Rust bindings are frozen since 2019, the maintained implementation is copyleft, and the system framework is deprecated on the Mac.
  • Upscaler and store SDKs: proprietary redistribution terms each; relevant only at the upscaling phase.

What was decided or recommended

Standardise on the table above. Prefer the single C windowing library over the three-crate windowing plus gamepad plus audio combination. Prefer the pure Rust allocator over the C++ one for the simpler ARM64 story. Take the maintained pure Rust physics engine and drop the idea that matching the original engine's physics family buys fidelity, since behaviour is rewritten rather than carried over. Write thin project-owned upscaler bindings at the upscaling phase instead of waiting for the ecosystem. The full versioned list with reasons, risks and rejected alternatives lives in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

  1. Query the package index API for each candidate crate and record version, licence, release date and download counts.
  2. Run package searches for the binding families where the crate name is uncertain (physics, spatial audio, video, networking) and confirm the maintained candidate by release date and repository activity.

Two searches returned misleading names. Verified A crate named exactly for the physics engine turned out to be an unrelated virtual machine project, and the crate named for the game's video format is a reserved-name stub; both wasted one lookup each before the package descriptions gave them away. Build configuration scanning missed several projects that use non-standard workflow filenames, which was corrected by listing one project's workflow directory directly. The oldest Vulkan binding release looked stale until the commit history showed active maintenance without recent releases, a reminder that release date alone misleads. Several platform claims rest on consistent secondary sources rather than primary documents because the time budget did not stretch to reading every upstream manual; those are marked as inferred in the report.

Establish which container and compression formats this build uses from file headers, then find, test and where allowed install the tools to list and unpack them, and prove the pipeline by extracting samples.

What was found

Verified The build uses two package-file versions: the audio banks use the newer one and the player-model archives plus one small data archive use the older one. Nearly all disc images are encrypted; four small ones are stored open. All loose resources share one container version and are zlib compressed. No lossless-console compression appears anywhere in this PC build, and no package entry uses the format's own compression flag.

  • Package files list 3,522 contained files; disc images list 52,718 entries, with zero failures in either set.
  • Audio bank entries carry content hashes instead of names; a public hash table resolves 99 percent of them to readable names.
  • Scripts ship only inside archives: 941 compiled scripts across eight archives, none as loose files.
  • The small data archive was the surprise: unlike every other package file, its file content is encrypted as well as its table, and it decrypts to a readable text file.

The Python audio-bank library resolves names and extracts correctly for audio banks but misreads model archives. The classic C# archive browser was evaluated from its source only; it supports this exact game version but needs a desktop install. The zlib libraries in both languages inflate identical bytes.

  • Scripted work should use the lane's small independent reader plus the Python crypto library: it is the only tested path covering all archive kinds, compression and the encrypted sidecar.
  • Audio-bank names should come from the MIT-licensed hash table behind a quiet wrapper.

How to reproduce it

Verified Run the lane's listing script from the repository scratch area: it loads the archive key from the owner's executable into memory, validates it by trial decryption without ever displaying or storing it, then lists every archive into a JSON file and extracts a handful of small samples into the asset cache. The audio-bank name table looks empty at first because its entries are hashes, not broken offsets; comparing against the Python library's hash table confirmed the bytes match. A first Rust attempt failed on a wrong argument type for the LZX crate and a bad relative path; both were fixed by reading the crate source and using an absolute path.

The largest regions are vehicle and police audio, car driving and door tasks, drive-by flags with seat and door logic, damage audio, and the get-in and get-out task family.

Games for Windows Live is gone without a trace, and the backend points at Rockstar Online Services instead. What was asked

Survey the networking subsystem from the executable alone: the classes, strings, code locations, operating system dependencies, public knowledge, timing behaviour, and rewrite notes, with a ranked list of what to understand first.

What was found

  • Verified Class names recovered through run-time type information show two layers: a game replication layer with per-entity-type sync wrappers, sync parsers, several dozen network event types, replicated task types, interpolation helpers, and array replication for pickups, player info and script variables; and an online services layer with session tasks, session events, wire message types, and a live-services manager with a Steam backend.
  • Verified Leaderboards dominate the class count: nearly fifteen hundred template bindings covering several hundred multiplayer mode schemas across ranked and standard boards for races, episodic content, team, competitive and co-operative modes.
  • Verified No reference to the old PC online platform remains anywhere: not in strings, class names, or imports. The replacement backend is named throughout: presence, party, invite, clan and sign-in events, matchmaking and clan web service endpoints, and Rockstar service hosts for auth, online services and cloud.
  • Verified Transport is raw sockets plus the engine's own HTTP client and statically linked TLS. Most socket imports are referenced from readable code in a select-loop client pattern with no listening sockets; all crypto imports are used for certificate checks and protected session-id storage.
  • Inferred The game replication layer and socket startup live mostly in the encrypted code region: most of its class tables and all of its diagnostic strings have no references from readable code. Parse the executable headers for sections, imports and relocations; scan read-only data for run-time type descriptors and validate complete object locators and class hierarchies against the relocation table; extract printable strings and filter by network keywords; resolve every relocation in the unencrypted code and keep targets matching network class tables, strings or socket and crypto import slots; group nearby hits into clusters; spot-check samples with a disassembler used only as a verifier.

The script native table: just over three thousand natives, all named

Verified The executable registers 3034 script natives into a single hash table, and every one now has a name from public databases. The older of the two known name-hash generations is the common Jenkins hash and checks out on all 2878 old pairs; the newer generation, which this build uses, is still unidentified, though its hashes have an unusual two-halves structure that constrains the search.

What was asked

Find the script engine's native function table using byte patterns published by the open-source script debugger scrDbg, enumerate every registered native as a hash plus handler pair, confirm the name-hashing function, and name as many natives as possible against public name lists.

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Script-engine anchors located10 of 10, each exactly onceThe published patterns fit this build precisely
Native registrations3034, each hash registered onceThe complete set this build can run
Named3034 of 3034No unknown natives remain in this build

Old name hashJenkins hash of the lowercase nameConfirmed on every old-generation pair

Verified Registration takes two shapes that both reach the same table insert routine: a small group carries its own failure check per native, while the large group calls through a shared wrapper that holds the check once. The table routines match the published open-table design entry for entry, including the probing rule and the empty-slot markers.

Verified Native name strings are absent from the executable, so scripts and the engine meet only through hash values. Seven cases where the two public databases disagreed on a hash were settled against the registered values: three favour one database, one was a misattributed name, and three turned out to be genuine alias pairs where both hashes are registered.

Inferred Roughly the first megabyte of the code section reads as high-entropy bytes rather than code, so it is likely decrypted by the start-up stub at load. Only the shared debug handler points into that region; everything else registered sits in readable code.

What was decided or recommended

  • The enumerated hash-to-handler list is the ground truth for this build's natives; later work should consume it rather than re-derive it.
  • The new name-hash algorithm stays open. The recommended next step is to extract the hashes that compiled game scripts actually call and attack the algorithm from those pairs, using the two-halves bit structure as the main constraint.
  • Handler code clusters into a few regions, which should make per-subsystem handler mapping straightforward.

How to reproduce it

  1. Search the executable's code for each published scrDbg pattern with wildcard bytes; each should occur once, pointing at the script-engine data.
  2. Read the table insert routine next to the table anchor and note its two-argument shape and probing loop.
  3. Find every push of a known native hash immediate followed by a call to the insert routine or its wrapper; pair each hash with the handler address pushed just before it.
  4. Match the collected hashes against the public SCO-Toolbox and HappinessMP lists to attach names, and hash the old list with the Jenkins function to confirm the old generation.

What was confusing or went wrong

Each hash in the small registration group appeared twice, which first looked like dual registration into two tables; disassembly showed the second push belongs to a failure-logging path, not a second table. The new hashes first appeared to have two bits structurally clear, which sent the analysis down a blind alley of masked and split-hash theories; the full-bit entries in the same list turned out to be old-hash placeholders, but the true new hashes really do keep those bits clear and the algorithm still resisted some sixty candidates plus seed-inversion, suffix, modulus and shift-family attacks. The shared debug handler points into the encrypted code region, so its runtime behaviour could not be checked statically.

What was asked

The owner reported that the published site did not seem to be working. The pages returned normally when checked a few minutes later, so what had happened?

What was found

  • Verified The coordinator had just started integrating lane results one commit at a time, pushing after each. Twelve commits went up within about a minute.
  • Verified The build history shows each push starting its own site build, and every build except the last of a burst ending immediately with "Page build failed". Only the final push of each burst produced a working site.
  • Inferred A build that is still running is cancelled or rejected when a newer push arrives, and it is reported as a failure, not as superseded. While a burst is in progress the site can serve an old version or fail to load.
  • Inferred Each failed build probably also sends the repository owner a notification.

What was decided or recommended

  • Commits stay one change each, but a batch of commits is pushed once, after the last one. The agent rules and the commit tooling now do this.
  • The status tick makes at most two pushes: one for the batch of integrated lane results and one for the progress files.
  • After a batch, check that the newest build reports "built" before telling anyone the site is updated.

How to reproduce it

List the repository's Pages builds through the GitHub API and compare their creation times, statuses and durations with the times of the pushes.

  • Verified the pageable resource system centres on a small base class with 8 typed dictionary instantiations covering animations, textures, drawables, physics bounds, particles and render mesh fragments, plus typed cross-file references that are resolved at load time.
  • Verified the main streaming scheduler classes have no type information at all: no descriptors exist for the streaming controller, the streaming module, the asset stores, or archive and resource manager classes, so they must be static classes or plain structures and can only be found through strings and code references.
  • Verified every virtual method of all 8 file-device classes and all parameter-stream classes points into the encrypted region, as do nearly all asset-loader methods. Readable code covers the media stream readers, the direct loader variant, dictionary plumbing and file-system call sites.
  • Verified 533 distinct subsystem strings, revealing a slot-based request model with active and requested state, per-area streaming set files, an on-disk cache with validation and a defragmentation pass, virtual paths split between shared and platform-specific data, streamed fonts, and a heavily duplicated resource-validation failure message in five languages.
  • Verified about ten code regions attributed to streaming through 492 specific references plus 73 direct file-system calls, all sample-checked as genuine code. They cover dictionaries, archives, async streaming, low-level file access, caching and cross-file references.

  • Inferred the readable streaming code is on the order of low hundreds of functions; the encrypted region holds most of the archive and scheduler method bodies, so no exact total can be measured from the file on disk.

What was decided or recommended

Rewrite work should start with the readable and documented parts in this order: local file device and virtual paths, archive reader checked against public format notes, decompression, resource block loading with pointer fix-up, dictionary containers, cross-file references, then the cache and the request scheduler last, since the scheduler needs dynamic analysis or a decrypted image. The archive format and the general resource design are publicly documented, but the streaming set files, the cache format, the defragmentation pass and the scheduling and eviction policy are not and remain the unknowns.

How to reproduce it

Parse the executable headers and relocation table, scan the data sections for C++ type descriptors and object locators, resolve base classes through the hierarchy descriptors, measure virtual tables by counting consecutive relocated code pointers, filter class names for streaming and resource keywords, filter the string table to trustworthy sections only, and collect relocation fixups in the unencrypted code that target subsystem tables, strings and file-system imports, then group nearby references into clusters and validate a sample by disassembly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two traps cost time. First, a case-insensitive name filter matched unrelated classes such as camera script instructions and destroy-car tasks, and a word-boundary pattern silently missed the whole file-device family; both were caught by inspecting the candidate list and the filter was rewritten case-sensitively. Second, clustering code by synchronisation calls produced bogus mega-clusters because every subsystem uses locks; synchronisation was excluded from attribution and the clusters were recomputed from subsystem-specific references only. Public sources were thinner than expected: the archive format page is thorough, but the canonical modding SDK repository and the resource-format notes could not be located in the time available and stay open leads.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite should target Visual Studio 2012 Update 1 semantics for matching purposes, and must account for whole-program optimisation effects such as custom register passing and missing frame pointers rather than expecting standard calling conventions everywhere. How to reproduce it

Read the bytes between the DOS stub and the PE header, unscramble them with the four-byte key stored next to the Rich marker, and split the result into eight-byte records of tool id, build number and object count. Map the tool ids with the richprint table, the Detect-It-Easy database and kirschju/richheader, and map build numbers to releases with the compiler version table on Wikipedia; the background format is documented in Pistelli's Rich signature notes. For corroboration, collect candidate function starts after padding bytes in the code section, disassemble the first dozen instructions of a few thousand of them, and measure frame setup, register argument passing and vector register use.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • An early check seemed to show the parsing library dropping the last Rich record. It was a bug in my own debug print, which truncated the list for display. The library and the hand decode agree on all 21 records.
  • The type names all sit in the writable data section instead of the read-only constants section, which is unusual and unexplained. Disabled string pooling is one hypothesis; a follow-up lane needs to confirm it.
  • The first register-argument measurement counted register saves as argument passing and overstated the result. Excluding save and restore instructions fixed it and the corrected numbers still support the optimisation finding.

Ordinal imports were resolved against the export tables of the matching system libraries, and crate licences were checked against the crates registry and lib.rs. The lane scripts and the resulting machine-readable tables are kept with the lane scratch work for the coordinator to integrate.

The biggest surprise is that every window-creation and message-pump import is dead, with no dynamic name string either, yet the program has a live window procedure and window-state code, and no shipped module creates the window for it. Unknown The call path is hidden from static analysis; the leading hypothesis is that the start-up stub resolves a window-API table that game code calls through, and a later lane should check cross-references to data pointer tables plus dynamic observation. Two smaller traps: the linker folds some string literals together with the import table own name entries, which at first looked like dynamic resolution reusing import names, and naive call counting misses a dozen imports used only through registers, including the two path-building functions that turned out to be among the heaviest shell users. Register-indirect counts stay approximate because some calls sit further from their pointer load than the pairing window.

Mapping the executable's data sections

The executable's data is now mapped: read-only data holds imports, over three thousand validated virtual tables, string and float pools; the writable area is mostly an eleven megabyte zero-initialised region with a few very heavily referenced globals; and the binary contains no C++ exception tables at all, which means later lanes never have to model C++ unwinding.

What was asked

Map every data section of the game executable so later lanes know what lives where: describe each section, break read-only data into regions with byte counts, count functions with C++ exception unwinding, find the most-referenced globals, list every resource, analyse relocations, and report anything unusual.

What was found

Verified The nine sections do not overlap. The code section is about eleven megabytes and the read-only data section about two megabytes. Writable data is thirteen megabytes in memory but barely over one megabyte on disk, so most of it is zero-initialised. The small entry-point stub section is writable and executable, and the one megabyte blob beside it is uniformly maximum-entropy, so encrypted or compressed.

Verified Zero functions use C++ exception unwinding: no exception tables exist anywhere in the image, and only plain system exception imports are present. The build was most likely compiled with C++ exceptions disabled.

Verified The most-referenced global is used from over two thousand code sites. The top fifty globals are nearly all in the zero-initialised area; the few named ones sit beside engine class names and a view-matrix global next to what look like viewport dimensions.

Verified Resources are seven icons, version information reading 1.2.0.59, a manifest, and one large embedded achievement database carried over from the console build, with achievement text in several languages. The manifest still asks for a much older C runtime, which looks vestigial.

Verified Of almost three hundred thousand relocations, about one hundred fifty-three thousand are code-to-data pointers and about forty-six thousand are data-to-code pointers, mostly virtual table slots. Seven percent of code relocations point at values that are not valid addresses and sit in maximum-entropy pockets spread across the whole code section.

Inferred The anomalous relocations are either stale linker output or bytes the startup stub restores at runtime. The small extra read-only section looks like a vector-constant pool from a statically linked library. Code also reads its own file headers, which suggests an integrity or version check.

What was decided or recommended

  • Treat C++ exceptions as absent: no unwinding support is needed in the checker or rewrites.
  • Treat the twenty thousand anomalous code relocations as untrusted input until a runtime lane diffs the code section after the startup stub runs.
  • Use the region map and the top-fifty globals list as the starting point for naming global variables.

How to reproduce it

All analysis ran directly on the executable file with small Python scripts using a PE parser and a disassembler library, without starting the game. The scripts parse section headers, directories, resources and relocations, scan for runtime type structures and exception records with pointer validation, and cross-check every structure against relocation references. The lane outputs are a full report, a region map file with start, size, kind and evidence for each region, and per-area detail files.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first type-information scan found nothing, because the type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, which is not the usual compiler layout. The locator scan then failed too, because the hierarchy descriptor here is four words wide rather than the documented three; decoding one known class hierarchy by hand revealed the extra field. The version-information library call also failed and had to be replaced with a manual parse. What remains unknown is why the descriptors sit in writable memory and what restores the high-entropy pockets in the code section, if anything does.

What was asked

Jump tables inside codeabout 2,260about 19,700Inferred

Verified The confirmed virtual tables name just over three thousand distinct classes, mostly engine and audio names. Inferred The largest dispatch table, with just over two thousand slots, points at evenly spaced stubs that each push an identifier, which reads like a script-native registration table. Verified Jump tables use plain 32-bit absolute addresses: for over a thousand tables the address baked into a nearby table-jump instruction equals the table address exactly. Three data-resident jump tables have byte-identical twins elsewhere in data, presumably backup copies like the encrypted code copy.

These are the functions reachable only through pointers, as an upper bound, since calls from the encrypted region are invisible. There are zero TLS callbacks. Unknown The static constructor count could not be established: every large null-delimited run proved to be something else, and the startup code that would anchor the real initialiser groups sits in the encrypted region.

What was decided or recommended

  • Later tools must not trust the relocation table for pointer detection; the lane's value-based tables ship as JSON instead.
  • Backup copies (the encrypted code duplicate and the twinned jump tables) should be deduplicated by content hash before any function counting.
  • The small unclassified runs still mix string fragments with real pointer pairs and need per-item review, starting with the ones flanked by encrypted-region pointers.
  • Static constructors stay unknown until an unpacking or dynamic lane reads the startup code; candidate groups are listed in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

Work only on a copy of the executable with read-only scripts. Map the sections and confirm the encrypted prefix by per-page entropy, then scan the file-backed data sections for runs of consecutive aligned words valued inside the code range. Drop runs whose bytes are UTF-16 or printable ASCII, confirm virtual tables through the type-descriptor name behind each table's header pointer, census direct calls by scanning readable code for call and jump opcodes, and verify jump-table encoding by comparing each nearby table-jump instruction's embedded address against the table address. The lane's scripts run in this order: layout survey, relocation probe, encryption probe, value scan, bridged and filtered passes, then relabelling.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full analysis trusted the relocation table and reported sixteen tables; the real count was thousands. That failure took one probe to diagnose and forced the value-based rewrite. The value scan then reported over eleven thousand runs, most of them strings, and the classifier initially labelled nearly three hundred string runs as initialiser tables — the byte-pattern text filter fixed that but certainly left string fragments among the small unknowns. Two self-checks were built on flawed reasoning and caught before shipping: a span comparison meant to test address encoding is translation-invariant and proves nothing, and a merge pass for split runs was unnecessary because runs already spanned encrypted-region slots. Both were replaced with direct evidence.

The start-up stub: a tiny loader, an encrypted first megabyte, and an external unlocker

The game does not start in its own code. A loader stub of about six hundred bytes runs first, loads a Rockstar wrapper module shipped beside the game, lets it prepare the process, then hands control to the normal C start-up routine. The first megabyte of the code section is encrypted on disk and a read-only section holds an identical backup copy of it.

What was asked

Explain what happens between process start and the game's real entry point: what the stub in the small executable section does step by step, what the one megabyte high-entropy section is, what runs before the real entry point, how the shipped launcher starts the game, and whether any of this interferes with analysis or with loading extra code into the process.

What was found

  • Verified The entry point sits at the first byte of a tiny writable and executable section. The stub finds the system library through the process loader list instead of using imports, then loads a wrapper module by name and resolves two single-letter functions from it by walking its export table by hand.
  • Verified The stub calls the first wrapper function once with no arguments, then calls the second one in a loop until it reports success, passing it the locations of the thread-storage and relocation tables. It then unloads the wrapper and jumps to the real entry point.
  • Verified The one megabyte section is byte-for-byte identical to the first megabyte of the code section, and that first megabyte is encrypted: maximum entropy, incompressible, and disassembles as nonsense. The boundary between encrypted and normal code falls exactly on a page boundary one page before the end of the copy.
  • Verified The encrypted region holds heavily used code: tens of thousands of call sites and over sixteen thousand linker-confirmed pointers from the rest of the program reach into it, including the call to the main window function from the C start-up code. It must be decrypted before the game can run.
  • Verified No game code references the backup copy. It is mapped read-only, so the game cannot corrupt it. It is most likely the wrapper's pristine reference for decrypting and integrity checks.
  • Verified Nothing runs before the stub except the operating system loader. The thread-storage callback list is empty, and the stub's own callback-dispatch code can never execute because its guard condition is always false.
  • Verified The real entry point is an ordinary C start-up routine of the expected compiler generation: cookie check, exception-handler setup, a check of the program's own headers, command-line retrieval, then a call into the main window function.
  • Verified The wrapper module exports only the two functions the stub calls. Its own code is obfuscated, and its imports show it can scan processes and modules, change memory protection, read process memory, terminate processes, and detect debuggers.
  • Verified Signature-checking functions are called from one cluster of game code far from the stub. The code verifies an Authenticode signature, treats a missing or bad signature as not verified rather than fatal, and inspects the signer certificate and timestamps. A separate pair of data-protection calls sits elsewhere and looks like save-data encryption.
  • Verified The game is normally started through a 64-bit launcher stub that reads two metadata files, supports store-specific launch paths with documented command-line flags, enforces a single instance, and hands off to the Rockstar Games Launcher, which starts the game itself.

What was decided or recommended

  • Inferred Static analysis of the first megabyte of code is blocked until it is decrypted; disassemblers will show garbage there, while callers elsewhere in the program stay visible. The import table is intact, so API usage remains readable.
  • Inferred Loading an extra module into the process is not blocked by the stub itself, but the wrapper scans the process before the game starts, so injected modules may be noticed. This needs live testing to confirm.
  • Inferred Replacing functions in memory at run time is mechanically normal, but the pristine backup copy and the wrapper's memory-reading ability mean integrity re-checks are plausible. Whether any run after start-up is unknown.
  • Inferred The wrapper's retry loop and the signature checks deserve dynamic observation in a sandbox before any lane depends on start-up behaviour.

How to reproduce it

All results come from static reads of the game executable and the two files shipped beside it, using a PE parser and a disassembler library from throwaway scripts. The checks were: section table and entropy survey; full disassembly of the stub section with manual decoding of its five embedded strings; byte comparison of the backup section against the code section; a page-by-page entropy scan to find the encryption boundary; counting linker relocation records that point into the encrypted range; reading the thread-storage directory and its empty callback list; disassembly of the real entry point; import-table review of the wrapper and launcher; and string and metadata review of the launcher. No game code was executed and no protection was defeated.

What was confusing or went wrong

Linear disassembly of the stub initially misread its embedded strings as instructions, which hid the real control flow until a raw dump revealed the call-and-capture pattern. A first scan for references to the backup section returned dozens of hits that all turned out to be misaligned decoding artefacts and coincidental numbers in graphics data, which only became clear after checking each one against aligned disassembly and the relocation table. The wrapper takes the thread-storage and relocation locations as arguments for reasons that remain unknown.

Correction: the first megabyte of the code is encrypted

About 9% of the code section is encrypted on disk, and the first look at the executable missed it. The first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section are indistinguishable from random data, and a separate section named .tbm holds a byte-for-byte copy of the same bytes. The remaining 9.9 MB is ordinary compiled code.

What was asked

A lane estimating the number of functions reported that the code section looked encrypted, which contradicted the coordinator's earlier reading. Which was right?

What was found

  • Verified Measured in 256 KB windows, the first four windows of the code section have an entropy of 8.00, 8.00, 8.00 and 7.97 bits per byte. Every window after that is between 5.6 and 6.6, which is normal for compiled code.
  • Verified The first four windows contain no standard function prologues and no padding between functions. Every later window contains hundreds to thousands of each.
  • Verified The .tbm section is exactly 1,028,096 bytes and is identical to the first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section.
  • Inferred The start-up stub in .rkstr probably decrypts this range in memory before the game runs, as part of Rockstar's protection for this build. A lane is analysing the stub; this has not been confirmed.
  • Unknown What code lives in the encrypted range, how many functions it holds, and why the same bytes are stored twice.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • The coordinator computed one entropy figure for the whole section, got 6.71, and wrote "not packed or encrypted". An average over 10.95 MB cannot show a 1 MB anomaly. The fix is to measure in windows, always.
  • The mistake was caught within minutes because an independent lane measured the same thing a different way. Two lanes looking at the same file from different angles is worth the duplication.
  • The Ghidra analysis had already started and was disassembling the encrypted bytes as if they were code, producing nonsense functions and call targets. It was stopped and restarted with that range split into its own block and marked non-executable.

What was decided or recommended

  • Until the range has been read from a running copy, every tool treats it as opaque data. It is excluded from function counts, from the queue and from the code map, and the progress figures state its size separately so the percentages are honest.
  • The coordinator first wrote that the project would never read this range from the running game, citing the anti-piracy rule. That was the coordinator's own over-reach, and the owner corrected it the same day: the anti-piracy rule is about piracy, not about analysing a copy the owner bought. The range will be read from the owner's own running, purchased copy and analysed like the rest of the code.
  • What is read that way is game code. It stays in the private, ignored folders and is never committed or published, like all other game code.
  • The project still distributes no game files, keys or cracks, and does nothing to help anyone run the game without buying it.

How to reproduce it

Read the code section with pefile, cut it into 256 KB windows and compute the Shannon entropy of each. Count the byte sequence of the standard function prologue and runs of padding bytes per window. Compare the first megabyte of the code section with the contents of .tbm.

Expect inlined callees, non-standard calling conventions on internal functions, and less regular function boundaries. This makes analysis and the emulator comparison harder.
Older code linked inInferred The same record shows small numbers of objects from Visual C++ 2003, 2005, 2008 and 2010 toolchains.These are probably third-party libraries built long before. They are candidates for exclusion as library code.
PackingVerified The code section is 10.95 MB with an entropy of 6.71 bits per byte taken as a whole.Corrected the same day: this row first said the code was not encrypted. That was wrong. The whole-section average hides an encrypted first megabyte. See the correction. The other 90% is ordinary compiled code that Ghidra can analyse directly.
Start-up stubVerified The entry point is in a 657-byte section named .rkstr that is both writable and executable. Beside it is a 1 MB section named .tbm with an entropy of 8.00.Unknown A Rockstar stub runs before the game's own start-up, next to an encrypted or compressed blob. What it checks or unpacks is not known. It matters for injecting replacements into the running game and must be understood before the harness phase.
Class namesVerified 3,618 type descriptor strings.Run-time type information is present, so class names and virtual tables can be recovered. The Xbox 360 build is reported to have 3,332 classes.
RelocationsVerified Present, 1.27 MB.Every absolute address the code refers to is listed, which makes resolving references to functions and data reliable.
SymbolsVerified The debug record names a file, GTA4_Win32_Final.pdb, which does not ship.Confirms there are no function names to be had from the file itself.

What it depends on

Verified From the import table. This replaces most of the inferred dependency list in the entry on dependencies.

ImportedMeaning
d3d9.dll, one function, and no d3dx9Direct3D 9 only. The helper library is statically linked or unused, so the engine needs no DirectX end-user runtime.
DSOUND.dllAudio output is DirectSound, not XAudio2 or OpenAL. An earlier forum claim of OpenAL was wrong for this build.
DINPUT8.dll, and no XInputThe engine itself uses DirectInput. The research lane had classed it as used only by mod loaders. Gamepad support through XInput, if any, is loaded at run time.
binkw32.dllBink video. The shipped DLL is version 1.9r.
WMVCore.DLLWindows Media, for user music or replay export.
WS2_32.dllThe engine uses network sockets directly.
WINTRUST.dll, CRYPT32.dllSignature and certificate checks, probably for the start-up stub.
No C runtime DLLThe runtime is statically linked, so the engine needs no Visual C++ redistributable.
No xlive.dll, no .NET, no Social Club importGames for Windows LIVE is gone from this build, and .NET and Social Club are not engine dependencies.

Verified Shipped beside the executable: a launcher, a video encoder helper, the Steam API library and one more DLL. The last two are not in the import table, so the game loads them at run time.

What was decided

  • Try Ghidra's stock Visual Studio 2012 signatures for tagging library code before building any of our own.
  • Treat link-time code generation as confirmed when designing the queue and the comparison: do not assume a function's arguments arrive the standard way.
  • Understand the start-up stub before the harness phase. It is now an explicit unknown.
  • Audio and input replacements target what DirectSound and DirectInput provide, not XAudio2 or XInput.

How to reproduce it

Copy the executable into the ignored orig folder and read it with pefile: file header, optional header, section table with per-section entropy, parse_rich_header(), the debug directory, and the import and delay-import tables. Count type descriptors by searching for the byte string .?AV. No Ghidra run is needed for any of this.

The first estimate was several years, and it was wrong in method as well as in size. It was reasoned from projects that predate agents. A search for 2026 results showed agent-driven decompilations finishing in weeks. The working estimate now rests on one comparable agent project and will be replaced by measured throughput after the phase 2 pilot.
